### The GPU clock lock (2026-10-10)

The user, after Matt Pharr's question on the heatmap: every GPU benchmark
runs with the GPU clock locked from now on. A GeForce boosts by power and
temperature, so an unlocked 5090 runs a light scene near 3.0 GHz and a
dense one lower, and a speedup moves with the load alone. Locking takes
root (`nvidia-smi -lgc`), which the session does not have, so
`apps/pbrt/gpu_clock.sh` (sourced by gpu_compare.sh and heatmap.sh) reads
the SM clock three times and refuses a run unless every reading is the
lock -- 2400 MHz by default (`--clock`, BONSAI_GPU_CLOCK), the card's
rated boost clock, which it holds at full power on every scene where 3090,
its maximum, is taken away by the power limit on the dense ones -- and
the memory clock at its maximum. The table's last line and heatmap.log
record the lock. Every number before 10-10 was taken unlocked. The first
form of the check misfired (00:20): an unlocked clock boosting under a
render of mine read 2400 three times and a sweep started unlocked, every
scene after the first refusing once the clock moved; the readings are of
an idle GPU now (no compute process, two seconds settled).

### Kroken's loss traced, and the baseline that was not one (10-10, 00:20-00:45)

The 0.3 s of host time per kroken render and its trace launch's growth
(REPORT.md, "pbrt's structure, matched"): nsys on one render showed
cuMemPrefetchAsync 1097 times a render, 267 us each (293 ms) -- the
driver's prefetch of every queue array, managed memory, before the
kernels -- and a memory sampler put the card at 32.2 of 32.6 GB during the
render. The scene is pbrt's exactly -- 287.9 M triangles in 248 meshes
by pbrt's own count (247.7 M from its displacement tessellation at load),
the dump's 2.6 M shapes plus ten instances holding 285.3 M -- but here
every triangle is a primitive with a 32-byte Geometric record (shape,
material, light, alpha, two media) and an 8-byte triangle record, 11.5 GB
over the 288 M, where pbrt's GPU keeps one material-and-media record per
mesh in the shader binding table. Measured with nvidia-smi during a
render: 32.2 of 32.6 GB on our side (the card full), 27.2 GB on pbrt's.
(The 348 MiB I first quoted from pbrt's statistics is one bookkeeping
category, "Redundant vertex and index buffers", not its footprint.) With
22 material queues of 302 B an entry (7.7 GiB of queue arrays at the
band's capacity) the managed memory oversubscribes and thrashes; with
eleven, and the mesh-entity series in the sweep's binaries, it fit. The
mesh entity is the per-mesh record; the dump on disk (21 GB, 20 s to
read) still writes a Placement per triangle and should write it per mesh
as pbrt's TriangleMesh carries it -- the follow-up once the series is in. The sweep
of 10-09 morning (compare-out-heatmap3) was run from scratch/wt-fix with
the uncommitted mesh-entity series, which removes the per-triangle
records and moved the ray launches by a third to a half -- so every
comparison of the matched structure against that sweep (REPORT.md's
tables of 23:00 and 23:40) has the series on one side only, and the
draws' share of kroken's and head's trace growth is unknown until the
series is in. The series (34 files, 4700 lines with its goldens) sits on
21712bee; HEAD has 42 commits since, four of its files changed (render.
bonsai, render_hook.cpp, CPP.cpp, CodeGen_GPU_Host.cpp), so landing it is
a port, the user's go first.

Two smaller findings from the same trace, both general codegen items: each
round's host work is 54 cuMemsetD32Async of a queue's count (0.9 us each)
plus the round guard's synchronous read, 38 ms per kroken render, where
pbrt zeroes every queue in one launch -- and the material queues' counts
are zeroed twice a round, in `rays!batch` ahead of the trace and in
`hits!exit` after their pass (one is enough; one launch for all of them is
pbrt's form). And the per-material queue entry is 302 B against pbrt's
MaterialEvalWorkItem's ~240: the entry carries the primitive's six fields
(shape, light, material, alpha, media) where pbrt carries the material and
the medium interface, and the bounce's ten sampler values (40 B) where
pbrt keeps them per pixel -- the cost of the draws' placement in bytes.

### The scene file as pbrt's representation (10-10, 01:30-)

The user (01:05): the mesh-entity series lands and is benchmarked ("it is
an effort to match PBRT's behavior"), and the scene dumper is fixed "so it
matches PBRT's representation exactly" -- benchmarking means nothing if
the two sides are not the same scene. Landed first: the series, ported
onto HEAD in scratch/wt-mesh (one conflict, Trees.cpp's node_bounds, where
HEAD's refusal of a bound that reads an annotation's parameter subsumes
the series' early return), 1534 tests, images matching pbrt on kroken,
head and killeroo; commit 1ed2eabb. Its kroken check put the card at 32.2
GB again: the series left an instance's object per triangle (`Inst.blas :
set[Geometric]`), and kroken's 285 million triangles are all inside ten
instances.

**The format (scene_geometry.fbs version 3, scene_io.h).** A `Mesh` carries
`kind` (triangles or bilinear patches), `prim_count` and its placement --
material, emission, the first triangle's light ordinal (a mesh's lights are
consecutive, pbrt's `areaLights[prim]`), alpha, the two media -- as pbrt's
GPU keeps the statement's graphics state once in the mesh's hit record. The
`Triangle` record (32 bytes a triangle: mesh, index, placement) is gone, and
with it the `triangles` and `instance_triangles` columns; a triangle mesh is
a primitive of the scene by itself. A `Definition` is a run of the instance
shapes and a run of the meshes; the scene's own meshes are the run
`top_first_mesh .. + top_mesh_count`. pbrt's CPU BVH is no longer mirrored
into the file (`--pbrt-tree`, `nodes`, `instance_nodes`, `prims`,
`Definition.root_node`, the LinearBVHNode mirror and the private-member
reach into BVHAggregate): it was a tree over a primitive per triangle, which
the file no longer has, and the driver builds its trees as pbrt's GPU
builds its own (a tree per mesh under the top one on the CPU, the 10-08
design; compare.sh's PBRT_TREE goes with it). A bilinear patch mesh keeps a
Patch record per patch (pbrt's GPU has a BLP build input per mesh with one
record too; a follow-up, rare in the scenes). The dumper's summary line
counts meshes and triangles as pbrt's statistics do.

**The driver.** The scene's own triangle meshes are the mesh primitives
straight from the file, each over its run of `tris` in mesh order; the
TriangleMesh records take the placement from the mesh (the material through
the renderer's slot). An instance's object is still a Geometric per
triangle on the device, made at load from the mesh as `triangle_geometric`
makes it on the device, each definition's run its shapes then its meshes'
triangles (DefRun); the light ordinals of a mesh's triangles map to the
mesh's emission. The tree-adoption path is gone with the file's trees.

**The instanced mesh as a primitive (10-10, 02:30-).** pbrt's GPU
(gpu/optix/aggregate.cpp, 1430-1560): per instance definition one GAS of
triangles with a build input per mesh (each input's SBT record the mesh's),
one of bilinear patches, one of quadrics; then ONE flat IAS whose
OptixInstances are the scene's own three GASes under the identity and, per
instance use, one per GAS of its definition under the instance's transform
-- no IAS inside an IAS; the hit programs read the instance's transform
from OptiX. A third tree level in the program (`Inst.blas : set[Object]`,
`Object = Mesh | Geom`) would be the literal transcription, and the tree
lowering (Lower/Trees.cpp, bind_elements) binds two levels today -- a
flatten over a tree whose arms are one element or one held tree -- so that
level is a compiler project. The same device representation without it:
a `Placed` primitive per instance use and mesh of its definition
(render.bonsai: `Placed(render_from_instance, instance_from_render, mesh,
tris : set[Triangle])`, `layout Primitive { Placed = tagged_index }`, a row
of a pool like an instance's, since it carries two matrices), its geometry
`map(triangle_geometric, tris)` as a Mesh's, the arms of transform,
untransform, hit_wo and the surface push the Inst's; `Placed.tris :
OptixTree from tris` / `MeshBVH from MeshNodes`. The definition's other
shapes -- quadrics, curves, patches -- stay the instance's `blas`, a
Geometric each. Driver: every triangle mesh has its run of `tris` once
(`mesh_first`), shared by its placements; the definition's mesh structure
is built once (`meshes_geometry` over its meshes, a build input per mesh)
and placed by each instance with `holder_per_input` (runtime/
bonsai_optix.h: the k-th input's records carry `holder + k`, the
instance's placed meshes lying consecutively in `prims` from its first,
in the definition's order -- pbrt's `sbtOffset` per instance with one
record set per definition). The top-level order on the hardware: own
shapes, own meshes, placed meshes, instances with shapes. On the CPU a
Placed's bounds are the mesh's box under the instance's transform and the
per-mesh tree is shared. So the hit chain is the Mesh's, record ->
prims[holder] (the Placed, its matrices one pool row away) -> meshes[mesh]
-> tris[base + prim] -> indices -> positions, and no record per triangle
is left on the device; kroken's 11.5 GB go, its queues fit beside pbrt's
27 GB. After it: the synthesized triangle set (the k-th element is
`Triangle{mesh, k}`), a layout construct to ask the user for, which
removes the 8-byte `tris` record per triangle (2.3 GB on kroken) that pbrt
does not have either.

Built and measured (03:10, scratch/surface/compare-placed): no compiler
change was needed -- the Placed arm is a mapped held tree like Mesh's,
and the layout binds `Placed.tris` beside `Mesh.tris`. Killeroo 36.1,
head 39.6, landscape 1012 (30034 instances of 32 objects, 254 thousand
placed meshes), kroken 779 ms of kernels at 16 spp (the sweep's 764,
pbrt's 1733) and 0.80 s of wall for 0.78 of kernels (1.20 for 0.90 under
the thrash); the card's peak over the whole compare 27.2 GB, pbrt's own.
Every image matches pbrt. Tests correctness/gpu/rtcore-placed (two
meshes as one definition structure of two inputs, placed twice with
holder_per_input) and correctness/cpp/placed-tlas (the arm on the CPU
trees, the mesh tree shared by two placements).

### One reset launch per round (10-10, 10:30-)

The user's ask after the structure work: profile, take the largest
slowdown first, and make general codegen improvements kept only when
they are a net gain across many scenes. While the 30-scene sweep ran
(compare-out-heatmap4, the clock unlocked and recorded), the first item
came from the kroken trace already in hand ("Kroken's loss traced",
above): a round of the gpu-optix schedule had the host issue 54
`cuMemsetD32Async` of one word each -- a queue's count zeroed -- where
pbrt's wavefront resets every queue a depth fills in one launch, `Do(
"Reset queues before tracing rays", lambda)` (wavefront/integrator.cpp),
a lambda on one thread. Read off the final SSA of the schedule
(scratch/surface/structure/final.txt, the host function `render`):
`rays!batch` zeroed the next ray buffer's count and the 22 material
queues' counts ahead of the trace (1 + 22); `hits!exit` zeroed the same
22 again after the material drains; and the nine lone queues
(medium_samples, medium_scatters, escaped, emissive, shadow, bssrdfs,
probes, exits, exit_shadow) each zeroed theirs at their own exit: 54. The
kroken nsys profile (two renders) had 82944 of them, 99 ms of host issue
and 23.5 ms of device-side memset time; and since the round guard's
synchronous read drains the stream at each round's start, the batch's 23
are issued while the device idles. On killeroo-simple at 16 spp -- 36 ms
a render, 96 rounds -- the 54 a round are some 5 ms of issue alone.

**Why the 22 were zeroed twice.** SSA/RoundGuard.cpp hoists an inner
queue's per-round header fill (`store hits_queue[k], make_struct(0,
arrays..)`) to the round loop's preheader and left a zero of the count in
its place "only when the loop does not already reset it" -- Defer resets a
stage queue after its pass, in `<queue>!exit` ("drained, so empty"). The
test compared roots through `root_name`, which asked `Value::get_argument()`
first; that answers for a *named instruction* too, so for the fill's slot
`@18 = gep(hits_queue, 0)` it returned "@18" rather than walking to
`hits_queue`, while the exit's reset, rooted through the thread-following
`rooted`, said "hits_queue". Unequal, so a second zero per arm per round. A
lone queue's header is no GEP, so its names agreed and it was zeroed once.
Reproduced in sixty lines (a three-arm specialized stage inside a GPU
round queue, now tests/bonsai/ssa/round-hoist-split): BONSAI_DEBUG_ROUNDS
printed "zero store in hits!exit roots at hits_queue against @18".

**The design: two general changes, no schedule construct.**

1. *The reset at the top of the round* (SSA/RoundGuard.cpp, RoundGuard.h).
   `root_name` takes the Argument proper (`std::get_if<Argument>`), so a
   slot's GEP walks to its queue. And the fill hoist now moves each inner
   queue's reset from after its pass to the top of the round body -- the
   in-loop target of the guard's `!go` dispatch, Defer's `pre` block,
   where the ray queue's reset of its other buffer already sits -- erasing
   Defer's exit reset of that slot (matched by slot: the queue root
   through threads and the constant arm index, so a split's arms are told
   apart) where the exit block's innermost loop is this round loop; a
   queue drained once per inner iteration keeps its reset where it is.
   Nothing reads a count between its pass and the next round's top -- a
   queue is filled only after the top and read only by its drain -- so it
   is the same word one round later, at pbrt's placement, and the resets
   of every queue the round fills are adjacent.

2. *A run of host writes into device memory as one launch*
   (CodeGen_LLVM::pending_device_stores / flush_device_stores,
   CodeGen_GPU_Host::flush_device_stores, CodeGen_PTX::add_store_kernel).
   `store_to_device` holds a word back; the pending run is flushed at the
   next point whose order against the stream matters -- a launch, a read
   from the device, a wait, a call or intrinsic, a free, every block's
   terminator -- as a memset each on a CPU host, and on a GPU host, from
   three words up (store_launch_minimum: a launch's issue is two or three
   memsets' and the kernel a memset node's, so one or two words stay
   memsets), as one launch of `_bonsai_store_words_<n>(ptr, u32, ..)`: a
   kernel of one thread that stores each word at its address, every
   operand a kernel parameter (12 bytes a word; the renderer's 32 are 384
   of the 4 KB), one kernel per word count, cached. pbrt's `GPUDo` of a
   lambda, as a lowering of what the host writes rather than a thing the
   program says.

Read in the renderer's final SSA (scratch/surface/reset/pbrt-final.txt,
compiled while the sweep ran): `rays!batch` holds 32 zero-word stores --
the next ray buffer's, the 22 material queues', the nine lone queues' --
and no block of the round holds any other; the object carries
`_bonsai_store_words_32`. So a round's host side is the guard's read, one
reset launch, and the kernel launches: 54 stream operations of a word
became one. Tests: ssa/round-hoist (re-blessed: the reset moved to the
top; its comment says so), ssa/round-hoist-split (new), correctness/gpu/
round-reset (new: three arms, so the reset is the store kernel; its
golden is the CPU's answer). The GPU runs -- the gpu tests, killeroo-
simple with BONSAI_KERNEL_STATS, then the 30 scenes at 16 spp against
heatmap4's rows, the user's net-gain rule -- wait for the sweep.

A smaller item seen in the same read, for later: `rays!drain`, once per
pass (per sample per band), still stores the 31 queue headers (a struct
each through the staging ring: a memcpy, a cuMemcpyHtoDAsync and an event
record), where pbrt allocates its queues once. The fills are loop-
invariant -- every operand is defined outside the sample loop -- and
could follow their allocations out of it (HoistAllocations hoists the
`alloca`, not the store).

### The draws made pbrt's (10-10, 12:00-)

The user (12:00), on the trace launch's growth with the draws in it: "our
draw cost must match pbrt's draw cost: the draw should be exactly the
same" -- investigate the differences and fix the specification to match
pbrt for draws; the placement itself (the draws in the trace launch) he
will look at and direct separately. So: sampler.bonsai and rng.bonsai
against pbrt's samplers.h, util/lowdiscrepancy.h, util/rng.h and
wavefront/samples.cpp, function by function, and the renderer's threading
of the sampler against pbrt's kernels.

**What matched, line for line.** Every per-draw function: RadicalInverse
(the loop, its `limit`, the final `min`), ScrambledRadicalInverse (the
digit-count condition, the permutation read at `digitIndex * base +
digit`), OwenScrambledRadicalInverse (`MixBits(hash ^ reversedDigits)`
over the 64-bit accumulator), the three Sobol' scramblers, SobolSample's
column loop, ZSobol's GetSampleIndex (our digit loop runs upward, pbrt's
downward; the bits are disjoint), SobolIntervalToIndex, PaddedSobol's,
Stratified's and PMJ02BN's `Hash(pixel, dimension, seed)` and
PermutationElement, the blue-noise read, the dimension wraps at the prime
and Sobol' tables' ends, and each sampler's StartPixelSample arithmetic.
The tables live where pbrt's do: `PBRT_CONST` is `__device__ const` on
the GPU, global memory, as our `extern` arrays are.

**What differed: the sampler's life, not its arithmetic.**

1. *The state travelled with the ray.* pbrt's GenerateRaySamples makes a
   fresh copy of the sampler object per ray per bounce -- a local, so
   registers -- reads the pixel from `pixelSampleState.pPixel[pixelIndex]`
   and starts it with `StartPixelSample(pPixel, sampleIndex, 6 + 7 *
   depth)`; nothing of a sampler is carried between kernels. Ours threaded
   `state : mut SamplerState` (40 bytes: a generator the low-discrepancy
   samplers never use, the pixel, the sample, the dimension, the index)
   down every function of the path and through the recursion, so the
   deferral kept it per ray in a record slot (`rays_state_slots`, 40 bytes
   a pixel) and every bounce read the slot, restarted the sampler from the
   pixel and sample it held, drew with the state's address as the `mut`
   parameter -- each draw's dimension step a global-memory load and store
   (the compiler item of 10-09 on `mut` aggregate parameters) -- and wrote
   the slot back. The same restart as pbrt's, around forty global memory
   operations more per ray per bounce, in the raygen's dependent chain.
2. *Two jumps where pbrt makes one.* Independent and Stratified restarted
   by seeding and advancing `sampleIndex * 65536` and then advancing
   `dimension` again; pbrt's StartPixelSample advances once by the sum.
3. *A jump of sixty-four steps.* `advance` ran a fixed sixty-four guarded
   steps of three 64-bit multiplies each, for a uniform trip count; pbrt's
   `while (delta > 0)` runs to the delta's top bit, some twenty for a
   sample's jump.

**The change** (sampler.bonsai, rng.bonsai, render.bonsai). `start_pixel_
sample_at(sampler, x, y, sample, dimension)` is pbrt's StartPixelSample
from nothing but its three arguments, each arm's dimension rule as pbrt's
(`max(2, dim)` for Halton, Sobol and PMJ02BN; as given for ZSobol and
PaddedSobol; one jump of `sample * 65536 + dim` for Independent and
Stratified), and `start_pixel_sample` is it at dimension zero. The
volumetric path's functions take the ray's pixel (`pixel_x`, `pixel_y`)
and the pass's sample index in place of the state, and vol_path_step
starts a local sampler per bounce and draws from it; the camera's state
stays the pixel kernel's local for its six draws; the CPU integrators
(Path, SimplePath, RandomWalk) keep carrying the camera's sampler down
the path as pbrt's CPU integrators do. `advance` runs while the delta has
bits. The draws' values are unchanged: a bounce restarts at the same
dimension from the same pixel and sample as before.

Measured (13:10, scratch/surface/reset/compare-draws, killeroo-simple at 16
spp, the reset launch of the morning in the same build): every image
channel byte-identical to the sweep's render of 10:20 (the values are the
same draws); the trace launch 18.45 to 17.49 ms (it was 12.81 with the
draws in the material kernels, and pbrt's sample kernel is 3.7 on this
scene: the draws now cost 4.7 ms in our launch, 1.26x pbrt's, from 1.5x);
kernel time 35.82 to 34.89; wall 42.9 to 38.7 ms, the host's gap over the
kernels 7.1 to 3.8 ms (the reset launch). The draw code itself set beside
pbrt's at the instruction level (scratch/surface/reset/draws_kernel.bonsai:
the bounce's ten draws as a kernel of their own, the sampler built as a
Halton sampler from runtime parameters so the match folds to that arm, as
pbrt's template instance is one sampler): ours 4096 SASS instructions and
48 registers, no spills; pbrt's GenerateRaySamples<HaltonSampler> 3576
and 55. The same work, give or take a seventh; what is left of the draws'
cost in the trace launch is the launch, not the draws -- the ten values
and the ray live across optixTrace, the raygen's occupancy -- which is the
placement the user is looking at.

Measured over the 30 scenes (13:35, compare-out-reset16: the 16-spp pass
of heatmap.sh with both changes of the day, against the morning's
compare-out-heatmap4 cell by cell; scratch/surface/reset/compare_tables.py
and trace-plus-draws-now.txt): wall faster on every one of the 30 cells,
geomean 1.074x (frame542 1.29x, dambreak 1.17x, rough-glass 1.16x, the
rest 1.02-1.13x); kernel time 1.017x; no cell slower; the same 27 images
match pbrt and the same three (pavilion-day, the two bistros) miss the
lit-pixel rule as before. The kernel side is the draws: our trace launch
with the draws in it is now 0.96 of pbrt's trace kernel plus sample
kernel summed (4036 to 3815 ms against 3975), ahead on 26 of 30 scenes;
the draws' own addition to the launch, read as the launch's growth since
the sweep that drew in the material kernels, is 1.17x pbrt's sample
kernel (932 against 798 ms; it was 1.44x), with landscape (2.0x), book
(1.9x), crown (1.7x) and villa-lights-on (1.6x) the far end and most
scenes near or under one -- what the instancing and routing changes of the
same interval add to those scenes' launches is folded into the figure. The
wall side beyond that is the reset launch. The memset-against-launch
microbenchmark (scratch/surface/reset/store_cost.cpp, a round as the
renderer issues it): the guard alone 4.1 us; N memsets 4.85, 5.81, 6.82,
7.90, 11.8, 19.5 and 33.6 us for N = 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16 and 32; one launch
7.3 us whatever N. So the launch pays from four words up and
store_launch_minimum is 4 (it was an estimate of 3); the renderer's 32
words went from 33.6 to 7.3 us of host issue a round.

### The sample pass on the same queue (10-10, 14:30-)

The user's direction, after the draws were made pbrt's: the schedule
should truly match pbrt's, which means a sample kernel of its own over the
ray queue ahead of the trace kernel, with the queue reused by both passes
(his option 2 of 13:20: "defer or stage with the same queue should result
in the queue being reused for the two stages"), and before building it a
rigorous semantics of every scheduling directive, written as the Halide
paper writes its model, in three groups -- loop transformations, hardware
binding, continuation styles -- with the leftovers under "other". Then
(20:00): finish the draws' placement with the step that keeps them out of
the downstream entries, specialize the camera and sample kernels on the
sampler as pbrt's templates are, leave the round loop's count read as the
one allowed structural difference, explain the hit chain's extra hop, do
the audits, and work in small verifiable chunks with the doc's examples as
real tests.

**The semantics.** docs/schedule-semantics.md: the parfor contract; the
SSA the directives rewrite (blocks with arguments, the call with its
continuation block, the parallel loop kept as a loop, tail position); a
running example -- one path per pixel, a wall on a line -- whose
unscheduled nest and whose nest under each directive are drawn in the
paper's `par for each` notation; each directive's conditions as a list;
and, for defer, stage and the new cut, the rewrite in the compiler's
printed SSA. Two things the review caught and the doc now says: a stage's
push follows the call at once, for every entry, a miss too (the whole of
`f` after the call is the drain's, and a push inside an arm is a deferral
of that arm's tail call, which is how gpu-optix routes with no stage in
it); and in `f.stage(g, q, l)` the second argument is the queue whose
drain already runs `f`, not one to push onto, and the third a fresh name
for the first pass, the second pass keeping the queue's name so the binds
written after it address the trace. The example is
tests/bonsai/correctness/llvm/semantics-render, and every schedule of it
in the doc is a test beside it printing the same film, with an SSA golden
of the same name: semantics-defer (4.2), semantics-stage (4.3 with 4.4's
split on the hit), semantics-draw and semantics-stage-same-queue (4.5),
semantics-reload-by-slot and semantics-reload-two-routes (the step 4.5
leaves), the last two also on the GPU. The example's `shade` ends with
pbrt's early return at max depth rather than a call inside an `if`, since
the deferral's tail test does not see through the merge block after such a
call -- a limitation worth lifting.

**The construct** (commit 4fb63990; SSA/Stage.h, cut_same_queue).
`f.stage(g, q, l)` and `f.defer(g, q, l)` cut `f` at its call to `g` as
the two-argument forms do (stage_tail, continuation_tail, now shared) and
then, in place of a deferral onto a new queue, split `q`'s drain into two
passes over the same entries in the same round: a copy of the drain's
block and body, named `l`, that the round enters first and that runs the
chain down to `f` and `f` up to the cut, and the drain as it was, keeping
its name, bounds and launch facts, whose body calls the rest with what it
handed the chain and with what the first pass stored. What is stored is
decided as an entry's fields are: each argument of the rest is followed
back through the chain's tail calls to the drain's own call, and one that
is a parameter all the way (an entry field, a uniform, a slot address, the
queue) is handed again; the others go into arrays of the record,
`<q>_<name>_slots`, one slot per producer iteration as a reducer's, at
the slot every chain function already carries (`_slot_<q>`), through a
pointer parameter per value (`_<name>_<q>`). The decision to store by the
record's slot rather than by the entry's index: pbrt's
pixelSampleState.samples is indexed by pixelIndex, which is that slot;
no entry grows, no push changes, and the downstream entries, which carry
the slot already, need nothing added to read the value back. The reset of
the other buffer goes with the copy, ahead of both passes, so a push made
before the cut is kept. Refused, each in its own words: a queue with no
drain yet, one split or whose drain is bound, a chain not in tail
position or with a caller outside it (the owner's own call has to be a
push, or it would run the first half alone), entries with no record slot,
a cut not every path reaches (the skip bit of 4.5 is not built), an
address of `f`'s frame live after the cut.

**The step it leaves** (4fc8ef18, f803bc35). pbrt's material, medium and
subsurface kernels read the samples from pixelSampleState.samples by the
work item's pixelIndex (surfscatter.cpp:184, media.cpp:57 and 271,
subsurface.cpp:33 and 67); ours stored them in every downstream entry,
since a deferral stores a value it is handed. The cut now records on its
queue the record arrays its first pass alone writes and where its second
pass sits (Function::OwnedQueue), and the entry analysis of defer() gains
a recipe beside the recomputed pure functions: an argument of the pushed
call whose owner-level definition at every producer call is
`load(gep(array, index))`, the array one of those, this deferral's every
producer in that round after the second pass, and the index the entry's
slot at that call, becomes `load(gep(array, slot))` built at the drain.
Three things the renderer taught on the way: the value has to be followed
route by route to the owner's calls (routes_to), not to one origin, since
`vol_route` is reached from the trace's drain and the medium kernel's and
is handed a different load at each; Definitions::parameter has to see
through a `let` (`vol_path_step!after` hands `rs`, the program's name for
its split parameter); and the loop form of specialize has to see a
parameter through the load of it a deferral hoisted before the loop
(`@2335 = load(sampler)` is how the sample kernel knows the sampler) and
read the tag before copying the loop, since in a round loop the threading
goes round the back edge through the drain's block, which gains an
argument the pre-copied selectors would not pass. With all three, no
queue of the renderer carries the draws, and the sample and camera
kernels are one per sampler, as pbrt's GenerateRaySamples and
GenerateCameraRays are (camera.cpp:25, samples.cpp:24).

**The schedule** (apps/pbrt/schedules/gpu-optix.bonsai):
`vol_path_step.stage(vol_ray_samples, rays, samples)` after the five
deferrals onto `rays`; `render.split(samples, samples_blk, samples_thr,
256, true)` and its binds beside the camera's; `render.specialize(p_blk,
sampler)` and `render.specialize(samples_blk, sampler)` after the binds
(the loop form comes late). The images: killeroo-simple at 16 spp is
byte-identical to the morning's render on radiance, albedo and normals
after each step.

**Measured, killeroo-simple 16 spp** (scratch/surface/samples/compare1-3,
against pbrt --gpu in the same run; pbrt's kernel total 49.4 ms, its
sample kernel 3.71, its trace 16.59, its camera 2.56): the cut alone took
our kernel time from 35.38 to 32.97 ms (2.76x to 2.88x pbrt), the raygen
from 17.49 to 11.46 ms, with the sample kernel at 3.87 -- parity with
pbrt's 3.71 where the draws' addition to the raygen had been 1.17x; the
reload rule changed nothing measurable here (33.01; this scene's material
kernels are not bound by their entries' bytes). Over the seven scenes the
30-scene sweep finished before I stopped it (compare-out-samples16-stage-
only against compare-out-reset16, cut alone): wall 1.037x geometric mean,
kernel 1.056x, no cell slower, book the far end at 1.13x kernel. The
sweep had to be stopped because it rebuilds build/compiler from source per
scene, and I had edited compiler sources while it ran -- never again
during a sweep. With everything -- the cut, the reload, the kernels per
sampler -- killeroo-simple is 31.17 ms (3.07x), the raygen 9.83 ms once
the hit program no longer loads and pushes the draws, the Halton sample
kernel 3.64 against pbrt's 3.71, the Halton camera kernel 2.75 against
2.56.

**The 30 scenes at 16 spp** (21:15-21:47, compare-out-samples16 against
compare-out-reset16, compare_tables.py): wall 1.057x geometric mean,
kernel 1.072x; faster on 28 of 30 cells, book 1.18x kernel, killeroo-gold
1.17x, frame542 1.16x, killeroo-simple 1.13x, coated-gold 1.13x, crown
and plume 1.11x, head 1.11x; the two lte-orb cells slower, silver 0.966x
kernel (89.8 to 93.0 ms) and rough-glass 0.996x. Against pbrt --gpu the
30-cell geometric mean went from 1.80x to 1.87x (the cells run from 1.25x,
landscape, to 2.91x, killeroo-simple); the same 27 images match
and the same three (pavilion-day, the two bistros) miss the lit-pixel
rule as before; the two zero-day frames are missing from both sweeps
because pbrt --gpu itself segfaults on them. lte-orb-silver, read off its
kernel tables: the raygen fell 34.95 to 27.09 ms and the PMJ02BN sample
kernel added 6.61 (pbrt's 6.09), but the CoatedDiffuse material kernel
rose 25.72 to 29.60 -- it now gathers the bounce's samples from the record
by slot, a 44-byte RaySamples struct per entry across two or three cache
lines, where it had read them from its own compacted arrays, and where
pbrt gathers its SOA<RaySamples>'s three Float4s and two floats. The next
step for those cells is to store a cut's values in the record as the
queue stores an entry, a struct of arrays by scalar (the leaves machinery
of SSA/Defer.cpp), which the reload would rebuild from.

**The entries, audited against pbrt's work items** (bytes an entry
stores, from the arrays the SSA declares; pbrt's from
wavefront/workitems.h): rays 181 against RayWorkItem's 184; escaped 161
against 164; emissive 165 against 192; shadow 112 against 124;
medium_samples 295 against 372; exits 252 against 330; hits 271 (311
before the reload) against MaterialEvalWorkItem's 252; probes 369 against
about 330; bssrdfs 382 (422 before) against 168. What is left in hits
over pbrt: pixel_x and pixel_y (8 bytes, recomputable from the slot and
the band -- the recipe analysis does not see the normalized-index
relation), `wave` (4, pbrt's wavefrontDepth, which is the round counter
and uniform per round: an induction on queue entries the analysis does
not know), `mat` beside prim.material (4), the primitive's tag and index
for hit_wo (5), prim.alpha and prim.light (8). bssrdfs carries the
SubsurfaceMaterial by value where pbrt carries a material pointer: a
program change (pass the index, re-read `materials[mat]` in the drain) or
the index-into-read-only-storage rule applied to an ADT payload. The
unread-leaf elision already drops prev_ctx, r_l, ray.o and the primitive's
other payload words from the material queues.

**The hit chain, and its extra hop.** Our closest-hit program (the SSA of
`_rt_trace0!hit`) reads the record (`base`, `holder`), takes the
primitive index from the hardware, and then: `prims[top]` for the
primitive's tag (parallel to the rest; its payload goes unread for a
mesh), `tris[base + prim]` for the Triangle, which is (mesh, tri),
`meshes[t.mesh]` for the mesh's record, then the mesh's indices and its
positions. pbrt's (optix.cu `__closesthit__triangle`,
Triangle::InteractionFromIntersection) reads its record, whose first word
is the mesh pointer (TriangleMeshRecord::mesh), then the indices, then the
positions: three dependent loads to our four. The hop is `tris`: our
Triangle record exists to say which mesh a triangle belongs to, and the
record already knows (one build input is one mesh). The fix is two
halves. The Mesh arm's `tris` becomes a set synthesized from the mesh and
an index range -- `Triangle{mesh, i}` for `i` in the mesh's count -- so
that `tris[base + prim]` is arithmetic, not a load; and the hit-group
record carries the mesh index beside `base` and `holder` (pbrt's
`rec.mesh`), so that `meshes[mesh]` is one hop from the record and the
`prims[top]` read serves only the instance arms. The first half is a
language and layout change -- a set defined by a range and a function,
which the tree binding must still enumerate for the build -- and the
second a change to `_RTRecord` and the driver's record fill; both are the
user's to approve.

**Open from this.** The skip bit for a cut not every path reaches;
recomputing pure functions of the entry in the first pass's stored set;
storing by entry index when the entries carry no slot; the loop form of
specialize copies the camera's prologue loop too (seven copies of a kernel
that zeroes the film, one launched); the round loop's count read stays by
the user's ruling (pbrt runs maxDepth rounds blind, launching over empty
queues).

### The work items matched, and the hit chain: the plan (10-11, 09:30-)

The user's directions this morning: a cut's stored values are a struct of
arrays by default, with layout specifications later, so the schedule needs
a handle to them as it has to a queue; a fresh three-count heatmap (queued
behind loom-f2's claim of the card, see below); the hit chain's extra hop
shown as the code we generate against pbrt's, with the compiler algorithm
that turns one into the other; and a plan that brings the hits and
bssrdfs entries to pbrt's bytes or under, with the code of each cause.
Everything here is a proposal; nothing of it is built.

**A cut's values today, and the handle.** `cut_same_queue` (SSA/Stage.cpp,
the `stored` loop) makes one array per stored value, typed as the value:

    s.array = make_alloca(*O, point, Array_t::make(type, as_expr(owned->second.size)),
                          queue.name + "_" + s.name + "_slots");   // rays_rs_slots : RaySamples[n]

so the draws are an array of 44-byte structs, read back whole by
`load(gep(array, slot))` (the reload recipe), where pbrt's
`pixelSampleState.samples` is an SOA (`soa RaySamples`: one array per
scalar). A queue's entry, by contrast, goes through `QueueLayout`
(SSA/Defer.h): the entry type flattened to leaves, one array per scalar,
bools packed, and `unread[q][l]` dropping the leaves a drain never reads.
Nothing in the schedule names a cut's storage: the queue is named by its
declaration (`rays = render.queue(p_band, ExternDevice)`, the name standing
for the storage and the drain loop), the first pass by `l`, the stored set
`S` by nothing. The proposal, in two steps:

1. The default. Give `S` a `QueueLayout` of its own -- the struct of the
   stored values as the "entry", flattened to leaves exactly as an entry
   is, one record array per leaf (`rays_rs_direct_uc_slots`, ...), and the
   reload recipe a load per leaf the drain reads, rebuilt into the value.
   The unread-leaf elision then applies to the reads: the Diffuse material
   kernel reads five of the seven draws (no subsurface pair), and loads 28
   bytes where it gathers 44 now and pbrt's SOA read of the whole
   `RaySamples` moves 40. This is the lte-orb fix and needs no new syntax.
2. The handle. The three-argument forms return it, in the one expression
   form the schedule already has for `queue`:

       draws = vol_path_step.stage(vol_ray_samples, rays, samples);

   `draws` names the arrays of `S` as `rays` names a queue's, for a storage
   word (`draws` in ExternDevice, as the queues are) and, later, a layout
   specification of the record's arrays, which the layout language has for
   neither a queue nor a record yet (the semantics, 4.1: "a layout for the
   queue that a schedule asks for may replace this; nothing here is the
   layout language's promise"). The alternative -- `l` naming both the loop
   and what it writes, as `q` names a drain and its storage -- is rejected
   because a loop name is what `split` and `bind` take, and a split of
   `samples` would then have to say which of the two it means.

**The hit chain: ours and pbrt's.** What the closest-hit program does for
a mesh hit, read off the SSA (`_rt_trace0!hit`, then `vol_route`'s
`hit_geometry` in the continuation `vol_path_step!after!hit`):

    // ours
    rec = rt_sbt_record()                 // load 1: {base, holder}, the input's record
    idx = rec.base + rt_primitive_index()
    top = rec.holder == OWN ? idx : rec.holder
    e0  = prims[top]                      // load 2: the Primitive -- its tag decides the arm
    switch e0.tag {
      Mesh:  t = tris[idx]                // load 3: Triangle {mesh, tri}
             m = meshes[t.mesh]           // load 4: TriangleMesh {first_index, first_vertex, material, ...}
             g = Geometric{Tri{t.mesh, t.tri}, light(m, t.tri), m.material, m.alpha, m.medium_inside, m.medium_outside}
      ...                                 // Geom, Placed, Inst arms
    }
    // the continuation: hit_geometry -> triangle_geometry
    m  = meshes[t.mesh]                   // load 4 again (the same row)
    v  = mesh_indices[m.first_index + 3*t.tri + k]   // load 5
    p  = mesh_positions[m.first_vertex + v]          // load 6

    // pbrt (optix.cu __closesthit__triangle, shapes.h Triangle::InteractionFromIntersection)
    rec  = *(TriangleMeshRecord *) optixGetSbtDataPointer()   // load 1: {mesh*, material, alpha, lights, medium}
    v    = rec.mesh->vertexIndices[3 * prim + k]               // load 2 (the mesh row), load 3 (the index)
    p    = rec.mesh->p[v]                                      // load 4

Six dependent loads to four. The two extra are `prims[top]`, read for
its tag alone (its payload goes unread on this path) and gating the rest
by a branch, and `tris[idx]`, a row that exists to name the triangle's
mesh when the record already knows it: one build input is one mesh
(trees/optix.bonsai, `Mesh.tris : OptixTree from tris`), so `top` is the
same for every hit on the input and `t.mesh` is too.

The algorithm that maps the one to the other is partial evaluation of the
hit program with the record as the static input and the primitive index
as the dynamic one (binding-time analysis; Jones, Gomard and Sestoft,
*Partial Evaluation and Automatic Program Generation*, 1993): 

1. Binding times. In `bind_elements` (Lower/Trees.cpp) `rec` is static,
   `rt_primitive_index()` dynamic, and every expression takes the join of
   its operands'. `own` and `holder` are static; `top` is static for a held
   input (`!own`), dynamic for an own one, so the split is per kind of
   input, which the driver knows when it fills the record (bonsai_optix.h,
   the records loop: `input.holder != BONSAI_OPTIX_OWN`). A load from a
   `const` extern array at a static index is static (`prims[top]`, then
   `meshes[mesh]` once `mesh` is).
2. Residualize. The static part becomes a host function per tree and kind,
   emitted beside the program (`bonsai_rt_record_<tree>(input, prims,
   meshes, ...) -> _RTRecord_<tree>`), which the driver calls where it
   writes `base` and `holder` today; the record type gains the static
   values the dynamic part reads -- the arm's tag (so the switch folds),
   the mesh's `first_index`, `first_vertex`, `material`, `alpha`, the
   media and `first_light` -- which is pbrt's TriangleMeshRecord, derived
   rather than written. Sound because the arrays are `const` for the frame
   and the record is read-only: the static part is a pure function of the
   input.
3. The `tris` row. `tris[idx]` is a load at a dynamic index and stays one
   unless the set has no rows: the Mesh arm's `tris` represented by an
   index function -- element `i` is `Triangle{mesh, first + i}` -- so that
   `stored(tris, idx)` is `Triangle{static mesh, first + (idx - base)}`,
   arithmetic. That is a representation of a set, so a layout-language
   form (`Mesh.tris : OptixTree by |i| Triangle{mesh, first + i}`, the
   driver's build input enumerating the mesh's own index buffer as it does
   now), with `first` and a count in the arm or the mesh row.

With 1 and 2 alone: record, `tris`, `meshes`, indices, positions -- five
loads and no branch. With 3 as well: record (the mesh's fields inline),
indices, positions -- three, one under pbrt, whose record holds a pointer
and pays the mesh row. Both are the user's to approve; 3 is the language
change.

**The hits entry, cause by cause.** What `hits!Basic!Diffuse` stores (the
SSA's `Entry_hits` less the leaves `BONSAI_EXPLAIN_DEFER` reports unread),
271 bytes, against pbrt's `MaterialEvalWorkItem`, 252:

    ray.d 12 | medium 4 | via {tag, payload_0} 5 | prim {shape 9, light 4, material 4, alpha 4, media 8} 29
    mat 4 | surf 128 | beta 16 | r_u 16 | depth 4 | wave 4 | _bits0 1 | eta_scale 4 | lambda 32
    pixel_x 4 | pixel_y 4 | _slot 4                                                      = 271

    material* 8 | lambda 32 | beta 16 | r_u 16 | pi 24 | n ns dpdu dpdv dpdus dpdvs dndus dndvs 96
    wo 12 | uv 8 | depth 4 | faceIndex 4 | time 4 | anyNonSpecularBounces 4 | etaScale 4
    mediumInterface 16 | pixelIndex 4                                                    = 252

The geometry is the same bytes on both sides (surf 128 + ray.d 12 =
pbrt's pi, eight vectors, wo and uv, 140); the spectra and depth are the
same; pbrt carries 19 bytes we do not (time, faceIndex, three bytes of a
bool, a wider medium interface, a pointer for a material). Our 38 over
pbrt, each with its cause:

- *`ray.d`, `via`, `prim.shape` (26 bytes) for `wo`.* render.bonsai,
  vol_surface: `wo = hit_wo(via, prim.shape, ray);` recomputes the
  direction the trace kernel already computed (`iwo = hit_wo(via,
  prim.shape, ray)` in vol_route, handed to emissive_contribution). pbrt's
  item carries `wo` and nothing it was made from; the comment above the
  line says as much. Fix, in the program: vol_route hands `iwo` to
  vol_surface and `ray` and `via` leave its signature; `ray.d` becomes
  `wo` (the same 12 bytes) and `via` and `prim.shape`, read by nothing
  else in the kernel, go unread (14 bytes saved).
- *`prim.light`, `prim.alpha`, `prim.material` (12 bytes).* vol_surface
  reads only the two media of `prim`
  (`get_medium`, the `ScatterPoint`), but hands `prim` whole to
  vol_subsurface, and `read_paths` (SSA/Analysis.cpp) counts a call's
  argument as read whole: `read(b, arg); // handed to the callee: a read`.
  Fix, in the compiler: a call's argument is read as the callee reads the
  parameter -- `read_paths` made interprocedural, memoized per function,
  the whole value for an extern, a recursion or a depth past a bound. The
  same fix takes `prim` to its two media in bssrdfs and probes.
- *`pixel_x`, `pixel_y` beside `_slot` (8 bytes).* pbrt stores
  `pixelIndex` and keeps `pPixel` in `pixelSampleState` by it. Ours are
  "stored: one value down the chain, but computed inside the producer's
  iteration (p_in!VolPath is a value of the iteration)": `cook`
  (SSA/Defer.cpp) sees a parameter at the push and stops, since
  `materialize` resolves a chain parameter only to a value in scope at the
  drain. Fix, in the compiler: `cook` follows a chain parameter to the
  owner's definition and cooks it there, with the producer's index -- the
  `SlotGroup`'s `index` at the producer -- standing for `Field(_slot)`;
  `pixel_x` is then the band's origin plus arithmetic on the slot,
  recomputed at every drain (eight bytes out of every entry of the family,
  seven queues).
- *`wave` (4 bytes).* The round counter: pushed as `wave + 1` by every
  pusher onto `rays` (vol_route's boundary crossing, vol_surface's next
  ray, vol_exit's), compared with `max_depth` in vol_route. pbrt's
  `wavefrontDepth` is a kernel argument. Every entry of a buffer holds the
  same value, by induction: the producer pushes a constant (li_vol_path's
  `0`), and every push inside the rounds pushes a function of the
  entry's own `wave` and nothing else. Fix, in the compiler: a field whose
  pushes all cook to `f(that field, uniforms)` with a uniform value at the
  producer is round-uniform, stored once per buffer beside the count
  (`Queue_rays.wave`), and handed to the drain as a uniform -- a new kind
  beside `Recipe::Kind::Uniform`. Four bytes out of every entry of the
  family.
- *`mat` beside `prim.material` (4).* Gone with the interprocedural reads;
  `mat` stays (pbrt's `material`).

After the four: 271 - 14 - 12 - 8 - 4 = 233 bytes against pbrt's 252.

**The bssrdfs entry, cause by cause.** What `bssrdfs` stores, 382 bytes,
against pbrt's `GetBSSRDFAndProbeRayWorkItem`, 168:

    ss {eta, scale, sigma_a, sigma_s, reflectance 20, mfp, table} 44 | medium 4 | prim 29 | mat 4
    surf 128 | hit.ns 12 | ctx {p, dpdx, dpdy, n 48, uv 8, dudx..dvdy 16} 72 | beta 16 | r_u 16
    depth 4 | wave 4 | eta_scale 4 | lam 32 | pixel_x 4 | pixel_y 4 | _slot 4 | _bits0 1    = 382

    material 8 | lambda 32 | beta 16 | r_u 16 | p 12 | wo 12 | n 12 | ns 12 | dpdus 12 | uv 8
    depth 4 | mediumInterface 16 | etaScale 4 | pixelIndex 4                              = 168

- *`ss` by value (44 bytes).* vol_surface pushes `*maybe_ss`, the
  Subsurface arm's payload of `materials[mat]` (bxdf.bonsai,
  material_subsurface). The semantics (4.2) say "a value selected from a
  read-only array by an index is stored as the index", but `cook` refuses
  every load (`!recomputable(in) || reads_memory(in) || ...`), so the rule
  is written and not built. Fix, in the compiler: a `Load` whose address is
  a `GEP` of an array that is `const` storage in scope at the drain
  (`materials`, every extern of the scene) with a cookable index is a
  recipe; the arm's extraction above it is pure and cooks already. The
  drain then reads the 128-byte Material row at `mat` as pbrt reads
  through `w.material`. Honest cost: a row per entry in the BSSRDF kernel
  in place of 44 bytes pushed and popped.
- *`surf` (128 bytes) and probes' `entry` (128).* vol_subsurface reads
  `surf.p` and hands `surf` to vol_probe as `entry`, whose only use is the
  initial `kept` of `vol_probe_step` -- the value `ProbeResult` returns
  when the walk found nothing, on which vol_probe returns at once. pbrt's
  `WeightedReservoirSampler` starts empty. Fix, in the program:
  `vol_probe_step` starts from a zero `SurfaceGeometry` and `entry` leaves
  vol_probe; vol_subsurface takes `surf.p`. 116 bytes out of bssrdfs, 128
  out of probes.
- *`ctx` (72 bytes).* `texture_context(hit, diffs)`, the material kernel's
  context with its differentials. pbrt's kernel builds its context from
  the item (workitems.h, `GetMaterialEvalContext`: `wo, n, ns, dpdus, p,
  uv`), no differentials, so its subsurface textures are read at level
  zero. Fix, in the program, pbrt's way: vol_subsurface builds the context
  from `p`, `n` and `uv` with zero differentials; the entry carries `uv`
  and `n` (20 bytes with `p` shared). 52 bytes, and textured subsurface
  scenes move toward pbrt's pixels.
- *`prim` to its media (21), `pixel_x`/`pixel_y` (8), `wave` (4):* the
  compiler fixes above.

After these: 382 - 44 - 116 - 52 - 21 - 12 = 137 bytes against pbrt's 168;
probes 369 - 128 - 21 - 12 = 208 against pbrt's SubsurfaceScatterWorkItem,
332.

**Order of work**, each a commit with its test: (1) interprocedural
`read_paths` (hits, bssrdfs, probes shrink; a test with a parameter handed
through two calls to a callee that reads one field); (2) the read-only
load in `cook` (ssa test: an entry stores an index, the drain reloads the
row); (3) the slot-function recipe (ssa test: `pixel = x0 + slot % W`
recomputed); (4) the round-uniform field (ssa+llvm test: a depth counter
stored once per buffer); (5) the program's three changes (`wo` handed, the
probe's empty start, the subsurface context), each byte-identical or
explained; (6) the cut's values as leaves with the reload per leaf (the
lte-orb cells); (7) the handle `draws = ...stage(...)` and its storage
word; (8) the hit chain's partial evaluation and, if approved, the index
set.

### The disk, the duplicate conversions, and the full sweep (10-11, 11:30-)

**What happened.** The morning's heatmap sweep (`compare-out-heatmap5`,
launched 10:24 on loom-f2's "done") lost its last twelve scenes at 11:30:
the root filesystem, 3.6 TB, was full. The sweep's own output was 32 GB.
What filled the disk was converted scenes: 1.1 TB of them under 55
compare-out directories in apps/pbrt, 180 GB more under scratch, 180 GB
under 25 compare-out directories at the repository root (the experiments
of 10-04 to 10-06), 117 GB under eval. Every cell of every sweep had
converted its scene again (`scene_dump --gpu --spp N` per cell), so a
scene had three identical copies of its geometry and texture sidecars per
sweep -- a scene's .geo and .tex are byte-identical across counts, only
the `sampler` line of the .txt differs -- and no sweep ever deleted them.
kroken's conversion is 10.6 GB (its 288 million displaced triangles, as
`pbrt --gpu` builds them), landscape's 4.5 GB.

**The cleanup** (the user: "do a big clean up of the unnecessary logs in
this repo, but obviously, do not delete anything important"; then "Can
the compare-out folders be deleted? what about stuff in eval?"). Deleted:
every converted-scene copy outside the shared folder below (1.6 TB in a
first pass that let the sweep resume, 117 GB in a second once the folder
held the thirty scenes); the 25 root-level compare-out directories whole
(their numbers are in this file's sections of 10-04 to 10-06); eval/out's
float renders (46 GB; its results.json and results.tsv and eval/plots
stay). Kept: every compare-out directory under apps/pbrt with its tables,
stats, logs, PNGs and float renders -- the sweeps REPORT.md cites and
compares (heatmap to heatmap5, gpu-sweep, gpu-fix, reset16, samples16)
and the variant sweeps of 10-06 to 10-08 -- bench-out's renders, scratch's
scripts and pinned worktrees. The disk went from 100% to 47% used, 1.9 TB
free. The sweep resumed at 11:57 and finished at 12:48.

**One conversion per scene** (the user: "We should never have duplicate
scenes converted. Please make a (not checked in, but gitignored)
apps/pbrt/scenes folder with each scene converted only once, and all other
copies deleted."). `apps/pbrt/convert_scene.sh <scene_dump> <dir/name>
[options]` prints `apps/pbrt/scenes/converted/<dir>/<name>.txt`,
converting when the conversion is missing or stale: a stamp beside it
hashes what the conversion is a function of -- the converter's sources
(scene_dump.cpp, scene_io.h, measured_io.h, the FlatBuffer schema, the
spectral and Sobol' tables), the pbrt binary's size and mtime, the options,
the scene file's size and mtime. The folder is a `converted/` subfolder of
apps/pbrt/scenes, beside the tracked test scenes, so that one .gitignore
line covers it and the .pbrt files stay tracked. The sample count is not a
conversion's: gpu_compare.sh converts with `--gpu` alone and renders with
the renderer's own `--spp N` (render_hook.cpp's sampler_at, pbrt's
override transcribed per sampler, which the eval tool's cells already
use), as `--spp` is pbrt's own on the other side. Verified with the
sweep's own render.out from the shared conversions: killeroo-simple at 64
(halton), lte-orb-silver at 64 (pmj02bn, whose sorting into pixels depends
on the count) and clouds at 16 (zsobol), each byte-identical to the
sweep's radiance, albedo and normals. gpu_compare.sh now also refuses to
start with under 50 GB free under --out. Open: compare.sh and render.sh
still convert into their work directory per run -- one scene at a time,
and their `--disable-pixel-jitter` and CPU form are other conversions --
and could take the shared folder keyed by option.

**Why the texture sidecars are three times pbrt's** (the user: "the scene
dumps should not be so huge! I thought we were making them memory
efficient"). landscape's .tex is 3.04 GB: 585 texture records, 6538
levels, 1013 million texels at three bytes each. The scene's image files
hold 186 million texels (191 files: 88 RGB, 52 grey, 47 RGBA, 4 palette),
250 million with their pyramids, 0.75 GB at three bytes a texel -- the file
holds each pyramid four times over. The cause is convert_image_texture
(scene_dump.cpp): it builds the pyramid and appends its levels per imagemap
*declaration* (its cache is by texture name and folded scale), and
landscape declares 861 imagemaps over those 191 files (Abies_concolor_tr_01_co.png
24 times, meadow_oldgrass01.png 22). pbrt shares them:
ImageTextureBase::GetTexture caches the MIPMap by TexInfo -- filename,
filter options, wrap mode, encoding (textures.h:505-549) -- one pyramid per
distinct file, and its stats for landscape count 990 MiB of ImageTextures
(793 MiB of image maps) against our 3.04 GB. The widening of a one-channel
image to three bytes a texel (the comment at the texel copy) costs another
0.11 GB here (52 grey images, 40 million texels, one byte in pbrt) and
matters less. Geometry is not bloated: landscape's .geo is 1.12 GB for
27.9 million triangles (40 bytes a triangle with normals and uvs),
kroken's 10.6 GB for 288 million, which is what `pbrt --gpu` holds too
(its stats: 5.36 GiB of acceleration structures for kroken). The older
dumps' .txt files were large (121 GB over 674 files, where today's are
kilobytes), a format since replaced; they went with the rest. **Deferred,
the user's to call:** key the pyramid in convert_image_texture by file,
wrap mode and encoding as pbrt does, so declarations share levels -- a
converter change, every conversion redone, the renderer unchanged, a
third of the texture memory and cache footprint on landscape, the sweep
measured after; and a one-byte texel format for grey images.

**The full sweep**, 30 scenes at 16, 64 and 128 spp against heatmap4 (the
sweep before the sample pass): REPORT.md "Where it stands (2026-10-11)".

### The cut's stored set as a struct of arrays (10-11, 13:45-)

The user's ruling (13:50): "the memory layout of the bounces must be SoA,
that should always be our default until we add in the extra memory layout
control for queues" -- step 6 of the morning's plan, first. And on a cap I
had written into the reload recipe (`most_reloads = 64`): "the compiler
cannot be built on shitty heuristics! Either justify it or we need a
replacement algorithm." It had no justification and is gone; the walk it
bounded is over the owner's SSA definitions, a finite graph, and ends on
its own, with a definition two operands share followed once.

**Built.** A cut on the same queue stores its set as a queue's entry is
stored (SSA/Stage.cpp, cut_same_queue; docs/schedule-semantics.md 4.5):
each value flattened to its scalars by `leaves_of` -- one array per
scalar, a short vector one packed array where no gang touches the queue,
bools eight to a byte, an ADT's padding nowhere -- `<q>_<leaf>_slots` per
array, a pointer parameter per array down the chain, the cut taking the
value apart (`take_apart`, `pack_bits`) into stores, and the second pass
putting it back together (`rebuild`, `unpack_bit`) from the scalars the
rest reads (read_paths; a scalar it never reads is undefined). The leaf
helpers moved out of Defer.cpp's anonymous namespace and are declared
beside QueueLayout in SSA/Defer.h, so both stores are one rule; the
entry's own bool packing and the push's bit packing now call the shared
`pack_bools` and `pack_bits`. The reload recipe (SSA/Defer.cpp) follows
the pure register operations that built a value at the owner's calls down
to the loads -- the struct put back together, a packed vector cast back, a
bit tested out of its byte, a constant pad -- and the recipe emitter at the
drain leaves a part of a rebuilt struct undefined when no read of the
callee's parameter covers its path (`covers`), so the drain loads the
scalars the callee uses. A scalar value's storage and names are what they
were (`rays_draw_slots`); the goldens of the scalar tests did not change.

**In the renderer.** `RaySamples` is seven arrays
(`rays_vol_ray_samples_{direct_uc,direct_u,indirect_uc,indirect_u,
indirect_rr,subsurface_uc,subsurface_u}_slots`). Every entry type is as it
was except two that shrank: `exits` lost its five draw fields (252 -> 224
bytes) and `probes` the same (369 -> 341) -- they were `LoadField`s of the
reloaded struct, which the old recipe, matching a load of the whole value
only, did not see; the new one follows the field read to the load. What
each drain loads of the seven: the exit kernel four (direct_uc, direct_u,
indirect_uc, indirect_u), the medium scatter four, the probe kernel five,
the material kernels all seven -- `vol_surface` hands `rs` whole to the
subsurface push, a call when read_paths runs, so the whole is a read (the
interprocedural read of step 1, made aware that a pushed argument the
entry reloads is not a read of the pusher's, narrows it; pbrt's material
kernel reads the whole SOA struct too) -- and the closest-hit program all
seven, to build an argument its continuation never reads: `rs` goes to
`vol_route`, whose pushes reload, so the parameter is dead and the loads
with it. The old shape loaded the 44-byte struct there for the same
reason. Removing a dead parameter from a function and the argument from
its callers, to a fixed point, is the standard pass (LLVM's
DeadArgumentElimination) the SSA does not have; the GPU backend's own
optimizer may do it on the device module, which the PTX would show.

instructions against a store at the push and a load at the drain) or go.

### Step 1: a call's argument is read as the callee reads it (10-11, 14:40-)

The user (14:40): "Yes, start step 1 now."

**Built.** `read_paths` (SSA/Analysis.h) takes the program's functions
and follows calls: the paths a callee reads of parameter k are the paths
read of argument k, each callee's reads computed once (memoized) and the
program followed through; an argument is read whole where the callee
cannot be followed -- not among the functions or no functions given, a
body-less extern, a callee on the cycle of calls being followed (a
recursion, whose reads across functions would need a fixed point and are
taken as everything), a run of calls (MultiCall). A deferred call that is
not yet a push is a call, so what its callee reads is what its queue will
store: this is the push-aware rule, and it needs no knowledge of the later
queue's layout. The entry analysis (SSA/Defer.cpp) and the cut's second
pass (SSA/Stage.cpp) pass the functions. Also in that function: the cap
`deepest = 8` -- a path longer than eight steps was taken as the whole --
is replaced by the type's own depth (a struct one more than its deepest
field, a vector one more than its element, a scalar nothing): no type
contains itself, so a longer path names nothing of the value and arises
only round a cycle of edges, where it means every field at every depth,
the whole. That is what ends the fixed point, and it is a fact of the
type, not a number.

**What the narrower reads uncovered.** A drain whose callee never reads a
field hands it `undef`; where that callee pushes the value on, the next
queue's analysis sees `undef` at that push and a real value at another,
and the slot and recipe rules asked every push to agree. In
semantics-reload-two-routes the pixel came through the detour queue as
`undef` (route hands it only to shade, which never reads it), and the hits
entry listed `p` as a stored field where it had been the slot. An
undefined argument is handed where nothing reads it, so whatever a recipe
computes there is read by nothing: the per-route slot match and the recipe
agreement skip an undefined push. The origin agreement of chain parameters
stays strict -- making `undef` agree there named one call's per-iteration
load the origin of every call, which the uniform rule then rightly
refused -- and the per-route rule, which matches each call against its
own slot, is the one that applies.

**In the renderer** (bytes an entry stores, the queue type's arrays less
the leaves the explain reports unread; the material kernels' is Diffuse's,
the same for every material):

    bssrdfs              382    345    168   prim 21, mat 4, ctx.n 12
    probes               341    316    332   prim 21, mat 4
    medium_samples       255    223    372   the hit's payload words
    shadow               112     80    124   lambda: shadow_contribution adds into L, no conversion
    exit_shadow          112     80          lambda
    emissive             165    149    192   lambda.pdf
    escaped              161    145    164   lambda.pdf
    exits                228    228    330
    rays                 181    181    184

The hits entry's three bytes over pbrt are `prim.shape` (tag, payload_x)
and `via`, read by `hit_wo(via, prim.shape, ray)` -- step 5's program
change, 14 bytes with `ray.d` becoming `wo`. The draws: the material
kernels still load all seven, since `vol_surface` hands `rs` to
`vol_subsurface` (a call, read whole: vol_subsurface hands it on to
vol_probe and so on; each is a real read until the push's entry reloads
it, which the analysis at this point cannot know), and the closest-hit
program all seven for its dead parameter. Both are the dead-argument
question, not a read question: once the pushes are lowered the parameters
are unused, and removing a dead parameter from a function and the
argument from its callers to a fixed point (the standard pass; LLVM's
DeadArgumentElimination) would drop the loads.

**Checked (19:50): LLVM already does it.** The claim above describes the
SSA, not the machine code. The renderer's GPU schedule compiled once with
`-b ptx` (the optimized LLVM IR of every device module beside its PTX,
scratchpad `dae/`): in the SSA, `__closesthit__trace$rays` does build the
draws with seven loads from the slot arrays and hand the struct to
`vol_path_step!after!hit`, whose parameter nothing reads once the pushes
are lowered. In the optimized IR of the OptiX module the closest-hit
program loads none of the seven arrays -- its launch-parameter loads are
the rays queue, the textures, the meshes, the materials, the shape pools
and the three target queues -- and in each of the 22 material kernels the
two subsurface slot arrays arrive as kernel parameters and are never
dereferenced (two address-space casts, both dead), while the five a
material reads are. Our device modules give LLVM everything the pass
needs: every function internalized (CodeGen_PTX), everything not
`[[noinline]]` inlined -- an inlined callee's dead parameter is a dead
value, plain dead-code elimination's -- and
`buildPerModuleDefaultPipeline(O3)`, which runs `deadargelim` after the
inliner for what stayed a call (`opt -O3 -print-pipeline-passes`, LLVM
23.1.1). So a dead-argument pass in the SSA would change no instruction
of the kernels; what it would tidy is the SSA itself and the dead pointer
parameters the kernels still carry (two to seven of 83, never loaded).
Not next: step 5's program changes (hits 255 -> 241) and the hit chain
(step 8) are what the closest-hit program still pays for.

### The camera-ray kernel against pbrt's GenerateCameraRays (10-11, 21:00-)

The one stage behind on 29 of 30 scenes (REPORT, 20:30). The two read
side by side before anything was changed: pbrt's
`GenerateCameraRays<ConcreteSampler>` (wavefront/camera.cpp, one kernel
per sampler type) and our `_kernel_p_blk$VolPath$<Sampler>` (the camera
loop specialized per sampler since 482c0de1).

**The same work in the same order.** The pixel from the launch index
(`pMin + index % xResolution`, `y0 + index / xResolution`; ours
`pixel_x0 + p % width`, `pixel_y0 + p / width`); StartPixelSample (the
Halton index from the two inverse radical inverses and the Chinese
remainder, as ours); the wavelength's draw and `SampleVisible`; the
camera sample -- the pixel pair, the filter table sampled by two binary
searches over its CDFs, the time, the lens pair -- with the same draws in
the same dimensions; `GenerateRay`: cameraFromRaster, the normalize, the
lens, RenderFromCamera through the interval transform. The radical
inverses, the digit permutations, the blue-noise and PMJ tables, the
filter's `PiecewiseConstant1D::Sample` and `FindInterval` are the same
loops over the same tables. Nothing of the draws or the ray differs, and
the measured times say so too: ours is **0.33 to 0.35 ns a ray on every
one of the 30 scenes** whatever the sampler (heatmap5 at 16 spp, the
kernel's milliseconds over pixels times spp), where pbrt's moves with the
sampler -- 0.27 to 0.34 on the Halton scenes, 0.29 to 0.33 on ZSobol,
0.20 on the two PMJ02BN scenes. A kernel whose time does not see the
difference between a table lookup and a dozen 64-bit divisions is not
spending it on arithmetic. The ratios: Halton 1.08x to 1.26x, ZSobol
1.04x to 1.18x, PMJ02BN 1.65x -- widest where pbrt's compute is least.

**What each stores per pixel sample** (pbrt's Halton instance's SASS, our
Halton kernel's PTX assembled with ptxas for sm_120; both read, not
guessed). pbrt: `pPixel` (two ST.E), `L = 0`, `lambda` (three ST.E.128),
`filterWeight`, and `PushCameraRay` -- ray o and d as six scalars (its
`SOA<Point3f>` is x, y, z arrays), time, medium (ST.E.64), depth,
pixelIndex, lambda, beta, etaScale, anyNonSpecularBounces, r_u, r_l,
specularBounce -- then `cameraRayWeight`: **212 bytes in 25 store
instructions**, nine of them 128-bit (its `SOA<SampledSpectrum>` is a
`Float4` per entry, sixteen-byte aligned). Its `VisibleSurface()`
initialization (18 `ST.E RZ` and a `.128`) is under
`initializeVisibleSurface`, false for an RGB film. Ours: the
`VisibleSurface` record slot -- `{n, ns, albedo, lambda, set}` as one
96-byte struct per slot (`rays_visible_slots : VisibleSurface[n]`),
written as eight stores of 81 bytes into a 96-byte stride; the `l` slot
(16); the filter weight (4); the `ran` byte, stored twice (a zero at the
iteration's start, a one after the push, with the push's atomic between
them so LLVM keeps both); and the rays entry -- o and d as packed 3-vectors
(three scalar stores each at a 12-byte stride), medium, beta, r_u, r_l,
depth, wave, eta_scale, `prev_ctx` (48 bytes: the constant origin context
li_vol_path passes, which vol_route reads only under `depth > 0`, so
pbrt's PushCameraRay never writes `prevIntrCtx`), lambda, pixel_x,
pixel_y, the slot, the bools' byte: **276 bytes in 58 store instructions**
-- STG.E x48, STG.E.128 x4, STG.E.64 x2, STG.E.U8 x4. The 48 scalar
stores are the point: every one of beta, r_u, r_l, lambda.lambda and
lambda.pdf is stored as **four scalars**, because the entry's leaf for a
4-vector was the *packed* vector, `[[packed]] f32x4`, whose LLVM storage
is `[4 x float]` -- sixteen bytes aligned to four -- and a sixteen-byte
store aligned to four is four `st.global.b32` in PTX and four STG.E in
SASS. The drains load the same way: the Diffuse material kernel's
optimized IR holds 418 scalar `load float` and two vector loads. Per warp
the four scalar stores of one spectrum touch sixteen sectors each (32
threads at a 16-byte stride) where pbrt's one ST.E.128 touches sixteen
once: four times the request traffic for the same bytes; the 96-byte
record slot the same, every one of its eight stores touching 32
half-filled sectors; the packed 3-vectors three times pbrt's for `o` and
`d`. Our 1.3x of pbrt's bytes is roughly 3x its L1-to-L2 requests, which
is what a PMJ02BN kernel of 1288 SASS instructions and 46 registers
(pbrt's: 2208 and 126) needs to be 1.65x slower than pbrt's.

**Built: the 4-vector leaf is the vector itself (`stored_vector_type`,
SSA/Defer.cpp).** A short vector whose natural storage is its components
back to back -- two or four of them, sixteen bytes or fewer -- is stored
in an array of the vector type, aligned as the vector is (eight or
sixteen bytes; what every allocation an array lives in gives: malloc's,
cuMemAlloc's, a std::vector's), so the push's store and the drain's load
are one `st.global.v4.f32` and one `ld.global.v4.f32`: pbrt's `Float4`.
A 3-vector stays packed (sixteen bytes of natural storage for twelve of
value), and so does anything wider than sixteen bytes (its natural
alignment is more than an allocation promises). `keeps_whole` beside
`packs` tells the rebuild that a whole-vector leaf may be the vector
itself; the push's `cast<[[packed]] f32x4>` and the drain's `cast<f32x4>`
are gone for the 4-vectors (and the `f32x2` draw slots of the cut). Tried
first and withdrawn: a codegen rule reading an element's alignment off
its stride (`[4 x float]` at a 16-byte stride in a 16-byte-aligned array
is 16-aligned). It is sound for the compiler's own arrays and the
driver's queue buffers but not for arrays in general: a runtime check at
`bonsai_buffer_wrap` found fourteen test drivers handing interior
pointers of structs and stack objects (8 mod 16) -- memory C++ does not
align to sixteen -- so the promise would have been one callers do not
keep, and a `movaps` or a `ld.v4` on it faults. The leaf's *type* carries
the alignment honestly; the compiler allocates those arrays (or the
driver does, by the queue-storage protocol, with cudaMalloc). The same
experiment showed one more thing, recorded for the user: a layout group
of `[[packed]]` rows is read on the GPU at alignment one -- ptx/rtiow-
primer's node fields were twenty `ld.global.u8` (byte loads of floats!)
that became word loads under the stride rule -- a layout-language
question (a group's alignment promise), not this renderer's, whose device
traversal is the RT cores'. Tests: ssa/defer-vector-leaves, semantics-
stage-same-queue-soa and semantics-reload-by-slot-soa re-blessed after
reading (the `s : f32x4[]` and `uv : f32x2[]` arrays, the casts gone,
numbering shifted); a new llvm golden defer-vector-leaves (the `<4 x
float>` store and load at `align 16`, the `[3 x float]` as before); the
non-GPU suites pass (1528) and the 64 GPU tests pass (10-12, 11:10,
once loom-f2 released the card). The assembly, read before the timing
(the device module recompiled with `-b ptx`, ptxas for sm_120,
cuobjdump): the camera kernel's stores went from STG.E x48, STG.E.128 x4
to **STG.E x28, STG.E.128 x9** on each of the Halton, PMJ02BN and ZSobol
instances -- the five spectra's twenty scalar stores are five 128-bit
ones; 58 store instructions to 43 -- the Halton instance's registers 62
to 56, the other two unchanged (46, 72). The drains the same way: the
Diffuse material kernel's stores STG.E x67, STG.E.128 x3 to STG.E x35,
STG.E.128 x11 (its pushes to the shadow and ray queues), its scalar
global loads 678 to 656 with the 128-bit loads 55 to 59.

**Measured (10-12, 11:20-11:45, `compare-out-vec4`):** the protocol's five
scenes at 16 and 64 spp against heatmap5 and the step-1 run, pbrt --gpu

-> 338.17 (644.9), 822.93 -> 815.00 (1336.7) at 64. Every cell faster,
**1.012x kernel as a geometric mean at both counts** (1.060x over
