### The bistro lit-pixel bias: pbrt masks an area light by its alpha texture (10-15 night to 10-17)

The 30-scene gate had three image verdicts standing against it after
heatmap5 (10-11): pavilion-day at 16 spp, the calibrated tolerance artifact
of 09-29 (pbrt's own CPU and GPU renders disagree there six times more
than we do with either), and bistro_cafe and bistro_vespa at every count,
where we light far more pixels than pbrt -- 2,044,954 against 1,880,575 at
16 spp on cafe, dim ones (median luminance 1.7e-4) in the restaurant behind
its windows and under the arch -- with the means agreeing to 0.04%. The
bias had been investigated on 10-05 and 10-07 and left at "the light tree's
choice, two thirds of it, and `uc` differing in its bits". It is neither.
The chain of probes that found it, each a scene under
~/projects/pbrt-v4-scenes (bistro/ and a new probes/ directory, untracked
there as the 10-07 probes are) rendered by `gpu_compare.sh` against
`pbrt --gpu` at 1 spp with maxdepth 1 -- emission and one light sample per
pixel, so a pixel's value names what the light sampler did -- and read
with scratchpad lit_diff.py (lit sets both ways, agreement, luminance of
the one-sided pixels, chromaticity):

- *The sampler is cleared.* killeroo-simple with `Sampler "zsobol"` in
  place of halton agrees with pbrt on 88.6% of pixels at 1 spp and 65.0% at
  16 (halton's figure is 65.6%): our zsobol draws are pbrt's at the bounce
  dimensions too, which the zsobol test covers only at the camera's. A
  halton bistro (bistro_vespa_d1h) diverges exactly as the zsobol one:
  +152,547 lit against +152,835, 1.2% agreement both.
- *The light tree, the sky and the triangle sampling are cleared in
  isolation.* One quad light over a floor: 100% agreement; the quad with
  vertex normals opposing its winding (pbrt orients the emitting side by
  FaceForward to the interpolated normal): 99.8%; bistro's sky alone over a
  plane: 95.2%; thirty-six quad lights (a 143-node tree) with and without
  the sky: the lit-pixel verdicts pass, 49.7% and 99.2% agreement.
- *Normal maps are cleared.* Bistro with every `normalmap` dropped from
  materials.pbrt keeps the bias (+161,164).
- *Alpha is where it arises.* Bistro with every `"texture alpha"` dropped
  from geometry.pbrt lights 591,463 pixels against pbrt's 591,292. Not
  because opaque trees block the sky on both sides -- the counts rise
  without alpha, since the cut-out quads become lit surfaces -- but
  because the counts agree to 0.03%.
- *The cutout test itself is right.* A quad whose alpha is a horizontal
  gradient 0..1 (probes/alpha_gradient.png, RGBA) over a floor, lit from
  above with the camera below the quad so only shadow rays cross it, and
  the same quad over an emissive floor seen from above so only camera rays
  do (alpha_shadow_d1, alpha_camera_d1): the pass fraction per column is
  the sRGB-decoded alpha on both sides, 92,626 against 92,713 lit pixels
  and 91,748 against 91,857 (scratchpad alpha_columns.py). A CUDA test
  (scratchpad srgb_test.cu) settled on the way that the texture unit does
  decode a one-channel 8-bit texture under the sRGB flag, which is how
  pbrt's GPU reads its alpha textures, so both renderers decode.
- *The first hits are the same.* Bistro rendered with `Film "gbuffer"` on
  both sides: every pixel hits on both, 99.3% of shading normals within
  one degree (scratch/gbuffer_compare_1016.sh). So the excess is in the
  direct lighting at the same points, and pbrt agrees with itself there:
  pbrt's CPU render of bistro_vespa_d1 lights 484,220 pixels to its GPU's
  483,217, with ours at 636,052.

What alpha changes besides the cutout is the *light*. pbrt hands a shape's
alpha texture to the area light it carries (scene.cpp, `Light::CreateArea(
..., alphaTex, ...)`), and DiffuseAreaLight is masked by it as the shape is
cut out by it: `L(p, n, uv, w, lambda)` returns zero after the one-sided
test where `AlphaMasked(Interaction(p, uv))` (lights.h), and `SampleLi`
returns no sample at all for a masked point (lights.cpp, "Check sampled
point on shape against alpha texture, if present"). `AlphaMasked` reads the
texture through the basic evaluator at the point and its uv alone, takes
one or more as never masked and zero or less as always, and in between
draws `HashFloat(intr.p()) > a` -- the hash of the point's twelve bytes,
not the ray's. The light tree is untouched (`Bounds()`'s phi has no alpha
in it, which is why pbrt's own dumped tree matched ours), and the uniform
sampler too, which is why the bias was smaller under it. render.bonsai's
AreaLight said "with no image and no alpha mask", on purpose, since
2026-09. Bistro's emissive streetlight glass declares
`"texture alpha" "alpha:textures/Emissive_StreetLight_BaseColor.png"`, a
16x16 one-channel image that is zero everywhere: in pbrt those lamps emit
nothing -- every sample of them is declined, every ray that lands on them
sees black -- and in ours they lit the street, dimly and from everywhere,
which is the signature the masks showed. The lantern and the curtains carry
partial masks of the same kind.

**The fix (render.bonsai, rng.bonsai, render_hook.cpp).** `AreaLight`
carries `alpha`, the emitting shape's texture index or -1, set per light
where the driver makes them (a shape's `prim.alpha`, a mesh light's
`m.alpha`; the emission table stays per declaration). `area_light_masked(
alpha, p, uv)` is pbrt's `AlphaMasked`, over `eval_float_basic` at a
context of the point and uv with no footprint, and `hash_float3(p)` is
pbrt's `HashFloat(Point3f)` (rng.bonsai: `hash3`, the twelve-byte Murmur
the layered BSDF already used). `area_light_l` takes the point and uv and
masks after the side test, as pbrt orders them; `light_l` and the emissive
hit's `emissive_radiance`/`emissive_contribution` carry `p` and `uv` (pbrt's
HitAreaLightWorkItem carries `p` and `uv` for exactly this), so the
emissive queue's entry grows by twenty bytes; the three CPU integrators
pass the hit's. `light_sample_li`'s DiffuseArea arm declines a masked
sample before asking the light what it emits. A probe for the rule:
probes/masked_light_d1 -- the gradient-alpha quad is the light, over a
floor, camera below.

**Measured (10-17, 23:30; apps/pbrt/scratch/alphafix-1016, gpu-optix
against `pbrt --gpu`, the least of three on each side, kernel
milliseconds; the 10-11 column is heatmap5's, whose images failed).**

| scene | spp | pbrt | ours (10-11) | ours now | kernel speedup | wall speedup | image |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bistro_cafe | 16 | 315.3 | 207.7 | 181.7 | 1.73x | 2.27x | matches |
| bistro_vespa | 16 | 327.4 | 216.9 | 188.9 | 1.73x | 2.16x | matches |
| bistro_cafe | 64 | 1269.2 | 830.6 | 727.3 | 1.75x | 1.85x | matches |
| bistro_vespa | 64 | 1309.7 | 863.1 | 751.5 | 1.74x | 1.92x | matches |

bistro_vespa_d1 at 1 spp matches too (it lit 636,052 pixels to pbrt's
483,217 before). Every image verdict of the 30-scene gate is "matches"
now but pavilion-day's 16-spp cell, the calibrated tolerance artifact.
The probe for the rule itself, probes/masked_light_d1 (the gradient-alpha
quad as the light, over a floor), lands 1.0% under pbrt in lit count
(177,461 against 179,282) and in mean (0.9903x), uniformly over the image
-- the lit fraction by column eighth runs 0.114..0.635 against pbrt's
0.115..0.639 -- with 77.8% of the shared pixels exact to 1e-3 and the
rest at ratios near 2 and 1/2 in equal numbers. Not understood yet; one
candidate is pbrt's `intr.p()` being the midpoint of the sampled point's
error interval rather than the point, so that its `SampleLi` and `L`
hash two different points when the midpoint rounds away and decline a
sample both would otherwise have taken, but that would make pbrt the
darker side. Left as the open detail it is: the scenes pass.

**Tooling found on the way.** `convert_scene.sh`'s stamp keys on the
scene file, not on what it includes: editing an `Include`d file leaves the
cached conversion in place, and one probe rendered a stale scene on our
side against a fresh one on pbrt's (a many-light probe whose quads faced
up in the cached copy). Delete `apps/pbrt/scenes/converted/<dir>/<scene>.txt*`
by hand after editing an include, or hash the includes into the stamp (a
debt). `check_differentials.sh` aborts in our `--print-differentials`
(a host buffer whose size was never given) -- rot since the GPU work, a
debt. scene_dump refuses the orthographic camera, so probes use
perspective ones.

### The megakernel's 1.5x since 10-02: not the driver, not the calls (10-15 to 10-18)

The compare of 10-15 found gpu-optix-mega 1.5x to 1.8x slower than on
10-02 (killeroo-simple at 64 spp: 306 ms then, 459 ms now) while pbrt and
gpu-optix got faster, and left the driver's closest-hit cost of 10-07 as
the first suspect. It is not the driver: the compiler of 85247b46 (10-02,
10:35, the last commit before that compare's build) rebuilt in a worktree
and run with its own renderer under today's driver renders the cell in
298 ms (apps/pbrt/scratch/mega-old-1015). So the slowdown is in the tree,
compiler or program, between 85247b46 and 6a36ceb1.

The PTX of the two binaries (`strings` on the compare's render.out; the
device module is embedded as text) names one structural difference. The
10-02 module has no `.func` at all -- every device function folded into
the programs, as CodeGen_PTX::finish means it -- and its VolPath raygen
is 170k lines; the current module has 24 `.func` definitions, the texture
graph's `[[noinline]]` levels eval_float_1/2 and eval_spectrum_1/2 (one
per integrator variant), and the VolPath raygen, 606k lines, holds 378
`call eval_float_2` and 70 `call eval_spectrum_2` -- the root evaluator
inlined at every texture read of every material arm, each composite arm a
real call. The texture graph (41e07971) landed at 23:57 on 10-02, after
the last megakernel measurement at 11:01, and its `[[noinline]]` levels
exist so the GPU build does not explode (above, "The GPU build ran out of
memory"); the wavefront never pays them on its Basic kernels since the
evaluator split of 10-09, but a megakernel inlines every arm into one
raygen. OptiX's continuation stack for that raygen is 768 bytes a thread
(BONSAI_OPTIX_STATS). A plausible cause, and wrong: two variants of the
renderer, built in the wt-bisect worktree with HEAD's compiler
(scratch/compile_schedule.sh compiles a schedule without rendering, so
the CPU work could run while another session held the card) and run on
the same cell, say so.

| renderer | `.func` | calls in the VolPath raygen | raygen PTX lines | kernel ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HEAD (6a36ceb1) | 24 | 448 | 606k | 459 |
| A: the root's composite arms return zero (no calls, no inlined leaves) | 0 | 0 | 592k | 468 |
| B: the calls kept, the callees made trivial | 8 | 1120 | 603k | 460 |
| 10-02 (85247b46) | 0 | 0 | 170k | 298 |

The call sites cost nothing measurable; nor does their stack. (A first
variant that inlined the leaves at every site instead was killed after
41 minutes at 5 GB in the backend -- the explosion the levels were made
to prevent, confirmed.) What the comparison does show is that the
raygen is 3.6x the PTX it was, with the calls accounting for little of
it, and that the any-hit and intersection programs beside it grew from
2.6k and 2.1k lines to 6.7k and 5.9k -- the shapes of 10-03 (cylinder,
patch, curve) and the alpha path -- while the closest-hit shrank from
111 to 47 lines (the 10-08 slimming). OptiX compiles a pipeline's
programs together, so a fat intersection program is not free to a raygen
even on a scene that runs it on one sphere.

A `git bisect run` over the 210 commits between (scratch/mega_bisect_run.sh:
a step builds the commit's compiler in the wt-bisect worktree, renders the
cell with that commit's own renderer and driver through its own
gpu_compare.sh, and answers good under 380 ms, bad over, skip when the
build or the render fails) is the honest instrument, run between the
other sessions' holds on the card. Its first run was not honest: after a
checkout that changed 44 compiler sources, make compiled nothing, and
the step measured 10-03's renderer under 10-07's compiler (the build log
shows no "Building CXX" line). Every step now builds from clean and
refuses one that compiled fewer than ten objects. The clean run, eight
steps, killeroo-simple at 64 spp, two renders a step, the least:

| commit | date | what landed | kernel ms | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 85247b46 | 10-02 10:35 | (the 10-02 compare's compiler) | 298 | good |
| cbee9449 | 10-03 08:37 | the bilinear patch | 302 | good |
| cc0095cf | 10-03 15:05 | coating textures, edge threading, spectral eta, FlatBuffer scenes, direct-descent skip, OptiX tmin, grid media, sphere quadric, read-only externs, three samplers (10-03 09:16-15:05) | 338 | good |
| 556acfc4 | 10-03 18:15 | foreign types, the nanovdb medium, spectrum reflectance | 360 | good |
| f9fb6edd | 10-03 18:37 | point and spot lights | 358 | good |
| **3206864a** | 10-03 20:27 | **subsurface scattering** | **428** | **bad** |
| c886960e | 10-03 20:36 | the film's crop window | 425 | bad |
| fc3d3f52 | 10-03 23:14 | the cylinder, sinh, the hair material | 455 | bad |
| 180b1319 | 10-07 | (the 10-07 matrix) | 458 | bad |
| 6a36ceb1 | 10-15 | HEAD | 459 | bad |

The first bad commit is the subsurface material (3206864a): seventy of
the hundred and sixty milliseconds, on a scene with no subsurface
material in it, from the probe walk, the BSSRDF table and the exit
shading compiled into the one raygen. The rest is the same thing in
smaller steps -- the morning's shapes, media and samplers +36, the
foreign types and the nanovdb medium +21, the cylinder and the hair
material +30 -- and nothing since 10-07 (+1). This is what a megakernel
is: every arm of the program in one kernel, paid in registers, stack and
instruction cache by every ray whether or not the scene reaches the arm
(Laine, Karras and Aila, "Megakernels Considered Harmful", HPG 2013,
which is pbrt's reason for the wavefront). The wavefront schedules never
paid it, their kernels being per stage and per arm and the unreached ones
never launched, which is why gpu-optix got faster over the same commits.

**The fix is the schedule's, and what it would recover (10-18).** The
answer a schedule has is the one gpu-optix already uses for its own pixel
loop and its shadow drain: copy the loop per value of a scene flag --
`render[VolPath].specialize(film_visible_surface)`,
`render.specialize(shadow, have_media)` -- so that the host dispatches
once and the scene without the feature runs a raygen with none of its
code. Written for the megakernel as `render[VolPath].specialize(
have_subsurface)` it does not compile: "render has no parameter
have_subsurface". `have_media` and `film_visible_surface` are parameters
of `render`; `have_subsurface` is a field of the VolPath variant of the
`integrator` parameter, bound by the arm that calls `li_vol_path`, and
the loop form of specialize names parameters. What the specialization
would buy was measured instead with the flags wired off in the arm
(scratch variants in the wt-bisect worktree, HEAD's compiler,
killeroo-simple at 64 spp, the least of three; the images match pbrt's):

| renderer | VolPath raygen PTX lines | kernel ms |
|---|---|---|
| HEAD | 606k | 459 |
| the subsurface flag false (what `specialize(have_subsurface)` makes for this scene) | 509k | 378 |
| the subsurface and media flags false (`specialize(have_media)` too) | 218k | 346 |
| 10-02 (85247b46) | 170k | 298 |

Subsurface is 81 ms of the 161 lost and the media code another 31; the
two flags together would give the megakernel back 113 of them, with its
raygen at a third of its text, and the 48 that remain are the shapes
and materials of 10-03 (the cylinder, the quadric sphere, the patch, the
hair, the spectral eta) that every scene's megakernel carries whether or
not it holds one -- the growth the wavefront's `specialize(material)` and
`specialize(evaluator)` keep out of its kernels, and which a megakernel
has no way to shed short of a copy per material set. Two ways to make the
first two flags schedulable, for the user to choose between: make
`have_subsurface` a parameter of `render` beside `have_media` (pbrt holds
all three as members of its WavefrontPathIntegrator, read off the scene at
construction, so the program is no less pbrt's for it; the Integrator
variant loses the field and the driver passes it as it passes
`have_media`), or teach the loop form of specialize to name a value the
integrator's arm binds from the parameter's payload (a uniform of the
launch like any parameter, one indirection away). Neither was done
tonight: the one is a program restructuring and the other a compiler
extension, each the user's to approve. The wavefront schedules are
untouched by either.

## The field form of specialize, and the megakernel per scene flag (10-18)

The user's rulings of 10-18 on the report above: a scene pbrt's own two
renderers disagree on more than we disagree with pbrt is rendered
correctly by us, so pavilion-day is fine and the heatmap is to be redone;
the megakernel needs more specialization, and the syntax for the flag the
integrator's arm carries is `render[VolPath].specialize(VolPath::
have_subsurface)` -- "to tell the compiler where to look for that
boolean" -- rather than `li_vol_path.specialize(have_subsurface)`, which
would be the same condition but could not unswitch the loop all the way
out of the renderer; and does the wavefront need the same?

**The compiler (9c823901).** The whole-function specialize names a
parameter of the function and copies its loops per variant of the
parameter's type or per value of a bool; `have_subsurface` is neither, it
is a field of the VolPath arm of `integrator`, bound by the match in
`integrator_li`, which the inliner has long since put inside the pixel
loop. The field form names it through its arm. What it does, in the terms
of SSA/Specialize.cpp: the parameter is found as the one whose variant
type has an arm `VolPath`; the loops copied are that arm's -- the copies
`render.specialize(integrator)` made, `p!VolPath`, which is why the field
form is written after it and on it (an error otherwise, saying what to
write first) -- and the copies are `False` and `True` as a bool
parameter's are. An arm's fields are stored in the payload's 32-bit words
at their byte offsets (Lower/WordStorage.h: C's rule), a bool as one
byte, and Lower/ADTs.cpp now records each inline arm's fields and offsets
beside the storage it already recorded (ir::Program::AdtStorage::
fields_of). The loop's block reads the byte -- `((words[k] >> shift) &
0xff) != 0`, the read the match lowering makes of the binding -- and
dispatches on it to the two selectors; each copy's value of the parameter
is the given one with the arm's tag and that byte of its payload set to
the copy's value (force_fixed_field: the word masked and or-ed, the words
rebuilt lane by lane), so that every read of the field, wherever inlining
put it, reads the constant as the match reads the tag; and a callee handed
the value is copied with the field fixed as it is copied with a tag fixed.
The fold is then two rules and one step: the copy's struct folds into its
reads (the LoadField rule, as for the tag); the pass folds the reads of the
words it built at a constant word (fold_forced_words); and the byte taken
out of the forced word folds to the constant by a known-bits rule new to
the simplifier -- what is known of an unsigned scalar's bits through and,
or and constant shifts, a result every bit of which is known being the
constant -- which also folds two goldens' constants (`(k & 3) & 0`, `1 <<
56`). Tests at the ssa, ptx and execution levels (specialize-field: under
a GPU bind the arm's kernel becomes two, neither reading the byte, one
doubling), and three errors by name: a field that is not a bool, an arm no
parameter has, the directive before the arm's loop exists.

**A rule tried and taken out.** The natural general rule, "a lane of a
vector built from its lanes is the lane", `extract_idx(make_struct(a, b),
1) = b`, folded the field too -- and 20 goldens with it, one from 622
lines to 4,198: SSA/SortRecursion.cpp recognizes a gang's run of calls by
its arguments being the lanes of one vector (`lane_of`: `extract_idx(v,
k)` for the k-th call), and with the lanes folded to the scalars they were
built from, the run of a vectorized traversal was no longer a gang's and
took Embree's scalar peel-and-insert chain in place of the lane sort. So
the fold is the specialize pass's own, on the words it built, and the
simplifier's ExtractIdx case says why. The rtq schedules are untouched;
the suite's 1684 tests pass.

**The schedules, and what they give back.** gpu-optix-mega and
gpu-optix-mega-ser gain, after `render.specialize(integrator)`:

    render[VolPath].specialize(have_media);
    render[VolPath].specialize(VolPath::have_subsurface);

so the volpath pixel loop is four raygens, one per pair of flags, and the
host launches the scene's. Their PTX (`strings -n 6 render.out`), against
the one raygen of 606,298 lines before: `p$VolPath$False$False` 219,744
lines (no media, no subsurface: the wired variant of 10-18 had 218k),
`$False$True` 248,659, `$True$False` 512,855 (the wired "no subsurface"
had 509k), `$True$True` 612,423. Measured on the protocol's three scenes
(apps/pbrt/scratch/mega-field-1018, `gpu_compare.sh`, kernel ms, the
least of three; the 10-15 columns are REPORT's table of that day):

| scene | spp | pbrt | mega 10-15 | mega now | mega over pbrt | mega-ser 10-15 | mega-ser now | mega-ser over pbrt |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| killeroo-simple | 16 | 49.5 | 116.2 | 88.3 | 0.56x | 73.4 | 49.3 | 1.00x |
| killeroo-gold | 16 | 149.4 | 317.4 | 183.2 | 0.82x | 266.4 | 159.6 | 0.94x |
| book | 16 | 152.8 | 338.8 | 240.9 | 0.63x | 277.7 | 210.1 | 0.73x |
| killeroo-simple | 64 | 198.0 | 459.5 | 349.8 | 0.57x | 298.2 | 197.8 | 1.00x |
| killeroo-gold | 64 | 597.6 | 1259.2 | 736.1 | 0.81x | 1073.4 | 652.2 | 0.92x |
| book | 64 | 617.0 | 1365.1 | 1001.1 | 0.62x | 1126.9 | 837.2 | 0.74x |

Every image matches pbrt's. The plain megakernel is 1.24x to 1.71x faster
than on 10-15 and the sorted one 1.27x to 1.66x; killeroo-simple at 64 spp
is 349.8 ms where the wired variant predicted 346 and 10-02's compiler
renders 298, so the 52 ms left are the shapes and materials of 10-03 that
every megakernel carries and no scene flag names. The sorted megakernel is
at pbrt's kernel time on killeroo-simple (1.00x at both counts; 2.23x and
1.31x on wall, where pbrt's process pays its fixed costs) and within 8% on
killeroo-gold; book, the scene with an interior node in its light tree and
the widest mix of materials, is the one still a quarter behind.

**The wavefront does not need it.** pbrt's wavefront keeps `haveSubsurface`
a run-time member: GenerateRaySamples branches on it per ray for the
dimension and the three extra draws (wavefront/samples.cpp:40, :58), the
subsurface kernels -- the BSSRDF evaluation, the random-hit raygen, the
out-scattering, the second shadow pass -- are their own launches, made
only when it is true (integrator.cpp:245, subsurface.cpp:19), and every
material kernel tests `w.material->HasSubsurfaceScattering()` per hit, a
tag dispatch over per-material constants, before pushing onto the BSSRDF
queue (surfscatter.cpp:227). gpu-optix has the same shape, and tighter:
the draws' branch is pbrt's; the four subsurface drains are the
`bssrdfs`, `probes`, `exits` and `exit_shadow` queues' kernels, gated off
by the owner's flag (SSA/GateDrains.h); and the material kernels are one
per material arm, in which `material_subsurface(material)` folds to
nothing for a material that is not subsurface, so the push is compiled
into the subsurface material's kernel alone where pbrt's dispatch sits in
each. Nothing of the wavefront's hot kernels carries subsurface code a
scene does not use, which is why it got faster over the commits that
slowed the megakernel.

**pavilion-day, and the rule as tooling (9bef802f).** gpu_compare.sh
renders pbrt on the CPU once per failing cell, untimed, at the cell's
count, by `volpath` with the scene's integrator parameters -- what the
wavefront runs whatever the scene names -- and compare_gbuffer.py holds
each failed check against pbrt's own figure for it (`--pbrt-spread`): the
lit-pixel gap against the gap between pbrt's two renders, the mean's
distance from one against theirs. On heatmap5's pavilion-day at 16 spp
ours is 2,058 lit pixels from pbrt --gpu where pbrt's CPU render is 5,529
from it, and the cell reads `ok: within pbrt's own disagreement`. Seven
seconds of wall per failing cell, three minutes of CPU.

## The probe walk's material handed undefined: every subsurface scene hung, every media scene's shadow rays on undefined wavelengths, since 10-11 (10-18)

**Found.** The 30-scene heatmap of 10-18 hung at its eleventh scene,
`head` at 16 spp: the renderer at 100% of the GPU for twenty minutes
where heatmap5's binary (10-11, 10:27) renders the cell in 0.096 s. The
binaries kept from the days between date it without a build: every
wavefront binary from compare-out-step1 (10-11, 15:31) on has a
`__raygen__probes` of 98 PTX lines where heatmap5's is 9,190, so the
regression is 28bd4aac or e07e53b4, the two commits between those builds,
and no later one. The 98-line raygen reads the probe's two points off the
queue, builds the segment once, and then `optixTrace; if hit, trace again`
with the same origin and direction in the same registers -- the walk's hit
handling, its reservoir and its loop-carried state are gone, so a probe
that hits anything traces forever. It is not the hit-continuation split
(`BONSAI_EXPLAIN_HIT_CONTINUATIONS=1`: "the raygen over `probes!False`
keeps its continuation: two calls on the way to the trace, `vol_probe!
False`'s and `trace`'s, go on after they return", and the closest-hit
programs beside the raygen are the 46-line generic ones in both binaries),
and the final SSA of `vol_probe_step` is right: the loop header
`vol_probe_step!loop(o, o_error, o_n, n_hits, steps, kept)` carries its
six changing values and the back edge passes `surf.p`, the error, the
normal, the count, `steps + 1` and the reservoir's pick.

**The cause.** The probes drain's call reads, in the final SSA,

    call vol_probe!False(p0, p1, bssrdf, medium, camera, spp_scale, prim, (i32)undef, entry, ...)

The eighth argument is `mat`, the material the walk compares every hit
against (`hit_prim.material == mat`, `vol_probe_step`). e07e53b4 made a
drain hand `undef` for what its callee never reads, as the entry stores
nothing for it, and the read analysis (SSA/Analysis.cpp, read_paths)
reported `mat` unread: `vol_probe` hands it to `vol_probe_step` and reads
it nowhere else, and inside `vol_probe_step` -- a loop since
`vol_probe_step.loopify()` -- `mat` is one of the parameters the loop does
not carry (`p1`, `mat`, `rng` are the same at every step), which the loop
header names without taking it as an argument and the loop's blocks pass
on under the name. The analysis keyed a reference to an argument by the
block it appears in, and no block of the loop declares `mat`, so the reads
of the name stopped at the loop's blocks and never reached the entry's
parameter. LLVM is then free to take `icmp eq %material, undef` and the
branch on it as it likes, and it took the hit path for unreachable: the
whole continuation after the trace went, the header's phis folded to their
initial values, and what remained is the raygen above. The same blind spot
was met and fixed for the contention analysis on 10-15 (43d8905a,
Origins::binding_block: "a loop header made by loopify() names the
function's parameters it does not carry without taking them as
arguments"); the read analysis had it too.

**Not the only victim.** Every `undef` the broken renderer's drains hand,
read off its final SSA against the callees' parameters: `mat` to
vol_probe and vol_subsurface; `lambda` to shadow_contribution and
exit_shadow_contribution -- the wavelengths the transmittance walk
(`vol_shadow_track`, loopified, `lambda` uncarried) reads at every step in
a scene with media, so the shadow rays of every media scene have been
traced on undefined wavelengths since 10-11 as well, in whatever way
LLVM chose to read that; `r_l`, `specular_bounce` and `prev_ctx` to the
material kernels and `uc`, `visible` and `path_lambda` down the
subsurface chain, which those callees indeed never read and which stay
unstored. The scenes without a subsurface material or a medium -- the
protocol's three, the bistros, the probe scenes, everything compared
since 10-11 -- were never exposed, which is how it lived a week.

**The fix (b6b09dc9).** read_paths keys a reference to a name the block
does not take by the nearest block above that takes it, up the dominator
tree -- the entry's parameter in the end -- as the contention analysis
resolves such a name. Tests: ssa/entry-reads-loop-named (a recursion made
a loop whose header does not carry `k`, handed by the drained function and
read inside the loop alone: the hits queue stores `hits_k` and the drain
hands it, `@30 = hits_k[hits]`, where it handed `undef`) and
correctness/llvm/entry-reads-loop-named (each pixel decays its hit by its
own k three times a bounce; 1.375 for pixel 0 is 0.125 + 0.375 + 0.875).
No other golden moves: nothing else in the suite had the shape. The
renderer's probe raygen is 9,117 PTX lines again and the shadow raygens
of a media scene 22,235 against the broken binary's 19,899
(apps/pbrt/scratch/probe-fix-1018). On the card, the evening of 10-18,
with that binary at 16 spp: head renders -- in a tenth of a second where
the broken renderer never returned -- and its image matches pbrt's,
dragon_10's matches, and explosion's, the media scene whose shadow rays
had the undefined wavelengths, matches (the three verdicts `ok: the image
matches pbrt`, same directory). The timings of the three are the
30-scene heatmap's, rerun with this compiler (REPORT.md), not this
check's one render each.

**What it says about the gate.** The 30-scene heatmap is the gate
(REPORT.md), and it is the run that found this; the compares in between
ran on scenes that could not. A compiler change to the deferral -- what
an entry stores, what a drain hands -- wants the heatmap, or at least
head and a media scene, before it is called measured.

## A pixel that is not a number passed the image check: kroken and watercolor at 128 spp, since 10-07 (10-18)

**Found.** The 128-spp row of kroken/camera-1 in the 10-18 heatmap reads
`mean 0.355477 vs nan (nanx)` and the verdict `ok: the image matches
pbrt`. It read so in heatmap2 (10-07), heatmap3, heatmap4 and heatmap5
too, and so did watercolor/camera-1's: three pixels, the same three in
every run -- kroken (592, 374), watercolor (473, 287) and (473, 415) --
are NaN in all three channels at 128 spp and finite at 16 and 64, so one
sample of each pixel between the 65th and the 128th is where a NaN is
made (the three are deterministic: the same sampler streams every run).
pbrt's pixels there are ordinary (0.54, 0.41, 0.23), and pbrt's film
`CHECK(!L.HasNaNs())`s what reaches it (film.cpp), so pbrt makes no such
sample: the NaN is ours.

**Why the check let it through.** compare_gbuffer.py summed every pixel
into the mean, one NaN made the mean NaN, and NaN is within every
tolerance because it compares false against all of them: `abs(ratio -
1) > 0.02` is False for NaN. The lit-pixel count did not see it either
(`v > 0` is False for NaN, so the pixel counted as unlit on our side,
one pixel of a 2,210-pixel allowance).

**The harness now (compare_gbuffer.py, README.md).** A pixel that is not
finite on either side is counted apart and left out of the totals, so
the mean is the mean of the finite pixels; one of ours fails the cell
(`FAILED: 1 pixels here are not finite (NaN or infinite), the first at
(592, 374); pbrt's film admits none`), and no disagreement of pbrt's
with itself covers it under the spread rule. The 10-18 heatmap's kroken
row at 128 spp is a failure under this rule (its mean, over the finite
pixels, is 0.871x: the regression of the section below), and
watercolor's 128-spp cell is too (its mean is right).

**The marking, revised 10-24.** The user: a cell that differs from pbrt by
less than pbrt's two renderers differ from each other is not marked. One
NaN pixel in 2.2 million at 128 spp (kroken), two and ten in 2.8 million
(watercolor at 128 and 256) are smaller disagreements than pbrt's own
lit-pixel gaps on those cells (115 and 11), and the finite pixels match
(0.99976x and 0.99997x of pbrt's mean). So compare_gbuffer.py no longer
fails an image for a non-finite pixel of ours; each counts as one
lit-pixel disagreement against the usual allowance (lit_gap_check: a
pixel we got wrong where pbrt wrote a value), named in every verdict so
it is never hidden, and thousands of them still fail the cell.
`recompare.py OUT_DIR` re-derives a table's verdicts from the images a
run kept; on compare-out-heatmap7 (120 rows, 10-24 10:14-10:19, under
the lock) exactly those three verdicts changed, FAILED to
`ok: the image matches pbrt; N pixels here are not finite ... counted as
lit-pixel disagreements`, and `plots/pbrt-gpu-heatmap.pdf` has no hatched
cell. The NaN is still ours and still open, below.

**The NaN itself: open.** What the two scenes share is their author and
their lighting: an `infinite` light through a `portal` (kroken's one
window, lights.pbrt; watercolor's two, lights-with-windowglass.pbrt),
textured interiors, `volpath` at a depth of 15, and no other scene of
the thirty has a portal. The portal light's direction from a uv
(render.bonsai, `PortalUV`: `tan(alpha)`, `tan(beta)` at the edges of a
portal, where pbrt clamps) and the equal-area square-to-sphere mapping
are where a direction can come out non-finite, and the pixel's 128
samples can be replayed one at a time once the renderer has a
`--pixel` switch (it has none; scene_dump's pbrt side renders a crop by
`--cropwindow`). To do, after the regression below.

## kroken's invisible sun: the alpha mask of 10-17 silenced a light pbrt keeps (10-18)

**Found.** The 10-18 heatmap's kroken/camera-1 is 0.871x pbrt's mean at
16 and 64 spp and lights 6,295 fewer pixels at 16, where it matched in
every heatmap before (0.9968x in heatmap3, 4 and 5); pbrt's own spread
covers none of it (pbrt's CPU render is 1.003x its GPU one). The
darkening is everywhere and strongest low in the frame -- 0.80 of pbrt
in the floor's quarter, 0.97 in the ceiling's. Rendered at 16 spp with
the binaries kept since (apps/pbrt/scratch/kroken-1018): 10-11 15:31
matches (0.99683x); 10-17 22:06, the alpha-mask build, is 0.87142x, and
the two 10-18 binaries are 0.87142x to the digit. The one change to the
lights between is b911a8a0, the area light masked by its shape's alpha.

**The cause.** kroken's sun (lights.pbrt) is

    AreaLightSource "diffuse" "blackbody L" 6500 "float scale" 50
    Shape "sphere" "float radius" 90 "float alpha" 0

a sphere light whose shape has a constant alpha of zero, and pbrt makes a
special case of exactly that (DiffuseAreaLight's constructor, lights.cpp):
"Special case handling for area lights with constant zero-valued alpha
textures to allow invisible area lights: we will null out the alpha
texture below so that as far as the DiffuseAreaLight is concerned, there
is no alpha texture and the light is fully emissive. However, such lights
will never be intersected by rays (because their associated primitives
still have the alpha texture), so we mark them as DeltaPosition lights
here so that MIS isn't used for direct illumination." The constructor
types the light DeltaPosition when the alpha is a FloatConstantTexture
evaluating to zero and keeps the alpha only for a light typed Area; the
wavefront then zeroes the BSDF density for such a light's sample
(surfscatter.cpp `IsDeltaLight(light.Type()) ? 0.f : bsdf.PDF(...)`,
media.cpp, subsurface.cpp). The 10-17 change applied the mask as the
texture said, as pbrt does for every alpha but this one -- Bistro's
zero-everywhere *image* alpha is masked by both -- and kroken's sun went
out: 13% of the picture, the sunlit floor most of all. The 0.3% it was
under pbrt before 10-17 is the other half of the special case: the sun's
sample was weighed against the BSDF's density by the power heuristic
when no BSDF sample can reach an invisible light, so a sliver of its
light was lost to a strategy that never pays it back.

**The fix.** `AreaLight` carries `delta` beside `alpha` (render.bonsai);
`light_is_delta` answers it for a DiffuseArea light, so the NEE of the
surface and medium kernels divides by the light density alone, as for a
point light; and the host (render_hook.cpp, mask_light) gives a light
whose shape's alpha is a constant texture of exactly zero no alpha and
`delta` true, every other light its texture and `delta` false. The
shape's own alpha test is untouched: the sphere stays invisible to every
ray, as pbrt's does. A probe for the case, probes/invisible_light_d1 (a
sphere of alpha zero between the camera and a diffuse floor, direct
lighting only, 16 spp), matches pbrt's image -- every pixel lit on both
sides, the mean 0.981x of pbrt's, within the rule, 66% of the pixels
within a thousandth (killeroo-simple's share) -- where the unfixed
renderer rendered a black floor. kroken at 16 spp after the fix
(apps/pbrt/scratch/kroken-fix-1018): 0.99985x pbrt's mean, the lit
pixels as before, `ok: the image matches pbrt`; killeroo-simple, whose
sphere light is a visible one, unchanged (0.99998x). The 30-scene
heatmap is rerun with this renderer, at 256 spp as well
(compare-out-heatmap6; the run with the dark kroken is kept as
compare-out-heatmap6-dark). The rerun (21:13 to 00:35): 117 of 120
cells match pbrt's image, kroken at 0.9998x of pbrt's mean at every
count, pavilion-day at 16 spp by the spread rule; the three that fail
are the NaN pixels of the section above, which no earlier heatmap could
see (kroken at 128 spp, watercolor at 128 and at 256 spp, where ten
pixels are NaN). Wall speedups: 2.01x mean at 16 spp, 1.75x at 64,
1.69x at 128, 1.65x at 256; kernel 1.65x to 1.68x; the least view-0
(1.18x to 1.29x), the most killeroo-simple at 16 spp (3.13x) and
watercolor above (2.40x to 2.43x). REPORT.md, "Where it stands
(2026-10-19, 07:00)".

**Open: the probe's 1.9%.** The probe passes, but its 0.981x is not
noise, and it is worth knowing what it is before the next light-sampling
change. Mapped (scratchpad probe_map.py, kept here in words): the floor
seen *through* the sphere -- the pixels whose camera ray crosses it,
radius 0.35 half-heights about the centre -- is exact to a millionth in
99% of its pixels; a ring from 0.4 to 1.2 half-heights is where the mean
drops, to 0.955 at 0.75, and it recovers to 0.999 at the frame's edge.
In the ring the pixel's deficit is quantized: a histogram of (pbrt -
ours) in sixteenths of the pixel peaks at one and again at two, so whole
samples of the sixteen are zero in ours where pbrt's are not; and 35k
pixels go the other way by the same one sixteenth (140k go ours' way),
so pbrt loses whole samples too, at a quarter of our rate. A sample lost
is a shadow ray occluded or a light sample refused; the sphere cannot
occlude in either renderer (its alpha rejects every hit; pbrt tests
quadrics in `__intersection__quadric`, optix.cu, shadow rays included,
and ours in `trace_any`'s conjunct), the floor is the only other thing
a shadow ray can meet, and the light sampler, the cone sample and the
facing test refuse nothing for a cap sample. The 10-17 probe
(masked_light_d1) showed a cousin of it at 1 spp: ratios of exactly 2
and 1/2 on 8% of the pixels both lit. To find it: the probe at 1 spp,
where a pixel is a sample, and two variants -- the same sphere visible
(`alpha` 1), and the invisible sphere above the camera so no camera
ray crosses it -- which say whether the loss is the alpha path's, the
camera ray's or the sphere light's in general (killeroo-simple's sphere
is far and small, and matches to 0.99998x). Deferred past the heatmap,
which holds the card.

## The entry stores what it is handed: the recipes extended (10-19)

**The question.** The user's, 10-18: the deferral's entry should store
the least that reaches the drain, and bssrdfs stores 345 bytes against
pbrt's 168, the subsurface material by value among them. How does the
analysis fail, and why by value rather than by index?

**What the analysis does.** A deferral stores the callee's arguments,
less three things. The read analysis drops the leaves the callee's chain
never reads and hands `undef` for them. A field that is an address into
the record is not stored but rebuilt from the slot index. And a field
that is a pure function of other fields, of values in scope at the drain
or of constants is recomputed at the drain -- a `Recipe` (SSA/Defer.cpp):
rematerialization in Briggs, Cooper and Torczon's sense (PLDI 1992), the
entry for the register file -- with one exception for memory, a value the
pusher's own drain loaded from a record array at the slot, loaded again.

**How it failed, read off `BONSAI_EXPLAIN_DEFER=1` on the renderer.**

- *A read of memory was never a recipe.* `ss` is `materials[mat]`'s arm
  taken apart in the pusher; the recipe rule refused any read of memory,
  so its eleven scalars were stored by value, and `mat` -- also an
  argument -- was dropped as unread, since the chain reads `ss` and never
  `mat`. The analysis had no notion that the two carry the same
  information. The materials array is a parameter the owner cannot write
  (no `mut`: the type says so), so a read of it at an index the entry
  holds is as recomputable as an add -- what Chaitin et al. (1981) called
  a never-killed value and Briggs et al. rematerialize rather than spill.
  The semantics (docs/schedule-semantics.md, 4.2) had promised exactly
  this -- "a value selected from a read-only array by an index is stored
  as the index" -- and the code did not do it.
- *The slot was not a leaf.* The index field has no parameter, so the
  recipe rule's "another field's value at this push" never matched it: a
  pure function of the slot -- the pixel's column and row from the
  sample's index, which pbrt's kernels compute from pixelIndex -- was
  stored, in rays and in every queue after it (explain: "pixel_x: stored:
  one value down the chain, but computed inside the producer's
  iteration").
- *Origins stopped at a drain's call.* A value that reaches the push as
  a parameter of the pushing function was followed to the owner's calls
  (routes_to) only for the reload shape; a round-uniform or a slot
  function arriving that way was "a value only the pusher has". And with
  a queue split by material, the 22 material kernels are 22 drain loops,
  each handing the pusher its own reload of the same hits field: "differs
  between calls (@4385 of hits!False!Basic!CoatedConductor!run at one
  call and @6218 of hits!False!Universal!ThinDielectric!run at the call
  in ...)" for `medium`, `prim`, `mat`, `wave`, `depth`, `pixel_x`,
  `pixel_y`, `r_u`, `surf`. Twenty-two loads of one field are one value
  by any sensible account, and the analysis demanded one definition.
- *A budget stood for a cost model.* `budget = 16` instructions a recipe
  might take, which would have refused the material's rebuild (a struct
  of eleven from a load) had the rule above admitted it.
- *The program handed a placeholder.* The probe walk's reservoir
  started as the entry's own surface, eleven vectors carried through
  bssrdfs and probes to be the value of `kept` before the first hit,
  where pbrt's WeightedReservoirSampler starts empty.

**The fix (SSA/Defer.cpp, render.bonsai).** One recipe rule at both
levels, the pusher's and the owner's: a leaf is a constant, a stored
field, *the slot* (slot_at: the index the owner's call hands, by site), a
value the drain has in scope (materialize), a cut's stable record array
at the slot (as before), or a read of memory rooted through address
arithmetic alone at a parameter the owner cannot write (read_only_rooted;
GEP and FieldPtr admitted as address ops); an argument of the pusher is
followed to the owner's calls (routes_to) and the recipe built there,
each call's value cooked on its own and all required to agree -- so the
22 drains' loads of hits' slot are each that drain's `slot_at` and agree
as the index field, and a function of the slot or a uniform survives any
number of hops. The `reloads == 0` guard that sent anything without a
reload back to the pusher's rule is gone; the budget is gone, with the
cost argument written in its place: every leaf is free (stored anyway,
the index, in scope, constant, or memory nothing writes), so a recipe
always stores less than the field it replaces, and the register
operations it costs the drain are cheaper than the store and the load
they stand in for; a cap of 1024 nodes is against a runaway expression,
not a cost. The slot group counts a recipe's reference as a read of it.
In the program, `ProbeResult.kept` is an `option`, the walk starts from
none, and `vol_probe` takes no entry surface. Tests: ssa and
correctness/llvm `defer-remat-readonly` (a row of a read-only array
stored as its index), `defer-remat-slot` (the pixel from the slot) and
`defer-remat-through-queues` (the slot function through two queues).
Built and run 10-19, 08:00: the three tests pass at both levels, and
eleven goldens moved, each read before it was blessed -- a read of a
read-only array at the slot reloaded at the drain in the two
demote-atomics-spawn tests, defer-spawn-join and spawn-then-spawn (through
two queues) and their LLVM and PTX twins; `values[7 - slot]` in
defer-split-unread; the slot-derived bools of defer-bools and the `k` of
entry-reads-loop-named recomputed. Three tests had been written on the
very field they lost and were rewritten to keep their point: defer-bools
and defer-split-unread read their per-iteration value off a `mut` array
(memory the type says may be written before the drain, which no recipe
reads), entry-reads-loop-named reads for the recomputed `k` where it read
for a stored one; and defer-remat-slot gained `drift`, a recursion handing
`x + 1`, whose entry stores `x` (routes_to refuses a caller handing
anything but its own parameter). The renderer's entries, counted array by
array off the drains' signatures (the convention of the hand counts above,
a vec3 as 12): bssrdfs 349 -> 225 bytes with the recipes alone -- pixel_x
and pixel_y out of every queue of the family, the probe's placeholder
surface (116 bytes) out of bssrdfs and probes -- probes 320 -> 184, hits
255 -> 247, exits 228 -> 220, medium_samples 223 -> 215, medium_scatters
120 -> 112; and `ss` still stored by value, for the reasons of the next
section, which takes bssrdfs to 180.

**Not yet: the cross-queue reload by position.** The hit-derived copies
every later queue carries -- wave, depth, medium, the primitive's media,
r_u -- are stored because the earlier queue's arrays are the only place
they live, and nothing says those arrays hold still until the later drain
runs. They do, within a round: hits is pushed by the trace and the medium
kernel, drained by the material kernels, and nothing pushes it again
until the next round's trace, after bssrdfs, probes and exits have
drained. With that argument made in the pass (the round structure is in
OwnedQueue: `rounds`, `round_header`, `second_pass`), a later entry can
store the earlier entry's position -- the subqueue and index, eight bytes,
or four for an unsplit queue -- and reload every hit-derived field through
the queue's array handles at the drain, as pbrt reads pixelSampleState by
pixelIndex: store-to-load forwarding through the queue, the push's store
and the drain's load of one slot (the memory-SSA form of GVN's load
elimination). It would take bssrdfs under 100 bytes.

## The material by index: a dispatch on a threaded constant, and a name reached from above (10-19)

**What still stored `ss`.** With the recipes extended, BONSAI_EXPLAIN_DEFER
still said of `ss`: "stored: differs between calls (handed @2464 ..., a
value of that function's own (defined in !then_186) that cannot be computed
before the producer loop)". Read in the kernel's SSA, @2464 is
`load_field(material_subsurface$r1341, 0)`: the material read off an
*option* -- the result of `material_subsurface(materials[mat])`, a match on
the material's tag folded into the kernel -- in a block that refers to the
option by name without taking it as an argument, the option itself a merge
of eleven arms: `make_struct<_option>(ss, true)` from the Subsurface arm,
the empty option from the ten others. Two things kept the recipe builder
from seeing through it, both general.

- *A dispatch on a constant that is an argument does not fold.* In the
  CoatedConductor kernel the tag the match dispatches on, `_t29497`, is the
  constant 2 -- the copy's own tag, which the first match's folded dispatch
  handed its arm as the constant it chose -- carried as an argument of 128
  blocks. fold_constant_dispatches asks `constant_of` of the value and sees
  an argument. So every one of the 22 material kernels compiled the
  subsurface push, each a producer of bssrdfs, and in each the option merge
  had eleven arms. pbrt's material kernels never had it:
  `HasSubsurfaceScattering` is a compile-time property of the concrete
  material.
- *A name reached from above was "unknown here".* The definitions analysis
  (SSA/Definitions.h), asked leniently about a name a block refers to
  without taking it, answered "defined here" -- by design for the rewrites
  (destination passing captures such a name for the continuation it hands
  it to) -- and the recipe builder took that for a value only the pusher
  has. The read analysis (b6b09dc9) and the contention analysis (43d8905a)
  had each met the same blind spot and each built a walk to the binding
  block of its own.

**The fixes (SSA/Simplify.cpp, SSA/Definitions.cpp, SSA/CodeGen_Stmt.cpp).**
(1) substitute_threaded_arguments: an argument every predecessor hands,
through however many blocks, one constant is that constant, at every use --
the trivial phi of Braun et al., "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA
Form" (CC 2013, 3.1), which the minimal SSA of Cytron et al. (TOPLAS 1991)
never builds and this form's threading makes freely -- and simplify()
repeats rules, substitution, dispatch folding and edge threading while any
of them moved. (2) Definitions gains a `bound` mode: with `lenient`, a name
reached from above resolves at the nearest block above that binds it (the
walk the two analyses had made their own, now the analysis's), for the
readers that want the value behind a name wherever it is read -- the
simplifier's common-subexpression key and the rule above, the deferral's
recipe builder -- while the rewrites keep "unknown here". Making it brought
out a latent flaw: resolving a loop header's argument reaches, through the
body, a merge of that argument with a constant; the edge back to the header
was skipped as "carried round unchanged", the merge answered with the
constant alone -- an answer good only inside that question -- and the
answer was memoized. tests/bonsai/ssa/cse-rebound-argument, the test
written for the rebinding, caught it the moment the walk exposed it (`walk`
returned 0). Now an answer reached by skipping an edge to an argument not
this one is provisional, never memoized, and the walk's answer is as
provisional as the binding's. (3) The SSA printer names a value computed
before a loop in the loop's condition where it inlined its whole expression
(inline_expr, as its own comment had promised).

**What moved.** 5 goldens for the constant rule: merge-variant-fold, whose
fold the test had always asked for and never got (the tag was carried as an
argument of its own; a run-level twin added), vectorize-switch-constant-
merge, whose branch now folds before the gang is linearized, and two mask
stores of a `let`-bound false. 32 for the bound key, read with temporaries
normalized: common subexpressions the key had missed -- a tree row's
address computed twice, a 75-line slab test computed twice in
arena-rows-vectorized -- and the renumbering that follows; the LLVM
goldens' instruction mixes identical or smaller, every prefetch count
unchanged. 1626 tests pass. In the renderer, bssrdfs has 2 producers, the
two Subsurface kernels, and `ss` is "recomputed at the drain from mat":
bssrdfs 349 -> 180 bytes in 22 arrays against pbrt's 168, probes 184
against pbrt's 332.

**Two things tried and withdrawn, for the record.** Pointing every argument
at the instruction or parameter it is threaded from -- the whole trivial
phi -- first miscompiled: a call's continuation read a value of the
producer loop's by name, and the deferral's drain is a function of its own.
In this form the arguments are also the scopes, so an instruction is in
scope only where every path back runs over jumps and dispatches; restricted
so, it still moved 88 goldens and lost the any-hit traversal's arm
prefetches (73 to 33 in the LLVM golden), since the mirror-loads and
linearize passes key on the threaded form, a loaded value carried by
argument being one read of memory. And resolving names at their binding for
every lenient reader turned destination passing more eager in
demote-atomics-loopify -- `series` was handed `&out[i]` for its `acc` --
and the atomic the test is about stayed (PTX atomics 3 -> 6). Hence the
constant alone, and the mode.

**Open.** The hit-derived copies (medium, prim's media, mat, surf.p,
hit.ns, ctx, beta, r_u, depth, wave, eta_scale, lam) stay stored: the
cross-queue reload by position of the section above. The 20 kernels that
no longer push to bssrdfs are smaller for it.

## The constant rule's first day: a provisional answer memoized, and every coated-diffuse surface black (10-19, 11:25-13:35)

**What the card said.** The GPU check of the three scenes at 16 spp, in
nacho-9b's window at 11:22: head matches (0.99951x, as heatmap6 had it);
dragon_10 is 0.288x pbrt's mean; killeroo-simple has 13,915 pixels lit by
pbrt and unlit here, a gap where 488 is allowed, with the mean still 0.996x.
The images say what the numbers do not: in killeroo-simple the floor and
the sphere light match and both killeroos render black with the coat's
highlight on them; in dragon_10 the subsurface dragon is right and the
floor and background are dark. The dark surfaces are the coateddiffuse
ones, both scenes, and head has none. The layered BxDF's walk contributed
nothing; only the entrance interface's reflection, which needs no walk,
survived. The 16 spp heatmap row was not run. All 76 GPU tests pass (the
first run showed seven failures, every one `clang++: not found`: ctest was
run outside the conda env; inside it they pass).

**Where the compilers agreed.** The renderer's SSA was dumped by the old
compiler (c9025e99, built in a worktree) and the new one, post-schedule
and final, and compared function by function with temporaries normalized,
with a renaming-aware canonical form, and with a structural hash of every
operand (the scratchpad's extract_func, canon_func, semdiff): the
CoatedDiffuse kernel differed from the Diffuse one in nothing that the
intended changes do not explain, the router pushed the same entry, the
drain read the same fields, the light sampler was identical, and the walk
functions themselves -- called with continuations, so printed in no dump
-- compile to the same answers on `-b llvm` (correctness/llvm/coated-
diffuse with --fast-math: identical output from both compilers). Every
comparison said the compilers agree. One of them had to be too coarse, and
reading harder would not have said which.

**Where they disagreed.** The scalar schedule on the CPU reproduces it:
killeroo-simple at 4 spp against heatmap6's pbrt, the old compiler leaves
sampling noise (18,435 unlit pixels, 327 of them with every neighbour
unlit), the new one a region (34,290 and 10,122), the killeroos black in
the image. No queues, no deferral, the same render.bonsai: the compiler,
and not the recipes. Four variant compilers, each a worktree, each run on
that reproduction in under two minutes: the old compiler with only the new
CodeGen_Stmt.cpp is fine, the new compiler with the old one is broken; the
new compiler with the bound key reverted is broken; the new compiler with
substitute_threaded_arguments returning false is fine. The constant rule.

**The flaw, read off the one function that showed it.** Of the 163
functions in the scalar dump, three differ; one difference is an argument
turned constant, and it is in `bvh_descend`, the light tree's descent: the
latch hands the header `(bool)1` for `done` where it handed `done`. The
descent sets `done` in the leaf arm and, inside the interior arm, in the
arm of zero importance, and leaves it as the header had it on the third
path; after promotion the merge before the latch takes `done` from the leaf
arm's edge, `true`, and from the interior arm's own merge of `true` with
the header's carried `done`. The definitions analysis, asked first about a
block inside the interior arm, followed the name to the header, round the
latch to the outer merge, into the inner merge, and skipped the inner
merge's edge back to the header's own `done` as carried round unchanged --
answering `true`, provisionally, as the 09:00 fix had taught it. The outer
merge then saw `true` from both of its edges. The skip was one level below
it; `via_other` marked only skips at the current level; so the outer
merge's `true` was memoized, and when the rule came to ask about the
latch's own argument it read the memo and wrote the constant. With one
light in the scene the tree is one leaf and nothing shows; with two the
descent would stop at the root. In the walk the same shape -- `dead`,
`escaped`, `valid` set in nested arms and carried round otherwise -- is
what went black, by the same mechanism; its functions are in no dump, and
the scalar reproduction stands as its witness.

**The fix** (SSA/Definitions.cpp, of_argument): an answer built on a
provisional one is as provisional as it is -- after an edge's definition is
fetched, if what the edge passes is an argument whose answer is in
`provisional`, this level's answer is provisional too. The binding walk had
already done this for its own recursion; the predecessor loop had not.
With it the scalar reproduction is the old compiler's to the pixel
(18,435 and 327), and the suite is 1626 of 1626 with no golden moved: the
flaw lived in no test.

**Why no test caught it, and the tests now.** The suite's layered BxDF
test runs on the LLVM backend, whose direct lowering asks the analysis in
another order and never met the flaw; the renderer compiles through the
C++ backend's statement lowering, which asks in the order that does. So
the shape has three tests: tests/bonsai/ssa/constant-argument-provisional
reads the latch's jump in the printed form (it showed `done = true` at the
latch under the unfixed compiler); correctness/llvm/constant-argument-
provisional runs it ({5, -1, 0, 7}); and correctness/cpp/
constant_argument_provisional runs it through the C++ backend from a C++
main, on the path the renderer takes, and WRONG under the unfixed
compiler. The GPU verification of the three scenes follows in nacho-9b's
next pause; the 16 spp heatmap row after it.

## The triangle range as a set the type describes (10-19, a proposal)

**What the compiler knows and does not.** The hit program is one program
for every record of a tree, a function of the record and the primitive
index, and the record holds `base` and `holder`. For a held tree -- a
Mesh element's `tris` -- the holder is one Mesh for every record, so
everything the hit program derives from the holder alone is a constant of
the record: the arm's tag, the mesh index, the mesh row's first index and
vertex, material, alpha, media, first light. Hoisting that into the record
is partial evaluation of the hit program with the record static and the
primitive index dynamic (Jones, Gomard and Sestoft 1993; the driver fills
the derived record where it fills `base` today) and needs nothing new
from the program: it removes `prims[top]` and the mesh row from the
chain, and folds the arm's switch. It is what pbrt's TriangleMeshRecord
is, derived rather than written.

The `tris` row is the other kind. That row i of a mesh's `tris` is
`Triangle{mesh, i}` is a fact of render_hook.cpp's fill loop, in C++, and
no analysis of the program can recover what the program never states. The
10-11 proposal was a layout clause, `Mesh.tris : OptixTree by |i|
Triangle{mesh, i}`, and the user's objection stands: a language feature
for one optimization, telling the compiler in the layout what the program
should have said.

**The proposal: say it in the program, in the type.** A mesh's triangles
*are* the integers 0 to count; pbrt's Triangle is (mesh, index) and
nothing else. The program says so with a set whose elements are its own
indices, a *range*:

    | Mesh(mesh : u32, count : u32)
    ...
    Mesh(mesh, count) => map(|i : u32| triangle_geometric(Triangle{mesh, i}), 0:count),

`0:count` the value of type `set[u32]` that a `for` already ranges over,
and `map` over it the mapped set the traversal already takes
(`maps_elements`). The layout then says what it says now -- `Mesh.geometry
: OptixTree from ...`, the build input the mesh's own index buffer -- and
the compiler knows from the *types* that the tree's element i is
`triangle_geometric(Triangle{mesh, i})`: a range set has no rows, so
`stored(tris, idx)` is `Triangle{mesh, idx - base}`, arithmetic, and the
8-byte row per triangle (2.3 GB on kroken) is not stored at all. This is
how the rest of the program already speaks to the compiler: `mut` says
what may be written, `reduce(+)` what is accumulated, `option` what may
be absent, `[[packed]]` and `inline`/`tagged_index` how a thing is laid
out -- a fact in a type, read by every pass, not a hint beside one
optimization. A range is the oldest set there is (APL's iota, Halide's
RDom, ISPC's foreach), and it belongs in the language whether or not the
hit chain existed. What the compiler would need: a range as a set value
in the frontend and IR (the loop form has the parser's syntax already),
`take_apart`/`bind_elements` (Lower/Trees.cpp) accepting a mapped range
as a tree's element set, and the derived record above. Asked for here;
nothing of it is built.

## The CPU wavefront with vectorized drains (10-20)

The ask (10-19, 23:15): get the CPU packet schedule to work, or at the
least make a vectorized CPU wavefront that beats the regular CPU
wavefront schedule. The regular one is `schedules/wavefront-volpath.bonsai`:
pbrt's wavefront for volpath on the CPU, a queue per kernel (camera rays,
the hits split by material, shadow rays, escaped rays, emissive hits,
medium samples and scatters), each drained after the other every bounce,
the drains running one entry at a time on every CPU thread. The new one
is `schedules/wavefront-volpath-packet.bonsai`: the same queues in the
same order, with each drain's loop split by sixteen and vectorized, so
that sixteen consecutive entries run as one gang on the AVX-512 lanes and
the trace drain's traversal is a sixteen-ray packet (`sort` then
`loopify(64)`, the packet order of item 6). The medium-sample and shadow
drains stay scalar: they call the foreign NanoVDB code, which has no gang
form. Nothing else differs between the two files, so the table below is
the drains' vectorization and nothing else.

**Seven compiler bugs stood between that file and an image**, each found
by the next compile or render of the renderer, each fixed at its cause
with an IR test, an LLVM test and an execution test against an
unscheduled twin:

1. The linearizer froze a uniform carried value of a uniform loop under a
   partial mask as if it were per lane (13da8c11, SSA/Linearize.cpp).
2. The induced storage of a queue read a gang's leaves with the scalar's
   shapes (c1d42be5, SSA/InducedStorage.cpp).
3. A split parameter's components were not found at the entry by name
   (15f1d9b0, SSA/SplitAggregates.cpp).
4. The uniformizer handed a use of a loop-defined value the block's own
   later redefinition of its name (e37a5e5a, SSA/UniformizeLoops.cpp): the
   Sobol scramble came out `v = hash ^ v` with both `v` the same value.
5. A copy of a function reused the names of its arguments (4175c22e,
   SSA/CloneFunction.cpp).
6. A gang variant of a function whose return does not depend on its
   arguments returned the scalar where the caller's continuation wanted
   the gang's shape (6e9d35bf, SSA/Vectorize.cpp).
7. The drain-gating pass read the material split's key off the drained
   kernel, which for a vectorized drain is the gang variant whose key has
   the widened type `Material$v16`; that matched no ADT storage, the
   split built no arm mask, the hits queue came out unfeedable, and the
   shadow queue kept only the medium kernel's push -- so the shadow drain
   was gated on `have_media` and, in a scene without media, never ran.
   Surfaces rendered black with the lights and the BSDF-sampled speckles
   left (78cf4c87, SSA/GateDrains.cpp; the key is read through the
   widening, tests ssa/gate-drains-gang and correctness/llvm/
   gate-drains-gang). Found by bisecting the schedule one gang drain at a
   time (only the hits drain's gang failed), then by a constant added to
   the reducer at each step of the material kernel (the kernel ran and its
   own write reached the film; what it spawned contributed nothing), then
   in the final SSA: `shadow!drain: dispatch have_media [exit, launch]`.
   `BONSAI_DEBUG_GATES=1` prints the pushes and the gates; the dump for
   the gang build said `0 masks` where the scalar build's said `1 masks,
   11 mask_alts`.

With the seventh fixed, the shadow probe and all five protocol scenes at
16 spp match pbrt under the full schedule (means within 0.15%), and the
gates of the vectorized build are the scalar build's to the bit.

**The table** (10-20, 21:12-23:26; compare.sh, both sides the best of
three, the machine otherwise idle, every one of the 24 images matching
pbrt's; render seconds, speedups over the pbrt column named):

| scene, spp | pbrt `--wavefront` (CPU) | vectorized drains | scalar drains | vectorized over scalar drains | pbrt volpath (CPU) | our `scalar` | vectorized over pbrt volpath |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| killeroo-simple, 16 | 5.50 s | 0.623 s (8.83x) | 0.600 s (9.17x) | 0.96x | 0.92 s | 0.679 s (1.35x) | 1.48x |
| killeroo-simple, 64 | 22.01 s | 1.900 s (11.58x) | 2.334 s (9.43x) | 1.23x | 3.59 s | 2.691 s (1.33x) | 1.89x |
| book, 16 | 20.01 s | 2.571 s (7.78x) | 3.193 s (6.27x) | 1.24x | 5.27 s | 3.703 s (1.42x) | 2.05x |
| book, 64 | 80.53 s | 9.125 s (8.83x) | 12.646 s (6.37x) | 1.39x | 21.11 s | 14.754 s (1.43x) | 2.31x |
| ganesha, 16 | 19.51 s | 2.877 s (6.78x) | 3.297 s (5.92x) | 1.15x | 4.14 s | 3.549 s (1.17x) | 1.44x |
| ganesha, 64 | 78.53 s | 9.516 s (8.25x) | 12.588 s (6.24x) | 1.32x | 16.21 s | 13.742 s (1.18x) | 1.70x |

Two pbrt references, because pbrt's CPU wavefront is its GPU design run
on the CPU, kernel by kernel over whole queues, and is six to twelve
times slower than our wavefronts on every cell; it is the like-for-like
algorithm the protocol asks for, and the images are checked against it,
but pbrt's ordinary CPU volpath (`VolPathIntegrator::Li`, a path to its
end per sample) is what a CPU renderer is measured against. Our `scalar`
schedule is that pattern, and beats it by 1.17x to 1.43x; the vectorized
wavefront beats it by 1.44x to 2.31x.

How to read the vectorized-over-scalar-drains column: the vectorized
drains win five cells of six, by 1.15x to 1.39x, and lose killeroo-simple
at 16 spp by 4%; on every scene the win grows with the sample count (0.96x
to 1.23x, 1.24x to 1.39x, 1.15x to 1.32x). A fit of T = a + b * spp to the
two counts of each scene puts the difference in a fixed per-frame cost:
a = 0.20 s (killeroo-simple), 0.39 s (book), 0.66 s (ganesha) for the
vectorized build against 0.02, 0.04 and 0.20 s for the scalar drains,
while the per-sample cost b is 26% to 30% lower with the gangs. The
per-sample win is the vectorization; the fixed cost is something the
vectorized build does once a frame, and is measured below.

**The audit** of the gang code (audit_gang.py over the `-b llvm` module of
the schedule, before timing): 76 gang functions, no vector integer
division, 16 i128 operations (the Sobol sampler's 64-bit multiply, per
lane), and 912 scalar libm calls -- 528 `sinf`, 352 `cosf`, 32 `tanf`,
about 57 trigonometric sites each lowered as sixteen per-lane calls, most
of them in light sampling (`light_sample_li`, 16 sites), the BSDF rho
estimate, the hit and surface geometry and the measured BSDF. A vector
lowering of the trigonometric functions (libmvec's `_ZGVeN16v_sinf`, or a
polynomial of our own as ISPC's stdlib has) is the first per-sample item
after the sort.

**Next**, in order: (1) the fixed per-frame cost of the vectorized build,
measured and removed; (2) the user's ask of 10-20 (21:15), a sort of the
rays queue before the packet traversal with the two-point key of Meister,
Boksansky, Guthe and Bittner (arXiv 2506.11273): the existing
`f.sort(g, |args| key)` on a call that `defer` sends to a queue sorts that
queue by the key before each drain -- the key computed at the push as an
extra argument of the deferred callee, so that it is a leaf of the entry,
the drain reading its entries through the sort's permutation -- with the
scene bounds the key quantizes against handed to `render` by the driver;
measured sorted against unsorted on this table, the sort's own time
inside the render time; (3) the trigonometric calls above; (4)
`packet.bonsai` itself, not retried since 09-22, and `wavefront.bonsai`,
which still fails to compile.

### The study moved onto pbrt's own structure (10-21)

The user's ruling (10-21, 00:05), told that the table above was built on
per-pixel queues: "please match PBRT's wavefront and then vectorize it,
and use that as a guiding schedule because I want to just investigate the
impact of vectorization on the same schedule"; `wavefront-volpath.bonsai`
and its packet form stay for schedule tuning. The base is therefore
`schedules/wavefront-frame.bonsai`, pbrt's `WavefrontPathIntegrator` on
the CPU: `reorder(p, s)` (a sample index outer, the pixels inner), the
pixels split into bands of `pass_pixels`, every queue on the band, the
drains run in pbrt's kernel order once per bounce over the whole band.
`schedules/wavefront-frame-packet.bonsai` (7c5907da) is that file with
each drain's loop split by sixteen and vectorized (the medium-sample,
shadow and exit-shadow drains stay scalar: NanoVDB), the binds naming the
gang loops; nothing else differs. `schedules/wavefront-frame-packet-
reorder.bonsai` is the packet form with the rays queue sorted before every
pass of its drain:

    li_vol_path.sort(vol_path_step,
                     |ray : Ray, scene_bounds : AABB| ray_sort_key(ray, scene_bounds));

the two-point key of Meister, Boksansky, Guthe and Bittner (arXiv
2506.11273): a Morton code of the ray's origin and of its estimated end,
origin first, both quantized in the scene's box, the end at a fixed
quarter of the box's largest extent along the ray. The key is computed
where the ray is pushed and rides in the entry (`_sort_key : u64`, a
leaf the recipe search leaves alone), `bonsai_sort_indices` builds the
permutation before each pass (Defer.cpp emits the sort in the round's
`pre`), and the drain reads its entries through it. `render.bonsai` gained
`ray_sort_key`, `spread_bits_6`, `quantize_in_box` and a `scene_bounds :
AABB` field on the VolPath integrator that every step passes along; the
driver computes the bounds from the top-level primitives on the CPU and
from every shape's bounds and the instance positions under OptiX. This is
the `sort` directive on a deferred call (30c36ffc, Lower/Sorts.cpp
`apply_queue_sort`, Defer.cpp; tests ssa/defer-sorted-queue and
correctness/llvm/defer-sorted-queue), with two stated limits: a split
(double-buffered) queue and a non-round drain are refused with an
assertion.

**The table** (10-21, 12:12-14:33; compare.sh, both sides the best of
three, machine otherwise idle under /tmp/benchmark.lock, all 18 images
matching pbrt's; render seconds, the speedups over pbrt's CPU wavefront;
pbrt's time is the least of its runs in the scene's six cells, 5.51 /
22.01 / 20.01 / 80.52 / 19.51 / 78.52 s). The two reference columns are
the 10-20 table's:

The plot the user asked for (five bars per scene and sample count,
normalized to pbrt's CPU wavefront) is published from
`scratchpad/plot/cpu-wavefront-speedups.html`.

What the table says:

- **Vectorizing the drains on pbrt's structure wins 15% on
  killeroo-simple, 1% on book, and loses 9% on ganesha**, the same ratio
  at 16 and at 64 spp on every scene. The 10-20 table's growth of the win
  with the sample count is gone, which confirms its cause: the per-pixel
  queues held only spp entries, so the gangs ran half-empty at 16 spp; a
  band's queue holds `pass_pixels` entries and the gangs are full at any
  spp. The ganesha loss is unexplained and is the first thing to measure
  when the machine is next free (perf stat of the frame and frame-packet
  builds at 16 spp, as fixed_cost.sh did on 10-20): ganesha is a single
  million-triangle mesh, and the candidates are the sixteen-ray packet
  traversal doing the union of the lanes' node visits on incoherent
  secondary rays, and the gather of sixteen entries from a band-sized
  queue that no longer sits in a core's cache.
- **The ray sort loses on the CPU, 2% to 10%**, and loses most where the
  trace is the largest share (ganesha). The paper's GPU finding was a
  1.3-2.0x faster trace that the sort's cost did not recover; here the
  packet traversal's gain from coherent lanes does not show at all
  against the sort (`tbb::parallel_sort` of (key, index) pairs per pass)
  plus the drain's indirect reads through the permutation. The sort stays
  available as a directive; the reorder schedule is kept as the
  measurement.
- **pbrt's band structure is itself the cost on the CPU**: our `scalar`
  schedule (a path to its end per sample, pbrt's CPU volpath pattern) is
  5.4x to 8.2x faster than pbrt's CPU wavefront and 1.17x to 1.43x faster
  than pbrt's CPU volpath; the band wavefront, scalar or vectorized, is
  1.3x to 1.8x faster than pbrt's; the per-pixel wavefront of the 10-20
  table is 6.8x to 11.6x. The queues of a band of `pass_pixels` entries
  stream through memory once per kernel per bounce; a pixel's queues
  stay in the core's cache.

**Next**, in the user's order (10-21, 13:10: "After the matrix, try the
per-thread wavefront next. And single-thread sorting should probably not

(runtime/bonsai_parallel.h) sorts sequentially below a million entries --
Intel's x86-simd-sort key-value quicksort where its header is installed
and the driver is compiled `-march=native` (compare.sh and render.sh now
are, as pbrt's build is), else an LSD radix sort of the (key, index)
pairs above a thousand entries and `std::sort` below -- and by TBB's
parallel sort from a million up. Measured on one thread, 60-bit random
keys, the least of seven: at 16K entries std::sort 495 us, the parallel
sort 155, the radix sort 117, x86-simd-sort 84; at 1M the parallel sort
8.6 ms, x86-simd-sort 8.9, the radix sort 16.2 (the table is in the
header). The machine, for the record, is an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D (Zen 5,
AVX-512), not an Intel part; x86-simd-sort dispatches on the ISA and
runs there. Test: correctness/cpp/defer_sorted_queue (the sorted-queue

per-thread wavefront: `split(p, p_thread,
p_in, chunk)`, `bind(p_thread, CPUThread)`, every queue on `p_thread`, so
