### The per-thread wavefront (10-21, afternoon)

`schedules/wavefront-thread-packet.bonsai`: `split(p, p_thread, p_in,
1024, true)`, every queue on `p_thread`, the drains as gangs, `bind(p_thread,
CPUThread)` -- each thread takes a chunk of 1024 pixels, owns the chunk's
queues (1024 x spp entries) and round loop, and drains them itself.
`wavefront-thread-packet-reorder.bonsai` adds `reorder(p_in, s)` after the
split, so a chunk is pushed sample-major (sixteen neighbouring pixels at one
sample per gang, pbrt's order within a band) rather than pixel-major. Four
compiler changes stood between the two files and an image, each fixed at
its cause with tests at the three levels:

1. **The record pass divided by a bound out of scope** (bd01d69a,
   SSA/Defer.cpp). The pass over a queue's record after the drain rebuilt
   the producer loops' indices from the slot by dividing by the inner
   loop's own bound -- `spp`, read inside the pixel loop -- which is not in
   scope at the chunk level where the pass runs; the count had already
   been settled before the nest for the queue's size, and the pass now
   divides by that settled copy (tests defer-nest-inner-bound).
2. **A chunk's queues overflowed the worker's stack** (ccd00344). A
   run-time-sized array inside a bound loop's body was a stack allocation
   of the kernel's frame -- right for a pixel's queues of a few hundred
   kilobytes, 80 MB an iteration for a chunk's, and the first `push`
   faulted. Now the CPU kernel takes such storage from a per-thread arena
   in the runtime (`bonsai_arena_mark`/`alloc`/`release`,
   runtime/bonsai_parallel.h; CodeGen_LLVM::in_cpu_kernel): a bump
   allocator whose blocks live for the thread, marked before the iteration
   and released after it, so that a thread allocates nothing after its
   first iteration -- MoonRay's per-thread queues, and what docs/
   schedule-semantics.md promised of a queue on a loop bound to CPUThread
   (tests defer-thread-queue: ssa, backends/llvm, and correctness/cpp,
   which runs the arena on the runtime's threads).
3. **The record pass ran the continuation for pixels past the frame's
   end** (0cd057bc, SSA/Defer.cpp). The deferral keeps a byte per slot
   when the call is not reached on every iteration, but tested that only
   over the innermost loop's body; a split's tail guard yields one level
   out, so the last chunk's skipped pixels had their film writes run on
   garbage records, past the film's end -- heap corruption on every scene
   whose pixel count 1024 does not divide (killeroo-simple, head,
   killeroo-gold; book and ganesha are 1920 x 1080 = 1024 x 2025 and
   passed). The test now walks every level of the nest for an exit that
   bypasses the inner loop or the call, and the bytes are cleared for the
   whole record by one `fill_bytes` (a new intrinsic, LLVM's memset) where
   the chunk initializes its queue, since a skipped iteration never begins
   the innermost iterations that cleared them before (tests
   defer-nest-guard). The band schedule had the same latent bug for a last
   band that `pass_pixels` does not fill.
4. **`reorder` through a split's tail guard** (7cc6f173,
   SSA/ReorderLoops.cpp). The interchange required the prologue to be one
   block ending at the inner loop; the guard put the inner loop one block
   in. The guard of a `split(..., true)` is now folded into the prologue
   and follows the body inward, as Halide's GuardWithIf does under
   reorder: its condition is a prologue value, recomputed in the new inner
   body (which skips the iteration), in the epilogue loop, and dispatched
   on by the prologue loop (tests reorder-split-guard).

Both schedules then compile (257 s each) and build; all five protocol
scenes at 16 spp match pbrt (killeroo-simple, book, ganesha, head,
killeroo-gold), and the twelve matrix images match. Timed 15:45-17:09 with
compare.sh (REPEATS=3, best of three each side, the machine otherwise
idle, lock held). Render seconds, speedup over pbrt's CPU wavefront, and
the ratio to the three builds already measured (the band matrix above, the
`scalar` schedule, and the per-pixel-queue `wavefront-volpath-packet` of
10-20, whose numbers are from the 10-20 compiler but whose `scalar`
control reads the same to 1%):

| scene, spp | pbrt wavefront | per-thread, pixel-major | per-thread, sample-major (`reorder(p_in, s)`) | over band gangs (`wavefront-frame-packet`) | over `scalar` | over per-pixel gangs (`wavefront-volpath-packet`, 10-20) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| killeroo-simple, 16 | 5.50 s | 0.663 s (8.30x) | 0.678 s (8.12x) | 4.68x | 1.01x | 0.94x (0.623 s) |
| killeroo-simple, 64 | 22.01 s | 2.988 s (7.37x) | 3.049 s (7.22x) | 4.15x | 0.91x | 0.64x (1.900 s) |
| book, 16 | 20.01 s | 2.837 s (7.05x) | 2.812 s (7.12x) | 4.62x | 1.30x | 0.91x (2.571 s) |
| book, 64 | 80.53 s | 12.029 s (6.69x) | 11.946 s (6.66x) | 4.38x | 1.23x | 0.76x (9.125 s) |
| ganesha, 16 | 19.51 s | 3.520 s (5.54x) | 3.878 s (5.03x) | 4.19x | 1.01x | 0.82x (2.877 s) |

Readings:

- **The band structure's 4-5x is the band, not the drains.** Per-thread
  queues over the same program, the same gangs and the same chunk-sized
  rounds run 4.2-4.7x faster than pbrt's band-pass structure at every
  cell: the band's cost was the pass over a band of 1920 x N pixels per
  round, shared by every thread through the global queues, with the
  record and the film touched once per round per pixel; a thread's chunk
  of 1024 pixels keeps its queues and record to itself.
- **Against the path-per-sample `scalar` schedule it is even on killeroo
  and ganesha and 23-30% ahead on book**, the scene with the most
  material variety (the gangs' sort by BxDF buys most where the scalar
  path's branch mix is widest), and 9% behind on killeroo at 64 spp.
- **Per-pixel queues (10-20) remain the fastest CPU wavefront**, by 6%
  to 56%, growing with spp. A pixel's queues of spp entries live in L1/L2;
  a chunk's queues of 1024 x spp entries are 20-80 MB and stream through
  L3 each round, so every drain re-reads its records from memory. The
  chunk size is the lever (256 pixels would be 5-20 MB; the to-do below
  sweeps it), and the gang fullness per kernel per round the measurement
  that says how small a chunk may go before the gangs empty -- the user's
  question of 13:10, to be answered before a `launch(count(q) >= 16)`
  directive is proposed.
- **Sample-major order within the chunk (`reorder(p_in, s)`) is a wash
  on book (1%), a 2% loss on killeroo and a 10% loss on ganesha**: the
  sixteen neighbouring pixels at one sample are more coherent for the
  camera rays but the sort by BxDF rebuilds the gangs after the first
  bounce anyway, and the pixel-major order keeps a pixel's spp records
  adjacent for the film write. The ganesha loss is of the same size as
  the band gangs' loss on ganesha (9%), and both are measured next with
  `perf stat`.

### The figure, from a script (10-22)

The user's rulings of 10-22 on the deliverable: the plot is code in the
repository and a figure file, not a page ("I need to make these plots for
a paper"); no number is ever typed into a CSV -- "you give a script that
runs benchmarks and PRODUCES a CSV"; the series names follow one pattern;
the line at 1 must be visible; the colours colour-blind safe, with pbrt
one colour and every Bonsai schedule the same colour told apart by hatch;
five scenes of varying complexity, the list one variable so it can grow;
and a per-thread wavefront with scalar drains beside the vectorized one,
as the band structure has. So:

- `cpu_compare.sh` runs the matrix (scenes x spp x schedules, one
  compare.sh run per schedule per cell, `scalar` against pbrt's volpath,
  the wavefront schedules against `pbrt --wavefront`) and writes
  `cpu-compare-out/cpu-results.csv` from the logs beside it; `--resume`
  continues a run. compare.sh gained `--pbrt-cache DIR`, which keeps
  pbrt's render (its least-of-REPEATS time and its radiance) keyed by
  scene, flags, depth, repeats and binary, so that pbrt is rendered once
  per cell and every schedule of the cell is measured against the same
  reference time and image.
- The five scenes, of rising cost: killeroo-simple, killeroo-gold, book,
  ganesha, sanmiguel-courtyard (`--scenes` takes any list scene_dump
  converts).
- `schedules/wavefront-thread.bonsai`: wavefront-thread-packet without
  its vectorize lines (the per-thread pair of wavefront-frame /
  wavefront-frame-packet).
- `plot_cpu_wavefront.py` draws the CSV: pbrt grey, Bonsai one blue with
  a hatch per schedule, the reference a dashed line labelled at the right,
  no numbers on the bars. The names are the user's encoding (10-22,
  evening): pbrt by its two schedules ("pbrt megakernel", "pbrt
  wavefront"); Bonsai as type-parallelism-SIMD-order[-sort] -- `wf`/`mk`,
  `b`ulk/per-`t`hread, `s`calar/`v`ectorized, `ps`/`sp` loop order, `-sort`
  for the rays sort -- so scalar = mk-b-s-ps, wavefront-frame = wf-b-s-sp,
  wavefront-frame-packet = wf-b-v-sp, wavefront-frame-packet-reorder =
  wf-b-v-sp-sort, wavefront-thread = wf-t-s-ps, wavefront-thread-packet =
  wf-t-v-ps, wavefront-thread-packet-reorder = wf-t-v-sp.

`*` the one image check of 150 that failed: sanmiguel-courtyard, 16 spp,
`scalar` against pbrt's volpath -- 853,111 pixels lit here against
pbrt's 856,648, a gap of 3,537 where 1,143 is allowed. It is pbrt's own
spread, not ours: pbrt's wavefront on the same cell lights 853,247 pixels
(compare_gbuffer.py on the two cached pbrt renders: pbrt's volpath is
3,401 lit pixels off pbrt's wavefront, "FAILED ... where 1134 was
allowed"), and ours is within 136 of the wavefront, which the program
follows where pbrt's two differ. Under the spread rule of 10-18
(gpu_compare.sh) the cell passes; the CSV keeps the verdict compare.sh
wrote, and the bar carries the vermilion edge until cpu_compare.sh learns
to hand compare.sh the cached other-renderer image as `--pbrt-spread`,
which is the right fix and is on the list below.

What the matrix says:

- **pbrt's own CPU wavefront is 2.7-6.8x slower than its megakernel**
  (PBRT mk over PBRT wf), the band structure's cost; the gap narrows as
  the scene's shading grows (sanmiguel 2.7x) because the drains, not the
  queues, come to dominate.
- **Our megakernel (mk-b-s-ps) beats pbrt's megakernel by 1.05-1.4x** on
  every cell: 1.33x killeroo-simple, 1.17x killeroo-gold, 1.4x book,
  1.15x ganesha, 1.05x sanmiguel.
- **The band wavefronts (wf-b-*) are 1.2-1.8x over pbrt's wavefront**,
  the same structure in our code: scalar drains 1.37-1.54x; vectorized
  drains gain 15% on the killeroos, 0-1% on book, 7-8% on sanmiguel, and
  lose 8-9% on ganesha; the band sort is 8-12% slower than unsorted on
  four scenes and 1% on sanmiguel.
- **The per-thread wavefronts (wf-t-*) are 3.0-8.3x over pbrt's
  wavefront**, 2.5-4.7x over the same drains in the band structure
  (wf-t-v-ps over wf-b-v-sp: 4.7x killeroo-simple, 4.2x gold, 4.6x book,
  4.2x ganesha, 2.5x sanmiguel), ahead of our megakernel on book, ganesha
  and sanmiguel, and behind it by 9-18% on the killeroos (except
  killeroo-simple at 16 spp), where the 1024-pixel chunk's queues at 64
  and 128 spp outgrow the cache and the megakernel's path-at-a-time wins.
- **Vectorized drains pay in the per-thread form where the shading is
  heavy**: 0 to -2% on the killeroos, 12-18% on book, 8-13% on ganesha,
  24-26% on sanmiguel (wf-t-v-ps over wf-t-s-ps) -- the opposite of the
  band, where ganesha lost. Sample-major (wf-t-v-sp) is level on the
  killeroos and book and 11-15% behind on ganesha and sanmiguel.
- **The per-thread sort (wf-t-v-ps-sort) never beats unsorted
  (wf-t-v-ps)**, and its cost grows with the pass size: killeroo-simple
  6% / 13% / 25% at 16 / 64 / 128 spp, killeroo-gold 7 / 11 / 19%, book
  3 / 8 / 15%, ganesha 7 / 13 / 20%, sanmiguel 9 / 6 / 8%. A chunk's rays
  queue is chunk x spp entries, so the sort runs over 16k to 128k keys per
  pass per thread, and the drain then reads the entries through the
  permutation -- a scatter that leaves L2 as the queue does. The sort was
  the paper's question (10-20); on this CPU, in both the band and the
  per-thread form, the packet traversal gains less from coherent rays than
  the sort and the permuted reads cost.

as `--pbrt-spread` for the scalar cell (compare.sh gaining the option);
the chunk-size sweep (256 / 128 pixels) for the per-thread wavefront,
which the sort cost's growth with spp and the killeroo 64/128 loss to the
megakernel both point at; the ganesha band loss under perf stat.

### The GPU matrix measured: five scenes, three sample counts, four OptiX sides (10-24)

The user's ask of 10-23 17:25: the CPU figure's twin for the GPU --
speedup over `pbrt --gpu` ("PBRT wf": pbrt's GPU renderer is its
wavefront, and it has no GPU megakernel) with the bars mk, mk-ser, wf and
wf with ray sorting, comparing only techniques that trace through OptiX
unless a software traversal ever wins. None ever has (gpu-wavefront ran
1.4x to 1.6x slower by kernel than gpu-optix wherever both were measured,
10-03 and 10-04, and the user set the software traversals aside on
10-04), so the figure's sides are the four OptiX schedules, and
`gpu_compare.sh`'s default list is now those four.

**The ray-sorted wavefront had to be built first.** `f.sort(g, |args|
key)` on a deferred call (Intrinsic::sort_indices) had only the host
runtime's sort (bonsai_parallel.h), so a sorted queue drained by a kernel
was impossible. Added (40c07dc4): runtime/bonsai_cuda_sort.cu, CUB's
radix sort of (key, index) pairs (Merrill and Grimshaw 2011; Adinets and
Merrill's Onesweep 2022, which is what DeviceRadixSort runs here) over
the full 64-bit key, the indices 0..n-1 written by a kernel, out of place
into a scratch kept and grown between calls, issued on the null stream
where the launches are, so the host neither waits nor reads back; built
by CMake as the shared library bonsai_cuda_sort when nvcc is found
(check_language(CUDA), cudart_static linked into the library alone) and
loaded by bonsai_cuda.h's bonsai_cuda_sort_indices with dlopen at the
first device sort -- BONSAI_CUDA_SORT_LIB in the environment, else the
path the generated header sets (CPP.cpp emits an initializer with the
compiler's build-time path), else the loader's search -- so the runtime
stays header-only and links no CUDA library, as it loads the driver. In
the compiler: the permutation array lives where the queue's header does
(DeviceGlobal for an ExternDevice queue, never an Extern parameter;
Defer.cpp); the residency analysis counts a sort_indices ahead of a
GPU-bound drain as the device's touch of its keys and permutation
(CodeGen_LLVM_SSA.cpp), and CodeGen_LLVM's sort_indices calls the device
sort when the permutation is device-resident. Tests: ssa/
defer-sorted-queue-device (the permutation allocated `device`, the sort
over the count the host read), correctness/gpu/defer-sorted-device (the
sorted drain on the GPU: the totals), correctness/gpu/sort-indices-cpp
(the device sort against std::stable_sort on 1,000,003 random 36-bit keys
with repeats, then a thousand equal keys). The schedule
`schedules/gpu-optix-sort.bonsai` is gpu-optix plus the one sort line of
the CPU sorted schedules. Found on the way: the driver had not compiled
on the OptiX path since 10-21 (the scene-bounds loop for the sort key
iterated a raw pointer); fixed in f36dc439.

The run: `gpu_compare.sh --out apps/pbrt/gpu-compare-out --spp "16 64
128"` with the three existing schedules, 18:19 to 18:53 on 10-23 (the
first cell 21 minutes, the OptiX compiles of the two megakernel programs,
cached for every later process; then about a minute a cell), and the new
schedule alone into `gpu-compare-out-sort` with its own pbrt, 19:08 to
19:20; three repeats a side, the least, pbrt's by its own timer and ours
by the driver's around the render, every image checked: 90 measured
sides, 60 images, all matching. The compiler was build/compiler at
40c07dc4 (HEAD plus the committed sort work; the first run's compiler
carried the same edits uncommitted, which change nothing for a program
without a sorted queue on the device). The figure:
`plots/gpu-wavefront-speedups.pdf` by `plot_gpu_wavefront.py` from the
two tables, each side's bar its speedup over the pbrt of its own run.

What it says:

- **The matching wavefront on the RT cores (wf) beats pbrt's on every
  cell, 1.38x to 2.92x by wall and 1.37x to 2.19x by kernel**, the
  margin narrowing with spp and with scene weight (sanmiguel at 128 spp
  is the least), as the heatmaps have shown since 10-11.
- **The megakernel (mk) wins only the killeroos at 16 spp** (1.17x,
  1.23x: pbrt's process pays its fixed costs there) and loses everywhere
  else by kernel, 1.3x behind on killeroo-gold and 3.2x behind on ganesha.
  pbrt's wavefront keeps a warp's threads on one material kernel; one
  raygen running every material's code over divergent paths does not.
- **Shader execution reordering (mk-ser) recovers between a fifth
  (ganesha) and all (killeroo-simple) of the megakernel's kernel-time
  loss**: killeroo-simple at pbrt's kernel time (49.0 ms against 49.5),
  killeroo-gold within 7%, book, ganesha and sanmiguel still 1.4x to 2.8x
  behind. The material key alone does not make a
  megakernel a wavefront.
- **The ray sort (wf-sort) never pays on the GPU.** By kernel it costs 9
  to 15% over the unsorted wavefront (the sort's own passes plus the
  permuted entry reads; the traces themselves gain nothing the hardware's
  own scheduling did not already have); by wall it costs 20 to 31%,
  because a sort is a dozen small launches and the wavefront sorts before
  every trace of every pass -- 96 sorts in a 30 ms render at 16 spp. The
  same verdict as the CPU's (the per-thread sort never beat unsorted),
  for the opposite reason: there the sort was the cost, here the launches
  are.

To do, from this: the device sort over the key's live bits -- ray_sort_key
is 36 bits, so five 8-bit passes instead of eight, with CUB's begin/end
bits; the width would come from the schedule (a bits argument on `sort`,
to be asked of the user) or from an OR-reduction of the keys per round;
the round's launches (sort passes and drains) captured in a CUDA graph to
take the launch gaps out, which pbrt's wavefront also pays for and which
would help every GPU schedule; the megakernel's ganesha loss under the
kernel profile (which material kernels diverge most), which is the paper's
megakernel-versus-wavefront point in numbers.

### The GPU schedule space explored: is the best schedule data-dependent? (10-24)

The user's question of 10-24 00:10: "The plot looks like Bonsai wf is
always the best schedule. Can you try exploring to see if there's any
better schedule, even if only better on a scene or scene x spp pair? I
want to know if there are data-dependent best schedules." And, on the
sort: "Definitely only sort the live bits for keys too ... Shouldn't the
compiler be able to analyze the possible bits set on the sort key?"

**The compiler reads a sort key's live bits off its arithmetic
(c9d0b824).** IR/KnownBits.h: `possible_bits(e, funcs)` is a mask of the
bits an integer expression may have set, over constants, masks, shifts by
constants, ors, xors, casts and selects, with a sound widening for add
(one bit past the wider operand), mul (the widths' sum), unsigned div and
mod (no wider than the dividend), everything else and any float cast every
bit of the type; a call to one of the program's functions is followed
into its body (to depth eight), read as straight-line statements with
branches (`let`, a plain variable's store, an allocation with its initial
value, if/else merged by or, return), and a body with a loop or an
indexed store gives every bit. Lower/Sorts.cpp's apply_queue_sort ors the
mask over every call site's key and leaves the width on the Sort
transform (`Sort::key_bits`); SSA/Convert.cpp carries it to the queue
(`QueueSpec::sort_key_bits`); Defer.cpp passes it as the fourth argument
of `sort_indices(keys, perm, count, bits)`; CodeGen_LLVM hands it to the
runtime, whose host radix sort runs ceil(bits / 11) passes (still skipping
a pass whose digit is constant) and whose device sort gives CUB `end_bit`
(ceil(bits / 8) passes). Tests: ssa/defer-sorted-queue-bits (a key of
`spread(x & 15) | (y & 1) << 12` through a function: 13 bits), the two
earlier IR goldens (a float cast's key: 64), correctness/gpu/
sort-indices-cpp (the device sort told 36 bits on 36-bit keys agrees with
std::stable_sort), correctness/cpp/defer_sorted_queue (the host radix
sort told 60 bits on 60-bit hashes).

**Found on the way: the two-point key was lossy (fixed in 508bc091).**
`spread_bits_6` used the every-third-bit masks of a 3D Morton code
(0x1249249249249249 and its ladder) while `ray_sort_key` ors six
coordinates at offsets 0..5, so coordinates two apart landed on the same
bits and the key lost information at every level. Every ray-sort
measurement before 10-24 -- the band sort of 10-20/10-21, the per-thread
sort of 10-23, the GPU wf-sort of 10-23 23:00 -- ran on that key. The
spread is now ten explicit terms, bit k to bit 6k, so the fine key is a
true 60-bit code; `ray_sort_key_coarse` beside it quantizes to six bits
per axis and masks them in the open, a 36-bit code (the analysis above
reads 60 and 36 off the two). The CPU sorted schedules are re-measured
with the fixed key below.

**The variants** (apps/pbrt/schedules/gpu-optix-*.bonsai, every one from
directives the language already had, nothing added): `b128` and `b512`
(the CUDA drains in blocks of 128 or 512 threads instead of 256); `fused`
(no hit queue: `vol_surface`, the material evaluation, the light sample
and the next ray's push, runs in the trace program right after the hit
is routed, as a megakernel's does; the material specialization goes with
the queue); `fused-ser` (the same with `vol_route.sort(vol_surface,
material)`, shader execution reordering before the switch); `sort36`
(the wavefront sorted by the coarse key); `mega-ser-ray` (the megakernel
with the material reordering and, on each call that continues the path --
`vol_surface`, `vol_route`, `vol_medium_scatter`, `vol_exit` calling
`vol_path_step`, the loop's back edges after loopify -- a reordering by
the top sixteen bits of the coarse ray key, so a wave enters each
bounce's trace with rays of one region and direction); `ps` (no
`reorder(p, s)`: a pass is a band of pixels with all their samples).
Two did not run. `ps` is refused by the compiler: without the reorder the
band's queue is made once per band iteration and cannot be hoisted to
the one allocation the caller's storage (ExternDevice) requires
(SSA/QueueStorage.cpp); withdrawn (deb8b53d), the pixel-major GPU pass
wants a queue sized by the whole band, a schedule question for later.
`fused-ser` fails OptiX's module compile: `Illegal call to optixReorder in
function __closesthit__trace with semantic type CLOSESTHIT` -- the
reordering hint was emitted into the closest-hit program, where OptiX
forbids it; Lower/Sorts.cpp's contract is that the hint is nothing
anywhere but a raygen (CodeGen_LLVM::codegen_rt_intrinsic), so the hint
has to be dropped or hoisted wherever the fused material stage is
reached from the closest-hit side. A compiler bug, first in the to-do.

**The run**: `gpu_compare.sh --out apps/pbrt/gpu-compare-out-explore
--spp "16 64 128"` with gpu-optix beside the six variants that compile,
03:12 to 03:39 on 10-24, three repeats a side, the least, every image
checked: 120 sides, all matching. The compiler at c9d0b824. The figure:
`plots/gpu-wavefront-explore.pdf` (`plot_gpu_wavefront.py ... --sides`
with these seven); the paper's figure stays the four-schedule one.

What it says:

- **Yes, there is a data-dependent best schedule, and it is the fused
  wavefront on sanmiguel.** With the materials inside the trace program
  (wf-fused) sanmiguel renders 4-8% faster by wall than the plain
  wavefront at every count (2.03x / 1.58x / 1.43x against 1.88x / 1.52x /
  1.38x) and 2% faster by kernel (106.1 / 423.8 / 850.5 ms against
  108.2 / 433.9 / 870.3), while every other scene is slower fused: book
  by 20% of kernel time (101.1 against 83.6 ms at 16 spp), the killeroos
  and ganesha by 13-15%. The queue a hit crosses costs a write of the
  record, a launch and a reload; the material switch inside the trace
  program costs the divergence of a wave that holds many materials. On
  sanmiguel -- the most materials and textures of the five, the heaviest
  shading per hit -- the queue's cost is the larger; on book the
  divergence is. (The "heaviest shading per hit" was a guess and the
  profiles say otherwise; see "The fused wavefront's trade read off the
  profiles" below.) This is the paper's point in one scene: the schedule
  that wins is a property of the scene, and both are the same program
  under two schedules.
- **The CUDA drains' block size is not a knob**: 128 is within 1% of 256
  on every cell (ahead by 0.5-1% on the killeroos and sanmiguel, which is
  the reference's own spread between runs: pbrt's killeroo-simple at 64
  spp read 0.26 s in the evening's run and 0.22 s in this one); 512 is
  0.5-2% behind. pbrt sizes each kernel by occupancy; one size for all is
  not what holds this renderer back.
- **The megakernel wants reordering by ray more than by material.**
  mega-ser-ray against mega-ser: killeroo-gold 1.91x against 1.38x at 16
  spp (kernel 115 ms against 159), book 1.40x against 1.11x (164 against
  208), ganesha 0.53x against 0.46x, sanmiguel 1.09x against 1.04x; on
  killeroo-simple the two are level (47.2 against 49.0 ms). It is the
  best megakernel measured and still behind the wavefront on every cell:
  the hardware's gathering by ray key recovers coherence for the trace,
  not the register pressure and the code size of one program holding
  every stage.
- **Sorting the ray queue never pays on this GPU, with either key, and
  the compiler's live-bits analysis is worth what the key's width lets
  it be.** With the fixed 60-bit key wf-sort is 20-36% behind wf by wall
  (kernel +8-9%, the rest the sort's dozen launches per round); with the
  36-bit key and five digit passes wf-sort36 is 8-10% faster than
  wf-sort by wall (its kernel time is the same, 29.7 against 30.2 ms, so
  the saving is the three passes' launches) and still 17-27% behind wf.
  A queue sort of the wavefront is the wrong place for coherence on
  hardware that reorders its own traversal; the megakernel's reordering
  hint is where the ray key earns its keep.

the sort key's live bits too (a 16-bit hint from a 36-bit key wants the
top sixteen, which the schedule shifts by hand today); the pixel-major GPU
pass as a schedule that sizes the band's queue by the whole band.

### The fused wavefront's trade read off the profiles; all GPU schedules on one figure (10-24)

few material types, the kernel profiles of the exploration run
(`gpu-compare-out-explore/*.stats`, read by a scratch script, nothing
typed) answer both. **sanmiguel has the most material types of the five,
not the fewest**: four material kernels run there (CoatedDiffuse,
Dielectric, Diffuse, DiffuseTransmission) against two on every other
scene. The trade, per scene and sample count -- the plain wavefront's
trace raygen and the sum of its material kernels against the fused
schedule's raygen, which holds both:

What it says:

- **The fused program's penalty is a per-scene constant, independent of
  the sample count**: 20% on killeroo-simple, 23% on gold, 22% on
  ganesha, 29-31% on book, and *nothing* on sanmiguel (2-3% below the
  sum). The win on sanmiguel is not that its hit queue is dearer; it is
  that fusing costs it nothing where it costs every other scene a
  fifth to a third of its trace-plus-shade time.
- **Shading is not heavier per hit on sanmiguel.** Its material kernels
  sum to 0.8 of its trace time (0.7 on gold, 1.0 on book and ganesha,
  1.1 on killeroo-simple), and two of its four material kernels run at
  the launch floor (9 and 19 us a launch against the 4 us of an empty
  one, 768 launches each at 64 spp): the wavefront's per-material
  launches are the most fragmented there, which is a few ms of the gap,
  not its 60.
- **What is different about sanmiguel is the trace itself**: 1.6 M
  triangles in 368 meshes plus 69 040 instances of 428 objects (a
  two-level traversal), the heaviest trace raygen of the five per sample
  (0.22 ms a launch at 64 spp against 0.15 on book). The reading this
  supports, not yet proven: the fused raygen's cost elsewhere is the
  bigger program's register pressure and divergence lowering the
  occupancy of the *trace*; on sanmiguel the trace is bound by the
  traversal's own latency, not by occupancy, so the shading rides along
  for free. The proof would be the fused raygen's register count and
  achieved occupancy per scene under the profiler, which crashes the
  driver on the heavy scenes (the standing rule: not without the user).
  An alternative to rule out: the per-hit payload the fused program
  avoids writing is larger on sanmiguel (textured materials carry more
  per hit), which a count of hit-queue bytes per scene would settle.

What it says, and what it corrects: **with a key that is not lossy, the
ray sort is a data-dependent win on the CPU too.**

- **The band sort (wf-b-v-sp-sort) now beats the unsorted band wavefront
  on killeroo-simple (1.83x / 1.84x / 1.82x against 1.77x / 1.77x /
  1.74x) and on sanmiguel (1.66x / 1.65x / 1.65x against 1.48x / 1.46x /
  1.47x, a 12% gain), is level on killeroo-gold and ganesha (within 1%)
  and 4% behind on book.** On 10-21, with the lossy key, it lost 8 to 12%
  everywhere; the sort was paying for itself and being charged for a key
  that scrambled half the rays' order.
- **The per-thread sort (wf-t-v-ps-sort) beats the unsorted per-thread
  wavefront on sanmiguel at every count (3.82x / 3.95x / 3.99x against
  3.75x / 3.78x / 3.80x, up to 5%) and on book at 16 spp (7.25x against
  7.01x)**, and it is the fastest CPU schedule measured on sanmiguel. It
  still loses where the chunk's pass is large: 3% at 16 spp growing to 18
  to 20% at 128 spp on the killeroos and book, 4 to 13% on ganesha -- the
  chunk x spp entries of a pass outgrow the core's cache and the sort and
  the permuted reads pay for it, as the 10-23 reading said; a smaller
  chunk at high spp is the remedy that reading pointed at.
- The ray sort's story is therefore the same on both processors: it pays
  where the shading is heavy and the rays incoherent (sanmiguel), and
  costs where the traversal is already cheap; and on the CPU, where the
  sort is one call per pass rather than a dozen launches, it pays more
  often. The 14:00 reading of 10-23 ("neither sort pays on this CPU") was
  a reading of the lossy key and is withdrawn.

## Feature gaps against pbrt --gpu, and the scene set reconverted (10-24)

The user asked whether the renderer is feature-complete with pbrt's GPU
renderer and whether it is spectral as pbrt is. It is spectral (four
wavelengths a ray, SampleVisible, the sigmoid RGB-to-spectrum tables,
TerminateSecondary at a dispersive interface, the sensor to RGB), and
scene_dump's refusals, read against pbrt-v4's wavefront sources, leave
these gaps where `pbrt --gpu` accepts and this renderer refuses:

- cameras: `perspective` only (pbrt's GPU also runs `orthographic`,
  `spherical`, `realistic`);
- the pixel filter: `gaussian` only (`box`, `triangle`, `mitchell`, `sinc`);
- lights: no `goniometric` or `projection`; no `infinite` with an
  `illuminance`; no area light with an image or a `power`; no bilinear
  patch with an `emissionfilename`;
- light samplers: `bvh` and `uniform` (`power`, `exhaustive`);
- textures: no `checkerboard`, `dots`, `bilerp`; the image filter
  `bilinear` only; a texture graph read three composites deep; `ptex`,
  which pbrt's GPU refuses as well;
- a subsurface material's `sigma_a`, `sigma_s`, `reflectance` and a hair
  material's `sigma_a` given as textures;
- lights and media placed through a named coordinate system; a shutter
  other than [0, 1]. Moving geometry is not a gap: pbrt's GPU warns and
  ignores animated shapes, and killeroo-moving converts here.

One gap was silent: `Film "spectral"` was not refused -- the film type
was only tested for `gbuffer`, so a spectral film rendered as an rgb one
without a word. scene_dump now refuses any film but `rgb` and `gbuffer`
(tried on a killeroo-simple with its Film changed: refused by name).

**Which gaps the scene set can test.** The converter run over the 29
top-level scenes of ~/projects/pbrt-v4-scenes that were not yet in
scenes/converted (the variants that share a converted sibling's geometry,
materials and lights -- kroken's and watercolor's other cameras, the
landscape views, the zero-day and transparent-machines frames, bistro's
variants -- were not rerun): **25 convert** -- all eleven hair scenes
(4 to 13 s each), bunny-fur, dragon_50 and dragon_250,
lte-orb-blue-agat-spec, sportscar-area-lights, sanmiguel's six other
views, dambreak1, watercolor camera-8 (which crashed the converter on
09-26 and converts in 39 s now). Four refuse, and these are the only gaps
the set exercises:

- sanmiguel-realistic-courtyard: the `realistic` camera;
- probes/alpha_gradient_d1: the `orthographic` camera;
- pavilion-night (`bdpt`) and contemporary-bathroom (`sppm`): integrators
  pbrt's GPU cannot run either; `pbrt --gpu` swaps in its wavefront
  volpath for them, so a `--integrator volpath` override in scene_dump
  would make the two comparable on equal terms.

(probes/manylights_grid.pbrt is an include file, not a scene: pbrt's own
parser rejects it outside a world block.) Every other gap above --
filters, the two light kinds, the two light samplers, the three
textures, the spectral film, the texture-valued subsurface and hair
parameters -- has no scene in the set, and would need a scene written
for it. The 25 newly converted scenes have been converted only; none has
been rendered against `pbrt --gpu` yet, and the hair set in particular
(curves and the hair material, built 10-04) is the untested part of the
renderer's feature claim. The scene_dump change moves the conversion
stamp, so every scene in scenes/converted is reconverted on its next use
(37 GB over the heatmap's list, kroken the slowest at about four minutes).

## The gaps the scene set exercises, built: the integrator override, the orthographic and the realistic camera (10-24 evening, 10-25)

The user: "start working on these features in order of simplicity; make
sure scenes including them beat PBRT's renderer across the spps". In
that order:

**1. The integrator override (scene_dump).** Under `--gpu` a scene whose
integrator this renderer lacks (`bdpt`, `sppm`) is converted as `volpath`
with the warning pbrt's WavefrontPathIntegrator prints ("Ignoring
specified integrator ... always uses a volpath integrator"), its
`maxdepth`, `regularize` and `lightsampler` read off the directive as
pbrt reads them; without `--gpu` it is refused as before, since pbrt's
CPU would run the scene's own integrator. pavilion-night and
contemporary-bathroom convert.

**2. The orthographic camera.** `camera.bonsai`'s element is now
`Camera` with a `kind` (0 perspective, 1 orthographic, 2 realistic);
scene_dump builds `camera_from_raster` from `Orthographic(0, 1)` for the
second, takes dxCamera/dyCamera as pbrt's OrthographicCamera does
(`cameraFromRaster(Vector3f(1,0,0))`), and the two generate functions are
pbrt's, both branches, lens included. probes/alpha_gradient_d1 converts.

**3. The realistic camera.** The lens system as data: cameras.h is
included in scene_dump with `private` opened (as lightsamplers.h is),
and `elementInterfaces` (focused), `exitPupilBounds` (64) and
`physicalExtent` are read off the RealisticCamera pbrt built -- the
64 x 1M-ray pupil search and FocusThickLens run in pbrt's own code at
camera creation. The renderer carries them as two extern arrays
(`camera_lens`, `camera_pupil`, vec4f each) and `trace_lenses_from_film`,
`sample_exit_pupil`, `generate_realistic_ray` are pbrt's operation for
operation (IntersectSphericalElement through `quadratic_f`, Refract
through `refract_`); the ray's weight (cos^4 / (pdf r^2)) multiplies the
path's radiance before the sensor, as the wavefront's `cameraRayWeight`
does; the differential version is CameraBase's finite differences. An
`aperture` shape or image is refused. sanmiguel-realistic-courtyard
converts: 13 interfaces, rear element at 14.3 mm, film 28.8 x 19.8 mm.
Compiler fix on the way: `(a < 0) != (b < 0)` on booleans had no LLVM
lowering (CodeGen_LLVM.cpp, `Neq` beside `Eq`; test
tests/bonsai/correctness/llvm/bool-neq; committed by bonsai-ac in
c7fdce07 with their backend work, credited).

**The one thing the camera needs that the compiler has not got: a
conditional deferred call.** pbrt's camera kernel pushes a ray only when
the camera gave one; for a vignetted sample the film still adds zero at
the filter weight. Written as `if camera_ray_valid { integrator_li(...) }`
the SSA deferral fails (SSA.cpp:699, "Var @N not in current block, and
current block is entry!", @N a `gep(rays_..._slots, rays_rest)`): the
continuation after the deferred call gains a second, direct predecessor
(the else edge), and the slot handles made at the push are not reachable
from it. Bisected on the CPU wavefront-volpath schedule (80 s a compile):
scalars extracted before the call still fail, the same program with the
call unconditional compiles. So the call is unconditional and a vignetted
sample's path is traced and weighed zero (its visible surface discarded,
as pbrt records none): the same image, at the cost of the path. **The
cost is real on this scene:** pbrt --gpu at 16 spp reports 19,844,697
camera rays for 1600 x 1100 x 16 = 28,160,000 samples, so 29.5% of the
samples are vignetted (the pupil bound is a box round a disc, and the
wide 22 mm lens at f/2.5 vignettes at the edges), and this renderer
traces 1.42x pbrt's paths on it. Beating pbrt there needs the conditional
deferral: the continuation's slot stores hoisted to where the captured
values are defined (the dominator of the `if`), the rest function run
for every entry of the band whether or not it pushed -- a Defer.cpp
change, and a semantics question (what runs the continuation of an entry
that was never pushed) for the user, with bonsai-ac's own Defer.cpp
extension in flight.

**Not yet measured.** The four scenes' gpu_compare against pbrt --gpu at
16/64/128/256 spp did not run: the first attempt died at its build step
(an edit of scene_io.h under it, my fault), the second was killed when it
started under bonsai-ac's --stars tables. It runs when the machine is
free; until then the three cameras are verified only to compile (scalar,
wavefront-volpath) and convert, and no image of theirs has been checked
against pbrt's.

## The conditional deferred call, built: pbrt's camera kernel as written (10-25)

The user's ruling on the paragraph above: no dummy path; the compiler
takes pbrt's shape. The semantics (the user, 10-25): a deferred call
stores its entry and ends the parallel iteration *only when the call is
made*; an iteration whose test fails runs the code after the call where
it stands, at once, as if nothing were scheduled. Directly in a parfor a
deferral is a store plus a yield; a function holding a conditional
deferral that stays out of line reports whether it deferred (an
`optional[ret]`, or a bool for void) and the yield propagates up to the
parfor. Nothing about an unconditional deferral changes.

**What failed, exactly.** `region_from(k0_entry)` gathered the owner's
continuation -- the call's cont block, then the merge after the `if`,
then the film write -- and the pass *moved* it into the record pass
(`k0_entry->preds = {run}`), while the else edge still jumped into the
merge from the producer. The merge's values (the slot handles made at the
push) were then wanted from a block whose predecessor chain reaches the
producer's entry: SSA.cpp:699. The precondition checked only that the
cont block had one predecessor; the merge inside the region was never
looked at.

**What was built** (src/SSA/Defer.cpp, `k0_rejoins`). When a block of the
continuation past its entry has a predecessor outside it, the
continuation is *cloned* into the record pass (`clone_region`, suffix
`!rest`) and the original stays for the path that skipped the call; the
blocks between the call and the merge, reachable from the call alone, go
dead in the producer and `remove_unreachable_blocks` takes them. The
`<q>_ran` byte, already allocated when not every iteration reaches the
call, gates the pass as before. One more bug under it: `clone_region`
keeps the names of block arguments that carry outside values, so the copy
and the original defined an argument of one name in one function, and the
record's SoA split (SSA/InducedStorage.cpp, which follows a handle by the
name the jumps pass it under) threaded the pass's handles into the
producer's merge -- the second SSA.cpp:699, on `@4070`. The copy's block
arguments now take fresh names (edit_argument, block by block: every use
inside a block is of the block's own argument). Tests:
correctness/llvm/defer-conditional-rejoin (the result),
ssa/defer-conditional-rejoin (the shape: `!merge_3` inline and
`!merge_3!rest` in the pass, `q_ran` dispatched on),
correctness/llvm/defer-spawn-conditional (a spawn under a test: the code
after it runs in the producer regardless, the reducer is read in the
pass), correctness/llvm/defer-conditional-in-chain (the result when the
chain returns without deferring; the inline shape for that case is the
to-do below). render.bonsai is back to `if camera_ray_valid {
integrator_li(...) }`, and wavefront-volpath compiles it.

**Spawn needed nothing.** A deferred spawned call pushes and jumps to its
own continuation (Defer.cpp, "the push is the spawn, taken up"); nothing
after it goes to the queue, so a test around it costs nothing -- all four
spawns in render.bonsai already sit under one. On the user's question
whether `spawn shadow_contribution(..); return;` is redundant since a
return joins (docs/parallel-semantics.md, section 1): in the program's
semantics it is -- `K` is empty and the return joins -- but section 4 lets
a deferral *move the join later, never earlier*, to after the drain, and
`spawn` is what tells the schedule that the call reports only through its
reducer and may be pushed past the function's return without capturing
the caller's rest (a plain deferred call's callers must do nothing after
the call but return). Whether that license should be the schedule's word
rather than the program's is the user's to decide.

**To do** -- each a test in the suite that fails on purpose until it is
built (the user, 10-25: the suite is not green while these stand).
(1) The chain reporting whether it deferred (the bool / optional return),
so that a test *inside* the chain -- `li` returning without having pushed
-- runs the owner's continuation at once rather than in the pass; today
the pass runs it for every slot, the same result
(ssa/defer-conditional-in-chain, red) -- **built 10-25 night, see
below**. (2) An explicit `Defer <entry> <queue>` terminator in the SSA for
the push that ends an iteration, which `lower_pushes` turns into the store
and the yield; today the push is an instruction followed by a `Return`
(ssa/defer-terminator, red) -- **built 10-25 evening, see below**. (3) The
GPU rest kernel binding every induced slot its continuation writes, not
only those it reads (CodeGen_LLVM.cpp:1756, seen with a store to
`visible.set` after the call under gpu-optix); the small form,
gpu/defer-store-after-call, passes, so the renderer's shape is not yet
reproduced in a test.

**Measured (10-25, 14:21-14:53, gpu_compare, gpu-optix against pbrt --gpu,
unlocked clock).** The orthographic probe: 3.14x / 1.64x / 1.62x / 1.61x
at 16 / 64 / 128 / 256 spp, the image matching pbrt's at every count. The
realistic camera, sanmiguel-realistic-courtyard: 1.86x / 1.45x / 1.41x /
1.45x, matching at every count -- with pbrt's shape, `if (cameraRay)`, and
no path traced for a vignetted sample. pavilion-night (bdpt as volpath):
2.08x / 1.75x / 1.63x / 1.61x but the image 0.83x pbrt's at every count,
where pbrt's two renderers agree to 1.02x -- a real defect, found by
region: everything lit by the sky and the two 3500 K sphere lights agrees
to 1%, and the candle lantern (a 2500 K blackbody at scale 25000, a mesh)
and the brightest pixels are 0.52-0.6x. Not the spectrum: the blackbody,
its normalization and the photometric scale are pbrt's own functions on
both sides. **The film's clamp.** pbrt's RGBFilm::AddSample clamps the
*sensor* RGB -- XYZ for the cie1931 sensor, imaging ratio included -- to
`maxcomponentvalue` and takes it to the output space only at GetPixelRGB;
this renderer applied the output matrix first and clamped the sRGB, so a
saturated orange sample whose XYZ sat under 50 but whose sRGB red stood
above it was capped where pbrt's was not. Fixed (colour.bonsai
`sensor_to_output_rgb`, the film block of `render`); every earlier scene
passed because none drove a saturated sample past the clamp.
contemporary-bathroom (sppm as volpath) never ran: scene_dump refused it,
"a shape names an area light the parser did not record" -- pbrt makes an
area light per *shape* (`scene->AddAreaLight` in BasicSceneBuilder::Shape;
the shape's `lightIndex` counts those) where the converter recorded one
per directive, so the bathroom's one directive over four filament meshes
indexed past the end. Fixed: `area_lights` is filled per Shape while a
directive is set, the directive carried on the attribute stack as pbrt's
graphicsState carries it. Both fixes await the machine for a rerun of the
two scenes and a regression check on three reference scenes.

**The third compiler fix (10-25, 6da5a6f7).** With the camera call under
a test, the deferral keeps a byte per sample slot (`rays_ran`) and clears
it as the band starts, a `fill_bytes` of the record -- which under the
OptiX schedule lives in the queue's device memory. The intrinsic lowered
to a host memset of the device address and the renderer died after
"lights and film" on every scene (SIGSEGV in `render`). A `fill_bytes` of
a device-resident array now crosses as `cuMemsetD8Async` on the stream
(runtime `bonsai_cuda_fill_bytes_async`), after the word stores held back
before it; gpu/defer-conditional-rejoin covers it.

**The second compiler fix the OptiX schedule needed (10-25, 0d33f9e5).**
With the film write inline beside the deferred path, the record's handles
(path_lambda's slot, the camera ray's) cross the merge after `if
(cameraRay)` as block arguments, and `render.specialize(p_blk, sampler)`
copies that body once per sampler. The record's SoA split
(SSA/InducedStorage.cpp) followed a handle through a jump by recording
"this argument's name stands for the same parts" and rewriting that
name's uses over the whole function -- and the variants' blocks carry
the enclosing scope's values under one name, so the Independent variant's
film write was rewritten to the PMJ02BN variant's slot addresses, off a
loop index no path of its own reaches (SSA.cpp:699 again, on `@17013`).
The split now splits the block argument as it splits a callee's
parameter: the argument renamed to a name of its own, one new argument
per leaf, every jump into the block appending its own parts (a part the
jump's block cannot reach, materialized on a path that never read that
leaf, goes as undefined; the arguments go with an unread leaf). Five
golden dumps changed in the expected way, the leaf addresses now named
as the arguments they are. A first attempt renamed every cloned region's
block arguments in `clone_region` instead; that broke the threading
convention a later `reach` relies on (an argument carrying an outside
value keeps its name) and failed six tests, so it was withdrawn.

**The spawn-join semantics, built (10-25 evening).** The user's ruling:
"The schedule cannot move a join! ... make spawn require an explicit join
or the end of the enclosing parfor ... The schedule should never indicate
program semantics, only the program specification should indicate
parallel semantics!" So (docs/parallel-semantics.md sections 1 and 4): a
`join;` waits for every call the *activity* spawned since its last join,
through the functions it called; a function's return joins nothing; the
end of a parfor body joins what the body spawned. Cilk's spawn and sync
without Cilk's return rule -- X10's async bounded by its finish is the
nearer model. Under a deferral the join is where the activity is
suspended: the owner's iteration runs on in place after its call into the
chain up to the join, ends there, and what follows the join runs in the
pass over the record after the drain; with no join before the iteration's
end nothing is suspended and the pass has nothing to run. The parser
(src/Parser/Parser.cpp, `Outstanding`): a reducer handed to a spawn is
outstanding outright; one handed to a call is outstanding provisionally,
if the callee leaves its parameter outstanding at a return, which is
settled once the whole program is parsed (`escape_rules`, a fixed point,
since a callee may be declared ahead of its body or be the function
itself); `join;` clears what this block and the blocks inside it made (by
block depth, so a join under a test does not clear an enclosing block's
spawns); a parfor body's entries are the body's alone. A read of a
reducer against a standing entry is refused where it was written:
tests/bonsai/error/reducer-read-after-callee-spawn (the caller parsed
before the callees). SSA/Defer.cpp: for a spawned deferral the owner's
rest begins at the join's `next` (`join_block`, `rest_jump`), the join's
block jumps to the iteration's end, and the blocks between the call and
the join stay in place -- tests/bonsai/ssa/defer-spawn-join-in-place
shows `marks[i] = ..` in the loop and `out[i] = total` in `q_rest`, and
correctness/llvm/defer-spawn-join-in-place runs it; two joins on
different paths, a join not reached on every path from the call, a path
to the join that skipped the call, and a lone call with no join are
refused as unimplemented, each with a message. SSA/Rewrite.cpp's
inline_call no longer turns an inlined return into a Join (loopify over a
spawning recursion: ssa/loopify-spawn-mutual's `main` now joins). Eighteen
tests that read a reducer after a chain's spawn write `join;` before the
read; their goldens change by one line each -- a dead slot address in the
loop where the rest no longer moves, or the join itself -- and the LLVM
and PTX dumps by value numbers alone. render.bonsai: one `join;` after
`if camera_ray_valid { integrator_li(...) }`, before the film write; under
wavefront-volpath and gpu-optix the join lands inside `rays_rest` right
before the film's reads of the radiance slot, and the spawned queues
(shadow, escaped, emissive, exit_shadow) have, as before, no rest of their
own, since the rays drain's iteration ends without a join. killeroo-simple
at 16 spp under gpu-optix against pbrt --gpu (18:40): 3.15x, the image
matching pbrt's, the kernel 27.66 ms against the afternoon's 27.62.

**The `Defer` terminator, built (10-25 evening; to-do 2).** The push that
ends an iteration is one terminator of the SSA, `defer q entry`
(Terminator::Defer, include/SSA/SSA.h): the store of the entry and the end
of the activity in one, where the deferral wrote a push instruction and a
return, two things for one. The deferral's site ends at it
(SSA/Defer.cpp push_entry, `ends`); the owner's own first push
(initial_push) and a spawned call's push stay instructions, since their
blocks go on. Every pass that walks terminators knows it -- no successors;
the queue and the entry its operands, cloned, renamed, substituted,
retyped, counted and read as a return's value is (about forty visitor
sites, each found by the compiler once the variant grew) -- and the
analyses that looked for push instructions see it as the push it is: the
distinct-slots count, the gate pass's push sites, the write and the
escape analyses, the refusals of collapse, of loopify's stack and of the
hit continuations. The vectorizer takes a gang variant's deferrals apart
into the predicated push and a yield before linearizing
(split_defer_terminators), and lower_pushes does the same first and then
lowers the push it left, so the lowered program is as before. Tests:
ssa/defer-terminator passes against the dump it had written by hand ahead
of the feature; defer-conditional-rejoin's dump shows `defer _queue_q @0`
for its push and return; eight goldens move by value numbers alone, the
push's name now drawn at the lowering. Built in a private worktree on the
branch ajr/ssa-defer-terminator and fast-forwarded, since the tree does
not compile between the variant's growth and the last visitor.

**The chain reports whether it deferred, built (10-25 night; to-do 1).**
The user's shape: `step` returns a bool -- `store (x, acc) q; return
true;` at the deferral, `return false` otherwise -- and the owner writes
`deferred = step(..); if !deferred { out[i] = acc + w; } else { yield; }`,
the deferred ones getting the continuation after the drained call. Built
as that (SSA/Defer.cpp `chain_conditional`, `reports`): a chain some path
of which returns without calling into the chain or the deferred call --
`step` calling `work` only `if x > 4.0`, a recursion's step ending its
path -- reports; every function of it returns a bool, or the option of its
value (`_option_<q> { value, set }`, as src/Lower/Options.cpp lowers one,
`set` false for "deferred"); the deferral's terminator carries the answer
(`defer _queue_q @1 ret (bool)1`, Terminator::Defer::answer, lowered as
the return's value), every other return answers `false` or `some(value)`
(and still writes the result slot, since the same return ends a path the
drain runs), and a tail call into the chain returns the callee's answer
onward -- through the empty blocks of a call under a test too
(`is_tail_call` follows them). The owner's call becomes `callc step(..)
q!deferred(..)`, which dispatches: "returned" to the continuation where it
stands, with the value taken out of the option; "deferred" to `q!end`,
which sets the slot's byte and ends the iteration; the pass over the
record runs the continuation's copy (k0_rejoins) for the slots whose byte
is set. The byte moves from the call to the dispatch. Not reporting: a
chain whose every path defers somewhere -- onto this queue or onto one
another directive defers or stages (QueueSpec::deferred_elsewhere, read
off the schedule in Convert.cpp: gate-drains-gang's `step` pushes onto one
of two queues) -- and the owner that makes the initial push, after which
every slot holds an entry (render.bonsai's rays queue: unchanged). Tests:
ssa and correctness/llvm defer-conditional-in-chain (the bool; the ssa
reminder's hand-written dump replaced by the real one), -value (the
option, the deferred value through the result slot), -deep (the test at
the bottom of a chain two deep, the answer returned onward), -middle (the
test in the middle, `b` always deferring); recursions report too, so
twenty-odd deferral dumps changed shape.

**Two defects found on the way.** (1) The record pass on the GPU read a
field the device call had just written as its pre-call value
(correctness/gpu defer-record-soa, defer-under-specialize,
defer-store-after-call: zeros where the inline path ran). The root walk
(SSA/Analysis.cpp roots_of) resolved a block argument to the instruction
of its name and took any other argument for a root of its own; a slot
address carried through a renamed argument -- the dispatch's, the copied
continuation's, the SoA split's `!arg` -- was a root the kernel never
wrote, so the loads through it were marked `!invariant.load`
(launch_readonly) and LLVM folded them to the store before the call. Now
an argument that is no instruction's follows what the jumps, dispatches,
calls' continuations and joins into its block hand it (argument_sources);
a loop body's arguments, the launch's captures, stay roots by name. This
is to-do (3), reproduced and fixed; the rtcore PTX dumps are unchanged to
the byte. (2) The JIT lacked the device byte fill (bonsai_cuda_fill_bytes_
async), met by the first managed-memory test with a `ran` array.

## The night of 10-25: the GPU schedule refused since 4e5419ee, the answer kept to the owner's side, and the evening's asks (10-25, 22:00 - 10-26)

**The regression.** The verification run's first compile died at 22:17:
`vol_path_step!False.stage(vol_ray_samples, rays!False, samples!False):
vol_path_step!False returns bool; a function on a drained chain returns
nothing` (Stage.cpp). 4e5419ee made every function of a chain report
whether it deferred as soon as *any* function of the chain could return
without deferring, and counted a return anywhere on the chain -- and the
trace kernel's step and the functions under it that push the next ray
(vol_route, vol_surface, vol_medium_scatter, vol_exit) end paths with
plain returns. So the whole rays chain was made to return bool, and the
stage on the same queue refused the step. apps/pbrt's gpu-optix schedule
had not compiled since that commit; it was not compiled after it, which
it should have been (the suite has no shape like the renderer's: a
non-owner function making the first push over a recursion cut by a
stage). Fixed in 629761b6, Defer.cpp alone: only the owner's side of the
chain can return to the owner -- the functions on a call path from the
owner's call that crosses no deferred call (`owner_side`: the camera
function that makes the first push; a recursion's step when the owner
runs the first step itself). What lies below a deferred call runs from
the drain alone; a return there ends an entry's path, not the owner's
call, and it answers nothing and goes on returning nothing. The walk for
a conditional return, the answer type, the passthrough of a callee's
answer, the answer at a return and the answer on a Defer terminator are
each confined to that side. The camera chain is back to its pre-4e5419ee
shape (integrator_li!VolPath!False called with rays!False!end as its
continuation, no callc, no option) and the schedule compiles. Tests: ssa
and correctness/llvm defer-answer-owner-side (the renderer's shape: a
camera function making the first push, a step cut by a stage on its own
queue, a route function that pushes the next step or ends the path --
refused at HEAD with Stage's message); ssa/round-hoist-split's
expectation is its 2df66fc7 one again, to the byte. Rule from it: a
change to Defer.cpp, Stage.cpp or the queue passes compiles the
renderer's gpu-optix schedule before it is committed.

**The verification (the 24 never-compared scenes at 16 spp).** Restarted
22:44 under the fixed compiler; `pbrt --gpu` itself segfaulted on
hair/hair-actual-bsdf (the reference side: pbrt-v4/build/pbrt, its log

**Ask 1 -- "There should be no shortcut".** The user, on the two-queue
item of the evening's status: the second defer should understand that
the function has already been turned into a defer-handler, so there is no
regular return and the continuation runs only in the queues' passes; make
a test with the right shape that currently fails. The shortcut is
QueueSpec::deferred_elsewhere (Convert.cpp reads every directive's callee
off the schedule, and a call to one counts as a push, so the first
directive never reports when another queue is in play). Where every path
of the function defers -- `step` pushing onto `a` when wet and onto `b`
otherwise, each in tail position -- the two directives compose today by
that shortcut, and the shape is right: `step` takes both queues and
returns nothing, the owner's call ends its iteration (`b!end`), no byte,
`b`'s drain chained after `a`'s and before the one pass over the record,
which runs the owner's continuation once per slot after both drains
(tests ssa and correctness/llvm defer-two-queues-one-chain, 629761b6,
pinned as the shape to keep). Where a plain return stands besides --
`step` pushing onto `a` for kind 0, onto `b` for kind 1 and returning
for kind 2 -- the first directive reports and the second dies: `Two
blocks named !step_call_cont_2!rest` (it rebuilds the owner's pass). The
red tests, in the worktree apps/pbrt/scratch/wt-mq (branch
ajr/ssa-multi-queue), not on ajr/ssa: ssa and correctness/llvm
defer-two-queues-and-a-return, the ssa expectation hand-written over the
one-queue dump (a guess at the spelling, to be blessed from the real dump
when the feature lands). The shape they pin:

    step(x, kind, acc, queue_a, slot_a, queue_b, slot_b) -> bool:
        kind == 0:  defer onto a   ret true      # the first directive's push
        kind == 1:  defer onto b   ret true      # the second's: answers too
        else:       ret false                    # deferred nothing
    owner:  deferred = step(..);                 # one dispatch, the first's
            if !deferred { continuation here } else { ran[i] = 1; end }
    drains: a's, then b's (chained), then the one pass over ran[]

The design, to build: (i) the second directive recognizes that the
owner-side chain already answers -- by a mark the first leaves on the
functions it retyped (`Function::answers_for`, the queue's name), not by
pattern-matching the owner's `callc`; (ii) it threads its queue and slot
down as today, turns its site into `defer _queue_b e ret true`, chains
its drain before the existing pass, and builds no dispatch, byte or pass
of its own; (iii) then, if no path of the owner-side chain can return
without deferring any more, the reporting is undone -- the owner's
`callc f(..) q!deferred(..)` becomes `call f(..) q!end()` with `q!end` a
yield, the byte's fill, store and gate go, and the chain's functions
return nothing again -- so that the every-path case comes out as today
without the shortcut; (iv) deferred_elsewhere goes from Convert.cpp. (iii)
is the heavy part: the byte is threaded through the owner's blocks as an
argument, so its removal wants a dead-block-argument cleanup, which the
simplifier may already have (to check). Separate and still open: a second
*continuation* of one function (`f!after exists already; f is staged
twice`, `f!g!k exists already; the call is deferred twice`) -- two
deferrals that each cut `f` -- is refused and stays refused until there is
a reason to have it.

**Ask 2 -- "What is the owner's own first push? Is something broken?"**
Nothing was broken in the program: with `run.defer(step, q)` beside
`step.defer(step, q)` the owner's call pushes the first entry instead of
running the first step (QueueSpec::initial_push), and the lowered program
was the same either way. What was odd was the SSA: every other push that
ends an iteration had become the `defer q entry [yield]` terminator in
2df66fc7, and this one was still `@n = push q entry` followed by `jmp
q!end` with `q!end` holding the yield. Built in the worktree (Defer.cpp,
the initial_push call of push_entry: `ends` when the owner loops over the
call, so the push is `defer q entry yield` and the `end` block goes; a
lone call's owner keeps the instruction and the jump to the drain, since
nothing of its ends there). Test ssa/defer-initial-push (red on ajr/ssa:
its expectation is today's dump with the terminator in place of the
push-and-jump, the `q!end` block gone and the drain's names one lower).
It found a real bug: Simplify.cpp's resolve_uses -- "points every use in
the function at what its value became" -- had an empty Defer visitor, so
when value numbering merged the owner's `gep(q_queue, 0)` with the entry
block's and dropped the one in the loop body, the Defer terminator kept
the dropped value and the lowering failed (`Var: @10 not in current block,
and current block is entry!`); fixed in the worktree (the visitor resolves
queue, entry and answer). Untested until a build is allowed (10-26);
Simplify.cpp is a shared file, bonsai-ac to be told before it lands.

**Ask 3 -- copies.** pbrt makes them: RayWorkItem, EscapedRayWorkItem,
HitAreaLightWorkItem and ShadowRayWorkItem (wavefront/workitems.h) each
carry depth, lambda, pixelIndex, beta, r_u, r_l and prevIntrCtx again;
the reload by slot was our own idea to beat pbrt's entry sizes, not a
fidelity matter, and stays optional.

**Ask 4 -- the hit chain, for approval.** Six dependent loads from the
hit to the material against pbrt's four (the 10-24 reading). The plan in
two parts. (a) The parts of the chain that are constant per hit-group
record -- the shape arm and the mesh row -- hoisted into the OptiX
hit-group record (the SBT) by partial evaluation in Lower/Trees.cpp: the
closest-hit program reads them off its record instead of following the
primitive index to the arm and the arm to the mesh; two loads gone,
matching pbrt's per-record `TriangleMeshRecord`. (b) The per-hit range
lookup, which needs "The triangle range as a set the type describes"
(the 10-19 proposal above): the range a set whose type carries its
bounds, so the index into the mesh needs no lookup. (a) alone needs a
build and a GPU image check -- after the machine is free; (b) is the
language change proposed on 10-19 and waits for the user's yes.

**Ask 5 -- the NaN pixels (kroken, watercolor at 128/256 spp; portal
lights suspected), the plan, uninvasive first.** (1) Narrow the sample:

**The tris array, from pbrt's source (the user's question, 10-26).** pbrt
has two data structures for a mesh's triangles, one per path. The CPU
path has exactly our rows: `Triangle::CreateTriangles` (shapes.cpp:272)
allocates one `Triangle` object per triangle, and the class is two ints,
`{meshIndex, triIndex}` (shapes.h:839, :1188), 8 bytes, with a
SimplePrimitive or GeometricPrimitive per triangle on top and the BVH over
those. The GPU path has no per-triangle object: `TriangleMeshRecord {mesh,
material, alphaTexture, areaLights, mediumInterface}` is the hit-group
record per mesh (gpu/optix/optix.h:26), and the closest-hit program names
the triangle by `rec.mesh` and `optixGetPrimitiveIndex()` (optix.cu:192).
So render_hook.cpp's `tris.push_back(Triangle{m, k})` loop is pbrt's
CreateTriangles loop, byte for byte -- not invented data -- but the
program fixes that one representation (`Mesh(mesh, tris : set[Triangle])`,
the rows the driver fills) where pbrt's GPU path shows the
representation-free statement: a triangle is (its mesh, its index), and a
mesh's triangles are the indices 0 to n-1. The right specification is the
one both pbrt paths agree on, stated in the program and left to the layout
to store or not: `Mesh(mesh : u32, count : u32)` with `geometry` mapping
`|i| triangle_geometric(Triangle{mesh, i})` over `0:count` -- the range as
a set value (the 10-19 proposal), with which a software-tree layout may
still store rows as pbrt's CPU does and the OptiX layout stores nothing
as pbrt's GPU does. Part (a) is pbrt's per-mesh record exactly: the mesh
row already holds material, alpha, media and first light, the record's
fields. Awaiting the user's word on the range as a set value before any
of (b) is built.

**Corrected within the hour (the user: "the layout language allows us to
specify how a reference type maps to the concrete value of the stored
type, right? That's how Scion's layout language works").** Right, and the
range in the program was wrong, as was "a new storage kind": the storage
kind exists. A layout `group` maps a reference -- its index -- to the
element's value field by field, each field stored (`name : type`) or
computed from the reference and the stored fields (`name = expr`,
ir::Materialize), and a group all of whose fields are computed stores no
bytes (Lower/Layouts.cpp stores_nothing: Embree's NodeRef, "the reference
is the data"); the tree leaves use computed fields already (`left = mnode
+ 1`, `data = range(tris, pOffset, nPrims)`). So pbrt's two storages of a
mesh's triangles are two layouts of the one declaration `Mesh(mesh, tris :
set[Triangle])`, with no change to the program:

    // CPU, pbrt's CPU: a Triangle object per row, 8 bytes
    group tris[tCount] k : u32 { mesh : u32; tri : u32; };
    // GPU, pbrt's GPU: nothing stored, the Triangle computed from its reference
    group tris[tCount] k : u32 { mesh = holder.mesh; tri = k - holder.first; };

The one thing missing: a computed field may name the group's index and
its own stored fields, not the *holder* -- the Mesh primitive whose run
of `tris` the element lies in -- although `Mesh.tris : OptixTree from
tris` binds the set to its holder and the Mesh arm stores the run's first
row and count. The extension is `holder` in the computed fields of a
group bound as a holder's set: general to every set a holder owns, no
program change, and on the OptiX side the holder is in the hit record
already (and its fields inline after part (a)). What (b) now is, with the
user's yes: `holder` in a group's computed fields, the OptiX layout above,
and Lower/Trees.cpp taking a computed group as a run's element storage
(`stored(tris, base + prim)` becoming arithmetic). The 10-19 range
proposal is withdrawn.

**Refined by the user ("make the GPU layout reference also take a holder
as the second argument to a reference").** Not `holder` as a name in
scope: the *reference* to an element of `tris` is the pair (holder,
ordinal), since a triangle is unique only within its mesh -- the minimal
bits naming a unique element, the rule references follow. pbrt's GPU
reference is exactly the pair (`rec.mesh`, `optixGetPrimitiveIndex()`);
its CPU reference is a row number into an array whose rows store the
pair (`Triangle{meshIndex, triIndex}`). Two layouts of one reference:

    group tris (h : Mesh, k : u32) { mesh = h.mesh; tri = k; };   // GPU: the pair, nothing stored
    group tris[tCount] k : u32 { mesh : u32; tri : u32; };        // CPU: a row storing the pair

What follows: the `group` index declaration takes a second component, the
holder's reference, when the group is bound as a holder's set (general to
every set a holder owns); the GPU side then needs no run -- no `base` in
the hit record, no `first` in the Mesh arm -- since the record's holder
and the primitive index are the reference as OptiX hands it over; a
query's best-hit record carries the pair (two u32, minimal bits still)
instead of the row and the holder it carries today; `stored(tris, ref)` in
Lower/Trees.cpp is the computed fields of the pair, no load; the CPU
layout keeps the row reference and the leaves' `range(tris, pOffset,
nPrims)`. (b) is now: the two-component reference in the layout grammar,
the computed group bound to a holder's set, trees/optix.bonsai written
that way, and the tree lowering producing (holder, primitive index) as
the reference and computing the element from it. To build after (a),
when the user says go.

**Built (10-26 afternoon, the user: "use this and make sure our codegen
strictly improves on the GPU and does not change on the CPU"; worktree
wt-mq, to land as one commit).** The layout language gains a group indexed
by (holder, ordinal): `group tris (h : Mesh, k : u32) { mesh = h.mesh; tri
= k; };` -- named, every member computed (`name = expr`), no size, no
bytes; ir::Group::holder_name/holder_t and Group::make_of_holder, the
parser's GROUP case (the pair in parentheses after the name, the holder
an element or variant by name -- element_type_of -- the two names scoped
to the body, so two such groups may both say `h`), the printer, the
layout comparison (Equality.cpp), Layout::count() (no rows). In the
lowering (Lower/Layouts.cpp) the group is registered in
LayoutTypeMap::of_holder and makes no array and no field; a stored-element
read through a field the schedule bound to it (`Mesh.tris : OptixTree
from mesh_tris`, LowerMatches::visit(StoredElement)) checks the holder's
type is the element the field is read off, substitutes that element's
value for `h` and the read's index for `k` into the members, and builds
the element in its own field order -- `Triangle{e0.mesh, idx}`, no load.
trees/optix.bonsai: `mesh_tris` for `Mesh.tris` and `placed_tris` for
`Placed.tris`, and no `tris`/`tCount` array; trees/bvh.bonsai untouched.
render_hook.cpp: `kTrisStored = requires(_tree_layout0 t) { t.tris; }`
decides whether the rows are uploaded and whether a mesh input's `base` is
its run's start or 0 (the primitive index is then the triangle's index in
the mesh, as pbrt's); the `Primitive_Mesh` row keeps its `tris` word
(unread by the hit chain now; a later cleanup). Lower/Trees.cpp is
untouched: `idx = base + prim` with `base = 0` is the ordinal, and the
`_RTHit` record's `idx` and `top` are the pair already. Found and fixed
on the way, at its root: SSA/Convert.cpp's lazy select (`ite(own, a, b)`,
the lazy select Trees.cpp makes of one own arm and one held arm) set the
arm's value before the call the arm made -- `block->make_instruction(..,
get_value(..))` reads the receiver before the argument splits the block
at the call -- so `@14 is not bound in __anyhit__trace` for a mapped arm
whose lambda calls (`triangle_of(t)`); the renderer never hit it (three
held arms, the match). Tests: backends/ptx/rtcore-holder-reference (the
closest-hit program reads the record, the primitive index, `prims[top]`,
the Mesh row and then the mesh's index and position arrays: no triangle
row; golden pinned at sm_90 as the directory pins) and
correctness/gpu/rtcore-holder-reference with its driver (two meshes and a
standalone triangle, the mesh inputs based at 0 with the mesh primitive as
holder and no row uploaded; five rays report the corner and the mesh,
right). Suite 1890 green. The renderer's gpu-optix schedule compiles
(6 m 31 s), its render.o 73 151 712 bytes against 73 176 024 with the
rows. The GPU and CPU measurements follow below.

`tris` word, unread by the hit chain now, and part (a) -- the arm and the
mesh row into the hit-group record -- which takes the chain from four
dependent loads (record, prims[top], the Mesh row, the mesh's arrays) to
pbrt's.

**Part (a), the holder element into the hit-group record (the user, 10-26
~15:00: "go ahead"; built and measured 18:40-19:30, below).** What a hit program derives from the record alone, before
any program function runs, is the holder element -- `prims[rec.holder]`,
a tagged index -- and its arm's row, two dependent loads; pbrt's record
holds the mesh pointer and the per-mesh attributes and loads the mesh
struct through it, so carrying the holder's arm in our record reaches
pbrt's count (record, the Mesh row `meshes[mesh]`, indices, positions);
the mesh row itself is the step past pbrt, which needs the slicing through
`triangle_geometric` and is not in this change. The general form, no
knowledge of pbrt in it: the program's `_RTRecord` is base, holder, `_tag`
(the holder's variant) and, for every arm of the flatten's match that
holds a tree, that arm's non-set fields, each named
ir::rt_record_field(variant index, field) (Lower/Trees.cpp
record_type_of; one record per program). In the hit programs a held arm
reads the holder as the new marker intrinsic `rt_sbt_element()` (typed as
the element), and the layout lowering turns every `Access(f, Unwrap(k,
rt_sbt_element()))` into the record's field read off `rt_sbt_record()`
(LowerMatches::visit(Access)) -- the pair-group's `h.mesh` included, its
bound expression lowered once more -- so no `prims[holder]` and no arm row
is loaded; which arm the holder is, the record's tag says (lazy selects
on `_tag` for the held arms, the own test before them; bind_elements).
The tree's own elements keep `stored(tree, idx)`. The driver fills the
record through a generated export, `bonsai_rt_record_fill(holder, out,
<the tree>)`: `stored(tree, holder)` matched on, a record built per arm
with its tag and fields and zeros in the others' (add_record_fill). The
runtime (bonsai_optix.h) sizes its records by the generated header's
`BONSAI_OPTIX_RECORD_BYTES` (= sizeof(_RTRecord), emitted before the
include; 8 for a program without a record of its own), takes the
element's bytes per input (`bonsai_optix_triangles::record`, for an input
with a holder of its own) or per placement per input
(`bonsai_optix_instance::records`), copies them when the geometry or scene
is built, and writes them into each hit-group record after base and
holder. The OptiX code generator loads the record at the intrinsic's own
type.

*Built (10-26 evening).* Two changes to the design above, from the first
renderer compile: the record carries only the holder fields the hit
programs read -- directly in the arm's expression, or through the layout
group bound to the arm's set field, whose members compute the stored
element from the holder (`mesh = h.mesh`; Lower/Trees.cpp fields_read) --
because with every held field it was 288 bytes for apps/pbrt (the Placed
and Inst transforms, four of them, which the hit programs never read; the
raygen reads the instance's row after the trace as before), and is 20:
base, holder, tag, `_1_mesh`, `_2_mesh`; the filler then needs the Placed
pool alone. And a placement with one holder carries one record, one per
input only with holder_per_input (bonsai_optix.h). Found and fixed at the
root on the way: the old two-word `_RTRecord` (ir::rt_record_type) beside
the program's was a second struct type of one name, which
common-subexpression elimination took for the same expression (`_1_mesh`
then read off the two-word one); every rewrite that rebuilds an intrinsic
from its op alone -- Mutator, CSE's Rename and LVN, RenamePointerToExpr,
the SSA-to-statement and SSA-to-LLVM code generators -- dropped a
program-typed intrinsic's type (Intrinsic::make_like, typed_by_program);
`#if BONSAI_OPTIX_RECORD_BYTES > 8` cannot see a `sizeof`, so the
runtime's record is a template on the count; the header always declares
`_RTRecord` (rtcore-alpha's driver found it missing); and the renderer's
filler, a host call made before the buffers are staged, aborted on
killeroo's empty Placed pool under --no-implicit-copies until the driver
stages its four buffers first as it does for every other generated call.
Tests: backends/ptx/rtcore-holder-reference re-blessed (the record read at
bytes 0, 4, 12; the held side straight from the mesh index to the mesh's
arrays; the own side loads its row under the holder test),
correctness/gpu/rtcore-holder-reference's driver fills the mesh inputs'
records (mesh 1 reports mesh 1, which only the record can say); every
other rtcore golden unchanged, their records being the two words plus a
tag. Suite 1892/1892 in the worktree.
