**The Mesh row's `tris` word gone (the user, 10-26 evening: "start with the
mesh row and unread tris word").** A set field bound to a group indexed by
(holder, ordinal) stores nothing: the holder is the element the field is
read off, so the stored Mesh is its mesh index alone and the stored Placed
its two transforms and mesh, where each kept a `tris` word -- the hardware
tree's run start, which a group computing its elements from the pair has no
run for -- that nothing read. Lower/Layouts.cpp binds such a field to no
reference type and leaves it out of the stored element; the reads through it
are lowered before the stored-type rewrite (LowerHolderReads, the computed
element factored out of LowerMatches), a build of the element drops the
field's value and a match arm its binding. The variant constructors follow
(`Primitive_Mesh(out, mesh)`, `Primitive_Placed(.., mesh, pool, fill)`), and
render_hook.cpp builds its mesh and placed primitives through a template on
whether the layout stores the triangles (make_mesh, make_placed), one call
per layout compiled; the CPU layouts store rows and keep the word. GPU
(gpu-compare-out-tris against gpu-compare-out-record): the same images, and
the kernel time within noise -- 27.51 -> 27.59, 118.32 -> 118.30, 729.77 ->
729.20 ms; a word per mesh primitive is not what these scenes wait on, and
the point was the layout's honesty. CPU render.o byte-identical for scalar
and wavefront-volpath.

**The mesh row into the record (the user, 10-26 evening: "start with the
mesh row"), built as partial evaluation of the hit programs with the
record as the static input (SSA/RecordHoist.h).** What a hit program
computes from the record alone -- the mesh row's fields at the record's
mesh, which pbrt's TriangleMeshRecord holds and ours loaded from `meshes`
first -- is computed once per record by the driver and read off the
record. A binding-time analysis over every function that reads the record
(the closest-hit, any-hit and intersection programs, the hit-side trace
variants) gives each value one of three times: the launch's (parameters,
constants), the record's (its fields, and what is computed from them and
from read-only storage at such indices), the hit's (the primitive index,
the ray, anything written, and what depends on them). The residual program
replaces each record-time *load* the hit needs -- directly, or through
record-time arithmetic, which stays in the program over the field -- by a
read of a new record field `_<arm>_h<n>`, the arm being the one whose
fields the load's address reads (a record over the tree's own elements is
never filled, so a load reading no arm field stays); the generating
extension is the filler (bonsai_rt_record_fill), which computes the field's
slice in that arm from the arm's record values and the arrays, zeros in the
other arms, the arrays added to its parameters under the programs' names.
The analysis sees through the calls a program makes: a call whose argument
carries a record part (the triangle built from the record's mesh and the
primitive index; a shape's payload packing both) is copied into the program
first (SSA/Rewrite.h's inline_call, after the hit continuations are split
and before the allocas are promoted), the simplification after each copy
folding the packing. Only loads are hoisted, never arithmetic, and a struct
read field by field hoists the fields read, not the row: the first renderer
compile carried `first_light < 0` as a bool field beside first_light, the
second a whole TriangleMesh row per arm, and the rule settled on loads,
field-wise. One computation is one field however many programs make it. Tests: ssa/blocks/record-hoist (the final SSA: the filler's Mesh
arm computing `mesh_first_index[mesh]` and `mesh_first_vertex[mesh]` and
building the record with them, the two arrays threaded to the arm as
parameters; the inlined triangle fetch reading fields 4 and 5 of the
threaded record before the indices), backends/ptx/rtcore-holder-reference
re-blessed (record read at bytes 0, 4, 16, 20; no mesh-array loads in the
hit programs), correctness/gpu/rtcore-holder-reference's driver passing the
two arrays to the filler. Suite 1896/1896 beside them.
BONSAI_EXPLAIN_RECORD_HOIST=1 prints what each program inlines, hoists and
keeps.

*apps/pbrt.* The record is base, holder, tag, the two mesh indices and,
per held arm (Mesh, Placed), the five fields of the mesh row that
triangle_geometric reads -- first_light, material, alpha, medium_inside,
medium_outside -- sixty bytes; the filler takes `meshes`, which
render_hook.cpp passes and stages with the rest. Not hoisted in the
renderer: the triangle's own vertex fetch (first_index, first_vertex). The
intersection test runs after the own and held sides merge their Triangle
(`_rt_e1`), and on the own side the mesh index is the hit's, so the row
read inside the test is hit-time; it stays one dependent load, as pbrt's
is (its record holds the mesh pointer and loads the struct through it).
Specializing the test per side -- the own side's triangle is never a mesh
triangle in a pbrt scene, but the compiler cannot know it -- is the step
after this one, worth taking only if a profile says the mesh row's load is
on the hit's critical path.

**`sort` on a call outside a ray tracing kernel is refused (the user,
10-26, after asking which pbrt schedules sort a queue and which apply
SER).** One directive, `f.sort(g, |args| key)`, means one thing -- the
calls to `g` that `f` makes run in ascending key -- and is had three ways:
exactly, when the calls are deferred onto a queue (wavefront-frame-packet-
reorder, wavefront-thread-packet-sort, gpu-optix-sort, gpu-optix-sort36:
the entries drained in key order); approximately, when the calls are made
in place inside a loop bound to OptixThread (gpu-optix-mega-ser,
gpu-optix-fused-ser, gpu-optix-mega-ser-ray: optixReorder before the
call); and not at all when the calls are made in place anywhere else,
which Lower/Sorts.cpp used to drop in silence and now refuses, naming the
two ways (in_optix_raygen: the sorting function is, or is called from, a
function with a loop bound to OptixThread). `trace.sort(primitives.
Interior, ...)` is the third kind, the traversal's child order, neither.
No pbrt schedule trips the refusal. Test error/sort-in-place-unbound;
docs/schedule-semantics.md's sort paragraph states the three cases.
lower/sort-call, which documented the in-place hint in a parfor bound to
nothing, binds its loop to OptixThread under `-p ssa` now and is
re-blessed: the three hints in their places, and each hint's let with a
name of its own (`_rt_reordered0..2`; the use counting refused the
shadowing that one statement with two sorted calls made). The
third argument of `defer`/`stage`, asked about the same hour, names the
first pass of a cut on the same queue (4.5), a cursor the directive
creates rather than a loop it takes -- the paper's signature table has it
as an input, and the grammar's own `C = f.transform(...)` convention would
put it on the left; left as it is in the language, noted for the paper.

**The composition built (10-26, landed as 190ffe86; apps/pbrt's gpu-optix
schedule compiles and its render.o is byte for byte 99c5de0d's).** A
deferral whose owner's call is an earlier deferral's
`<q>!deferred` dispatch -- found through Function::OwnedQueue::Reporting,
which a reporting deferral now leaves on the owner's queue: the dispatch
and end blocks, the pass's gate blocks, the copied continuation and its
original, the byte's allocation and fill when the reporting alone made
them, the retyped functions, the answer type -- composes with it: it
leaves the call alone, makes its pushes in those functions answer
"deferred" in the earlier answer's terms, chains its drain after the
earlier one's and before that pass, and builds no dispatch, byte or pass
of its own (its `k0` is empty: the rest of the iteration is the earlier
pass's). Its tail-position check, and Convert's choice between defer and
defer_continuation (has_nontail_call), accept a call followed only by the
chain's answer -- `work_b(..); ret (bool)0`, or the option of the call's
value -- as a tail call (SSA/Stage.h returns_chain_answer): the deferral
replaces that answer with its own, so nothing of the function's runs after
the call. The walk for a plain return covers the earlier deferral's
functions too and treats a call into one of them as a call into the chain.
When it finds none (undo_prior), the reporting is undone at the end of the
pass: the owner's call is made plain by the ordinary branch (a fresh
`<q2>!end`, the dispatch and the byte's store unreachable), the pass's
gate on the byte becomes the jump it guarded, aimed at the original
continuation instead of its copy (whose returns become yields), the byte's
load and address, allocation, fill and induced-storage registration go,
the chain's functions are retyped to void with their Defer answers and
answering returns cleared, every call that took the answer drops it (its
continuation's first argument removed), and the block arguments that
carried the byte and the answer for nothing are removed by a new
simplifier utility, remove_dead_arguments (Simplify.h; not part of
simplify(), which has no such pass -- the Defer undo calls it after the
dead instructions are gone). QueueSpec::deferred_elsewhere no longer reads
the schedule's other `defer`s: the every-path case now goes first
directive reports, second undoes, and comes out as the pinned shape, less
one dead `out` argument of the owner's loop body that the cleanup takes
with the byte (ssa/defer-two-queues-one-chain re-blessed: that argument
and renumbering; gate-drains-gang the same route, renumbering only). The
set still holds the `stage`s' callees: the Stage pass refuses a reporting
chain ("a function on a drained chain returns nothing") and does not
compose with one, so a `stage` after a `defer` on the owner's side of its
chain would otherwise make the chain report and then be refused -- the
remaining shortcut, to go when Stage composes as Defer now does. Tests:
ssa + correctness/llvm defer-two-queues-and-a-return (the reporting kept:
`defer _queue_a @e ret (bool)1`, `defer _queue_b @e ret (bool)1`, `ret
(bool)0`, one `callc step(..) a!deferred(..)`, `a!end` setting the byte,
b's drain between a's and the gated pass; values 102.5, 107, 104, 107, 116,
107, 111.5, 125) and defer-two-queues-one-chain (the undo); the two error
tests' expectations changed by the assert's line and text only. Suite 1884
green in the worktree.

## 10-27: the megakernel against Dr.Jit's -- one thread per path, one launch per frame, and the field specialize that stopped at the call

**The question (the user, 10-27 morning).** Why are our megakernel
schedules so slow, when Dr.Jit's megakernel is 2.14x faster than
`pbrt --gpu`? Dr.Jit (Jakob, Speierer, Roussel, Vicini; arXiv 2202.01284,
Fig. 5 and 6, an RTX A6000: Staircase at 3 bounces and 64 spp, Living room
at 12 bounces, Glass of water at 32 bounces) reports its megakernel at a
geometric mean of 2.14x over PBRT 4 --gpu and 3.70x over Mitsuba 2, and its
own wavefront -- "every loop and polymorphic call unrolled into separate
kernels that communicate through global memory", not pbrt's queue
wavefront -- 2.0 to 7.7x slower than its megakernel on the GPU. Ours
(gpu-compare-out-b, the night of 10-26, kernel ms at 16 spp): killeroo-gold
pbrt 149, wavefront 68, megakernel 182, megakernel with the SER sort 134;
ganesha pbrt 177, wavefront 95, megakernel 560 (0.32x of pbrt), 490 with
the sort; and the megakernel's time is linear in spp where pbrt's is not
quite. So the question is what Dr.Jit's megakernel does that ours does
not. What it does, from the paper and drjit-core's source
(https://github.com/mitsuba-renderer/drjit-core: src/optix_core.cpp,
src/call.cpp; https://drjit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference.html):
(a) it is a tracing JIT, so the kernel holds the types the scene
instantiates and nothing else -- a scene of two materials compiles two
BSDF arms, where our raygen compiles every material, shape, light and
texture of pbrt (`__raygen__p$VolPath$False$False` is 220,872 PTX lines
with no media and no subsurface, `$True$True` 613,340); (b) one lane per
sample of the pass: the launch is pixels x samples-per-pass threads, each
lane one path, the passes sized to memory (Mitsuba 3's spp_per_pass);
(c) a polymorphic call is a direct callable under OptiX
(`__direct_callable__<hash>` program groups, `optixDirectCall` selected by
the instance's index out of an offset table) or an indirect `call` through
a `.callprototype` under CUDA, with the callee's unreferenced inputs and
outputs pruned and identical callees deduplicated by hash, which the paper
puts at 2.5x on OptiX for its polymorphism-heavy scenes (§3.5, (d));
(d) loops stay loops in one kernel (registers and labels), with "loop
tracing inconclusive on the GPU" and ~65% of a loop's state variables
removed by its optimizations; (e) its OptiX modules leave
`maxRegisterCount` at OptiX's default (0) and `optLevel` 3, `maxTraceDepth`
1, two attribute values, a trivial `__miss__`, the continuation stack
`cssRG + max(cssCH, cssMS, cssAH + cssIS)`; (f) shader execution
reordering at the trace and at `reorder_threads`. Against ours, four
hypotheses, in the order they were tested: (1) `render.bind(p, OptixThread)`
gives a thread a pixel and has it run the pixel's samples in turn, so a
warp's lanes drift apart in sample and bounce and the warp executes the
union of their paths, where lanes that all start a path together lose only
the ones that end early; (2) every arm in one raygen -- the code size and
register pressure of 09-22's entry and 10-15's bisection (the two flags,
have_media and have_subsurface, bought back 113 of 161 ms; the rest of
the arms are still there); (3) the continuation stack a path keeps live
across `optixTrace`; (4) divergence at the hit, which the SER sort already
takes 1.36x out of.

**Hypothesis 1 measured: 1.74x, and one launch per frame 1.86x.** Two
schedules. gpu-optix-mega-pass is gpu-optix-mega with
`render[VolPath].reorder(p, s)`: the sample loop outside the pixel loop,
the per-pixel prologue (the AOVs' zeroing, 36 PTX lines, a raygen of its
own with a continuation stack of 0) distributed into a loop before the
nest, and then a raygen launch per sample over the frame's pixels, one
thread one path -- which is what gpu-optix-mega's header said could not be
done ("the pixel loop does work of its own before its samples, so the two
loops cannot be collapsed into one thread per sample"); the reorder's
distribution is exactly what does it. gpu-optix-mega-flat adds
`render[VolPath].collapse(s, p, ps)` and `render[VolPath].bind(ps,
OptixThread)`: the interchanged nest collapsed into one loop over
(sample, pixel) pairs, the pixel fastest, one launch of spp x pixels
threads for the frame -- Dr.Jit's shape (b), and the shape 09-22's entry
proposed for the software megakernel as its first item ("the block is the
wrong shape"); the pixel's sum is then the atomic the program wrote, in
whatever order the lanes finish, which is the trade render.bonsai's pixel
loop says a schedule may make. Through gpu_compare.sh (compiler f2e47a10,
the worktree's build; gpu-compare-out-mq and -mq2; killeroo-gold and
ganesha at 16 spp; every image `ok: the image matches pbrt`, the flat
schedule's included):

| kernel ms, 16 spp | pbrt --gpu | gpu-optix-mega (a pixel's samples in turn) | gpu-optix-mega-pass (a launch per sample) | gpu-optix-mega-flat (one launch) | gpu-optix (wavefront, night run) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| killeroo-gold | 149.4 | 181.2 | 104.0 | 97.4 | 67.6 |
| ganesha | 177.0 | 560.6 | 321.8 | 316.4 | 94.9 |

The samples in turn cost 1.74x on both scenes (181 -> 104, 561 -> 322),
and the launch per frame another 6% on killeroo-gold and 2% on ganesha
(the per-launch tail -- the frame's longest path -- paid once instead of
sixteen times, and sixteen launches' gaps). The megakernel is now ahead of
pbrt --gpu on killeroo-gold (1.53x on kernel time, 2.26x on wall) and at
0.56x of it on ganesha; the wavefront is still 1.44x and 3.3x ahead of the
flat megakernel. The continuation stack (BONSAI_OPTIX_STATS) is 384 to
736 bytes a thread for gpu-optix-mega's four volpath raygens, 544 to 704
for the reordered ones; hypothesis 3 is not what moved.

**The compiler bug on the way: the field form of specialize stopped at
the call.** The pass schedule's `$True$False` raygen came out at 613,688
PTX lines with 8 trace sites, the same as `$True$True`, and `$False$False`
at 250,080 with 4, the same as `$False$True` (gpu-optix-mega: 513,925 / 4
and 220,872 / 2): both copies of each pair carried the subsurface arm,
have_subsurface no longer a constant in either. A small reproduction
(ssa/specialize-field-callee) shows why, and that it never worked for a
callee that is not inlined: `render[VolPath].specialize(
VolPath::have_subsurface)` copies the loop and forces the field's byte in
the copy's value of the integrator (SSA/Specialize.cpp force_fixed_field),
and SSA/Specialize.h says the callees handed the value are copied with the
field fixed as they are with a tag fixed -- but specialize_callees knew
the value only by its name, or through a load of it, and after
`render.specialize(integrator)` the call's argument is no longer the
parameter: it is the first copy's struct, `build<Integrator>(3u, pad,
payload)` of the parameter's own fields with the tag a constant, which the
tag specialize put in place of every read. So `integrator_li!VolPath!True`
(the have_media copy) stayed shared by both have_subsurface copies, each
handing it a struct whose byte was forced by arithmetic (`word &
0xFFFF00FF`, `| 0x10000`), and the byte folded only where LLVM inlined
`integrator_li` into the raygen and saw that arithmetic -- which it did
under gpu-optix-mega, and not under the reorder: the forcing is pure
arithmetic on an invariant read, so reorder() hoists it before the nest
(SSA/ReorderLoops.h), which under `bind(p, OptixThread)` is the host, and
the kernel received the finished struct as a launch parameter, in which no
byte is a constant. Fixed at the root in specialize_callees: `names()` now
also recognizes the value rebuilt with constants put in -- a MakeStruct of
the value's type whose tag is a constant equal to this variant's and whose
every other operand is the value's own field at that index (LoadField), or
at the payload its words rebuilt lane by lane with a byte forced
(force_fixed_field's shape: ExtractIdx of the value's payload per lane,
masked and or'ed with constants), which is what a field fixed earlier
leaves -- and a slot an earlier copy made that stores nothing but the
value. Nothing looser: a struct the program builds from some of the
value's fields is not the value. With it the field form clones the callee
per value of the field (`apply!Sum!False`, `apply!Sum!True`; in the
renderer the four `integrator_li!VolPath!{False,True}!{False,True}`, each
raygen copy calling its own), and the field is a constant in SSA, where
fold_forced_words and the known-bits rule fold the arm's `if` -- nothing
left to the backend. In the renderer (the post-schedule dump of
gpu-optix-mega-pass under 927fa485) `integrator_li!VolPath!True!False`
hands `li_vol_path` the literal `(bool)0` for have_subsurface, where
`integrator_li!VolPath!True` handed it `@110 != 0u`, a byte extracted
from the word the host had forced; the arm's `if` below is folded on a
literal argument. Tests at every level:
ssa/specialize-field-callee (the two clones, the `* 2f` in True alone,
each loop copy calling its own), ssa/specialize-field-reorder (the
renderer's shape: the nest interchanged after the field form, the forced
struct hoisted before the nest and the clones called from the inner
body), correctness/llvm/specialize-field-callee (the three answers run).
The 68 specialize-family tests and the 60 that name callee copies pass;
the suite 1916 of 1916 on the rebuilt worktree compiler (927fa485 on
ajr/ssa-multi-queue, cherry-picked onto ajr/ssa as b80bfa6d). A design
note from the way
the bug surfaced: reorder()'s hoisting of pure arithmetic on invariant
reads is right by its own rules and moves that arithmetic across the
kernel boundary under a GPU bind -- a value LLVM could have folded in the
kernel becomes a launch parameter; harmless once the SSA holds the
constant, but worth remembering for any other value a specialize forces
by arithmetic.

**What remains of the gap, and what Dr.Jit does that we do not --
proposals needing the user's word.** Where the day ends: the megakernel
at 16 spp is 2.5x of pbrt --gpu's kernel time on killeroo-gold (181 ->

of pbrt on ganesha (561 -> 270), 2.8x behind the wavefront (94.9). So
the answer to the morning's question is in two parts. Most of the

samples-per-pass, which `reorder(p, s)` plus `collapse(s, p, ps)` now

the scene instantiates, where `__raygen__p$VolPath$False$False` carries

holds a 544-byte continuation stack live across every `optixTrace` --
and (b) polymorphic calls as OptiX direct callables with pruned
inputs and outputs, so the raygen's register allocation is not the
union of every arm's. The register cap is not among them (mq4). Which of
the two it is on ganesha cannot be told from kernel time alone, and the
GPU profilers stay off OptiX without the user's word. Proposals, each a
new construct and so asked before built: (1) a `specialize` on the
variants a table holds -- `render.specialize(materials)` copying the
loop for the set of material tags the scene instantiates, decided at
scene load, so that the raygen a scene runs carries its arms alone (the
set form; the copies would be per distinct set seen, the dispatch at the
launch); or, Dr.Jit's own answer, (2) a bind of a match's arms to OptiX
direct callables (`materials.bind(DirectCallable)`), the raygen keeping
the dispatch and each arm compiled apart; (3) the profiler on ganesha's
two kernels (ours and pbrt's wavefront's trace) to settle (a) against
(b) first. Also asked: whether the GPU wavefront figure
(plot_gpu_wavefront.py, plots.sh's GPU_TABLES) should gain the flat
megakernel sides -- gpu-optix-mega-flat and -mega-ser-flat -- which
needs the five-scene, three-spp sweep (about 2 h of card); and the full
pbrt redo (CPU and GPU) owed anyway once the loopify exit rewrite lands
on top of aa4dbaaa's min/max change, into which that sweep would fold.

the harness-only speedups (2, 3, 4) after the sweep lands").** Edited
after the runs ended, untested until the first free card window
tomorrow (after bonsai-ac's stars table and the 08:30-08:50 profiler
slot), then committed. gpu_compare.sh compiles every schedule in
parallel, each into OUT/<schedule>/ -- the compiler's render.h and
render.o there, the driver linked as render.out, compile.log, and
render.key -- where it compiled them one after another into
apps/pbrt/render.{h,o} because the driver's `#include "render.h"` found

time'); render_hook.cpp and nanovdb_shim.cpp now include the macro

gpu_compare.sh passes each compile's own. The shim and the schema header
are built once before the compiles (both write under apps/pbrt).
render.key is a sha256 over the compiler binary and its flags, every
.bonsai under apps/pbrt and the stdlib's, the schedule and the trees,
the driver's sources and headers, the runtime headers, the shim's
source and build script, the GPU and the C++ compiler; `--reuse DIR`
copies a schedule's renderer from an earlier run whose key is this
run's and compiles only what has no match, `--resume` reuses this run's
own renderers under the same test and recompiles one whose key moved
(a renderer without a key -- every run before today's -- is compiled
again); the converter (scene_dump, 16 s a run) is keyed and reused the
same way. heatmap.sh passes `--reuse` through, so a heatmap after a
sweep under the same compiler skips its one compile. Expected from
today's timings: the seven-side sweep's compiles from an hour to about
ten minutes (seven compilers at once on 32 cores and 186 GB; the peak
memory of one is to be read off tomorrow's compile.log), and the
heatmap's from six and a half minutes to none. The 'one compare at a
time' rule still holds for compare.sh, render.sh, check_hits.sh and
check_differentials.sh, which write apps/pbrt/render.{h,o} as before.

**The A/B under a53c8f84 (07:41-08:04): the remainder is the
funnel's.** The two flat megakernels compiled at once through the
compiler at a53c8f84 (585 s each) and ran on killeroo-gold and
killeroo-simple at 16 spp (gpu-compare-out-ab-a53c8f84, every image
matching pbrt). Kernel ms, a53c8f84 / 39c67ab9 (the night) / 9846e3e6
(run c): mk-ser-flat on killeroo-gold 59.62 / 64.28 / 71.55 -- mq3b's
59.40 of 10-27 afternoon reproduced on the pre-funnel base with the
device min/max and the specialize fix in, so the 8% the fix left is
the funnel's own shape, with no stack cost (the SER raygens'
continuation stacks are the pre-funnel widths exactly); mk-ser-flat on
killeroo-simple 23.53 / 24.68 / 26.08, the fixed funnel 4.9%; mk-flat
on killeroo-gold 87.02 / 86.15 / 88.69 and on killeroo-simple 42.05 /
42.01 / 43.98 -- the flat megakernel without SER pays nothing for the
fixed funnel, 1% in its favour on killeroo-gold. bonsai-ac's reading
of the night (the saved PTX): every exit of a loop leaves a body block
by a conditional branch, and LLVM places the funnel phis' copies in
that block before the branch, so they run on every iteration -- the
medium march's latch carries eight slot copies, seven zero fills and
the tag per iteration under 39c67ab9 (the slots shared by type, so no
slot can coalesce with the loop state's register; the +392 bytes of
spills are 5 edges x 10 slots x 8 bytes), the SER raygen's bounce loop
thirty zero fills before each of its six exits; NVPTX requires a
structured control-flow graph, so the backend splits none of those
edges, and PHI elimination's early exit (a value whose only uses are
phis) is target-independent, so the copies sit in the body on the CPU
too, where the greedy allocator's live-range splitting and
rematerialized zeros hide them: their wosx solver CPU table under
39c67ab9 (01:37-03:25, 114 cells) is a tie with the pre-funnel one,
0.9997x geomean, no cell below 0.97x. They will propose to the user a
payload keyed by SSA value (a slot per value, undefined on the edges
that do not care, the back edge's own argument on the latch's exit for
a loop-header parameter so that the phi cannot fold, zero only where a
fold would stretch a value), so that the funnel needs no copies in the
body: about a day of compiler work and every table again -- the
user's call. Until then the funnel's standing on apps/pbrt is: the
wavefront's medium march 26% slower on explosion (1.14x the frame),
bunny-cloud 1.06x, disney-cloud 1.055x, plume 1.03x; the SER
megakernels 5-8% slower on the killeroos; everything else within 2%.

**The profiler on ganesha (07:39-07:41: Nsight Compute, the full
section set, the user's approval of 10-27 for this scene).** Our flat
megakernel's raygen, `__raygen__ps$VolPath$False$False` of
gpu-optix-mega-flat at 16 spp (33.2 M threads: 1920 x 1080 pixels x
16 samples, one launch; 384 ms under the profiler's replay, 315
unprofiled; Nsight names every OptiX launch `optixLaunch`, so the
filter is the launch's ordinal -- the first try on the raygen's name
profiled nothing). What it reads: 128 registers per thread (the cap),
so at most 16 warps of 48 per SM, 14.3 achieved (29.7% occupancy);
issue slots busy 11.6% (0.46 instructions per cycle per SM); a warp
eligible to issue in 11.6% of cycles, 0.13 eligible per scheduler of
3.58 active; 30.8 warp-cycles per issued instruction, of which 14.0
with no instruction to issue (the fetch after a jump or an
instruction-cache miss -- a kernel far larger than the cache, its
warps at different places in it), 9.3 stalled at a barrier (our raygen
has no barrier of its own, so this is OptiX's: the warp's wait for the
traversal hardware's answer), 2.9 on a memory dependency, 2.0 on a
fixed-latency one, 1.0 issuing, the rest under one; 9.1 of 32 lanes
active per warp instruction (8.6 not predicated off): a warp is mostly
finished paths and skipped arms. Memory is not the wall: L1 throughput
8%, L2 35%, DRAM 11%, L2 hit rate 97.7%; no register spill at all (the
spilling counters are zero), but 1.87 G local loads and 1.80 G local
stores of 4.8 G sectors each -- the OptiX continuation stack (1024
bytes configured) saved and restored around every optixTrace --
against 1.43 G global loads, the stack two thirds of what reaches L2
(L1 hit 42% on its loads, 22% on its stores). 72.6 G warp instructions
issued, 5% branches. Against the two readings of 10-27: (a), the
raygen the size of every pbrt type, is what the profile shows -- the
instruction fetch is the largest single stall and the stack the
largest memory stream -- and (b), the register allocation as the union
of every arm, is what holds the occupancy at 16 warps, so that nothing
hides those stalls; the lanes' 29% is the megakernel's own (paths of
unequal length in one warp), which SER mends in part (mk-ser-flat 277
ms against 315) and the wavefront does not have (gpu-optix 95 ms). So
the step that would move ganesha, if one is taken, is the one that
shrinks the raygen's hot code and its register union: the match arms
as direct callables (proposal (2), "probably fine"), or a build of the
scene's own types alone (proposal (1) in its build-time form). pbrt's
trace kernel (`__raygen__findClosest`: launches of 1,036,800 threads,
540 scanlines of 1920 per pass, 128 registers, an 8192-byte stack
configured) recorded launch statistics only -- kernel replay
collected no counter on pbrt's three launches and logged no error --
so its rerun with application replay (five to six minutes of the
card) is asked of bonsai-ac's next gap. The reports (ours complete,
pbrt's as it is) and the raw metrics are kept under
apps/pbrt/scratch/ncu-ganesha-10-28/.

### pbrt's trace kernel profiled, and read against the megakernel's (10-28, 11:47-11:53)

The route, since the morning's run recorded nothing for it. pbrt is
built against OptiX 7.7's SDK (PBRT_OPTIX_PATH in its CMake cache),
and under the current driver its launches reach Nsight Compute as
"cmdlist workloads": application replay refuses them outright
("Cmdlist workloads are only supported in kernel replay mode", no
kernel profiled, 11:47), and kernel replay with the full set or with
named sections records the launch statistics and the two sampling
passes only -- every hardware counter n/a, no error, the "Profiling
optixLaunch: 0%" line and nothing after it -- where a --metrics list
of eight or twelve names at a time comes back complete. So six pbrt
runs of five seconds each (11:52-11:53, scratchpad/profile_pbrt_
groups.sh, copied beside the reports), one metric group per run, the
first trace launch each time and the first three launches in the
last. Our raygen's profile of 07:40 (OptiX 9.1, the full set) has the
same metrics, so the table below is the same counters on both sides;
the morning's pbrt report also holds its PC-sampling stall counts,
which were valid all along, and the sampled shares agree with the
counters on both sides (pbrt: 54% long scoreboard, 33% barrier, 1% no
instruction; ours: 45% no instruction, 30% barrier, 10% long
scoreboard). bonsai-ac's card was mine 11:38-11:53; 'done' sent.

What pbrt's launch is. `__raygen__findClosest` over 1,036,800 threads
(540 scanlines of 1920 pixels, one camera sample each): the raygen
reads its ray from the ray queue, one optixTrace, the closest-hit
program gathers the triangle's vertices, normals and uvs, builds the
surface interaction and writes it to the next queue. The first three
launches of the frame: findClosest at bounce 0, 811 us; the shadow
ray at bounce 0, 86 us; findClosest at bounce 1, 419 us (the rays
still alive, 19.8 lanes of 32). The shading is in CUDA kernels
between the launches, not profiled here. Ours is the whole frame:
every bounce, every shadow ray, the shading, 33,177,600 paths.

| | pbrt findClosest, bounce 0 | ours, gpu-optix-mega-flat raygen |
|---|---|---|
| duration | 0.81 ms (one bounce's trace of 1.04 M rays) | 384 ms under replay (315 plain), the frame |
| registers per thread | 128 | 128 |
| warps per SM achieved (16 fit at 128) | 15.9 (33.2%) | 14.3 (29.7%) |
| issue slots busy | 4.7% | 11.6% |
| instructions per cycle per SM | 0.19 | 0.46 |
| eligible warps per scheduler (of active) | 0.06 of 3.99 | 0.13 of 3.58 |
| warp-cycles per issued instruction | 85.3 | 30.8 |
| ... waiting on a memory load (long scoreboard) | 45.7 | 2.9 |
| ... at the barrier (the traversal's answer) | 28.0 | 9.3 |
| ... load/store queue full (lg_throttle) | 4.2 | 0.1 |
| ... a fixed-latency dependency | 2.1 | 2.0 |
| ... no instruction to issue | 0.95 | 14.0 |
| lanes active per warp instruction | 31.3 of 32 | 9.1 of 32 |
| warp instructions issued | 59.5 M (1,838 per warp) | 72.6 G (70,000 per warp) |
| global load / store sectors (32 B) | 23.0 M / 30.0 M | 3.54 G / none |
| local load / store sectors (the OptiX stack) | 3.5 M / 11.1 M (8192 B configured) | 4.83 G / 4.74 G (1024 B) |
| L1 hit / L2 hit | 19.9% / 73.7% | 44.5% / 97.7% |
| SM / L1 / L2 / DRAM throughput, of peak | 6.1% / 28.6% / 57.0% / 51.5% | 11.6% / 8.0% / 35.1% / 11% |

The reading. pbrt's trace kernel is a memory machine at full lanes:
31 of 32 lanes on every instruction, and 54% of its warp-cycles
waiting on loads from DRAM (half of DRAM's peak, L2 hits only 74%) --
the ray read from its queue, the hit's gathers from the mesh, the
interaction written (30 M sectors stored per launch, about 900 bytes a
ray: the wavefront's queue traffic, 1.7 GB through L1 per million
rays). The traversal's barrier is a third; the fetch is 1%, a kernel
that fits the instruction cache. Ours is an instruction machine at a
third of the lanes: 9 of 32, 45% of its warp-cycles with nothing
fetched, 30% at the barrier, 10% on memory; DRAM at 11% and L2 hits
97.7% -- the path's state in registers and the continuation stack in
L1 and L2, no queue. Both sit at the register ceiling (128, so 16
warps per SM) and neither hides its stalls (pbrt issues in 4.7% of its
cycles with 0.06 eligible warps, we in 11.6% with 0.13), but pbrt has
little to hide: 1,838 instructions per warp per launch, a million rays
traced in 0.8 ms, the cost moved into the stores and loads of the
queues and spread over the frame's launches. The megakernel's cost is
in instructions: 70,000 per warp per path, each at 9 lanes, each 30.8
cycles, 14 of them the fetch. (A sentence here at 12:05 said the
traversal hardware was "asked three and a half times as often" because
our instructions carry 9 lanes to pbrt's 31; the user asked why, and
it was wrong: the same rays are traced either way, and 9.1 is the
lane count averaged over every instruction of the megakernel, the
shading included, not at the trace. What the report's per-instruction
page says instead (the SASS of our raygen, which OptiX splits at each
optixTrace into continuations, `_ss_0` before the first trace, `_ss_1`
and `_ss_2` after one): the prologue up to the camera ray's trace runs
at 31.9 lanes (7.2 G of the 69 G warp instructions, 8% of the stall
samples); the continuations after a trace run at 6.0 lanes (47.6 G
and 14.4 G instructions, 71% and 21% of the samples); the closest-hit
program runs at 12.3 lanes, the miss programs at 7.9 and 6.8. No
trace instruction appears in the SASS -- the traversal runs between
the continuations -- so the lanes at the trace are between the
continuation's 6 and the hit program's 12, and the hardware's work per
ray is the same as pbrt's. What the lanes cost is on the SM side:
after the first bounce every shading instruction of a path is issued
at 6 lanes of 32, so the frame's shading costs five times the warp
instructions it would at full lanes, each fetched at 30.8 cycles. And
the barrier wait per instruction is 28.0 in pbrt's launch against 9.3
in ours: in pbrt's trace launch every warp of the SM is at the trace
and the traversal hardware is the bottleneck, saturated, which is the
ideal; in the megakernel a warp reaches the trace while the others
shade or fetch, waits less per trace, and the hardware sits part
idle. The traversal is not where the megakernel loses on ganesha.)
So the morning's reading holds and gains a third part: (a) the
raygen's size is the fetch, 45% of the cycles; (b) the register union
is the 16-warp ceiling that hides none of it (pbrt is at the same
ceiling and loses nothing to it because it has nothing to hide); and
(c) the lanes -- after the first bounce a megakernel's warp carries 6
live paths of 32, so every shading instruction is paid at a fifth of
its width, which SER mends in part (mk-ser-flat 277 ms against 315 on
ganesha) and the wavefront never pays, its warps full at every
launch. The steps that would move ganesha are unchanged -- the match
arms as direct callables (proposal (2)) or a build of the scene's own
types alone (proposal (1), build-time) for (a) and (b) -- and (c) is
the wavefront's argument on this scene, which the figure already
makes (gpu-optix 1.80x at 16 spp). The
reports of both sides (ours one .ncu-rep with the full set; pbrt's
six, one per metric group, with their logs; the morning's pbrt report
with its sampling data) and the three scripts are under
apps/pbrt/scratch/ncu-ganesha-10-28/. The one method note for a next
time: an OptiX 7-ABI process is profiled under kernel replay with
short --metrics lists, never --set or --section.

### The profile figure: the wavefront's trace kernel against the flat megakernels, on ganesha and on killeroo-gold (10-28, 12:10-16:25)

The user's ask at 12:10, after the morning's two profiles: a figure for
the paper with the relevant parts of this information, clean like the
other plots, for ganesha (where the wavefront wins) and for a killeroo
scene (where the megakernel wins), comparing our wavefront's trace
kernel to our megakernel. Built: `profile_kernels.sh` (one OptiX launch
of a renderer gpu_compare.sh compiled, chosen by its ordinal in the
process, under Nsight Compute; `--list N` prints the first N launches to
tell them apart; `--single-pass-timing` is explained below),
`plot_gpu_profile.py` (a row of three panels per scene: the launch's
SASS size on a log scale, the lanes active per warp instruction of 32,
and where a warp's cycles between issues go as shares of the cycles per
issued instruction -- the instruction fetch, the wait on the traversal
hardware, memory, the rest -- with a .txt beside it listing every
launch's numbers and the lanes of each function in it), and the fourth
fixed name of plots.sh, `pbrt-gpu-profile`. The data is in
apps/pbrt/profile-out/ (untracked, 400 MB a report); the renderers are
the GPU figure's, gpu-compare-out-d, built under 39c67ab9, so the figure
and the sweep figure are of one compiler. The card was bonsai-ac's for
the walk on stars table until 14:26 and for their build, suite and walk
A/B from 14:30 to 15:18; my windows were 14:26-14:29, 15:08-15:14 and
15:19-15:31 (and 16:16-16:17, see the slip below), each under the lock
with 'timing' and 'done'.

**Which launches.** Nsight names every OptiX launch `optixLaunch`,
whatever its raygen, so the launch is chosen by ordinal and the listing
says what each is. The wavefront (gpu-optix) launches only bands:
every one of its first twelve launches on ganesha has 1,036,800
threads (half the frame's 1440 x 1440 pixels; the frame at 16 spp is 32
bands), on killeroo-gold 701,952 (half of 1368 x 1026). Launch 0 is the
first band's closest-hit trace: 430 us at 31.2 lanes on ganesha, 285 us
at 31.5 on killeroo-gold, the launch whose functions are the trace's
raygen (85 instructions before its optixTrace, 268 after), the
closest-hit program (14,530 instructions: the hit record written) and
the miss program. The flat megakernels launch twice: launch 0 the
per-pixel prologue (2,073,600 threads at 64 registers, 172 us) and
launch 1 the frame -- for mega-flat 33,177,600 threads (16 x the
pixels) at 128 registers, 384 ms on ganesha and 100.7 ms (22,457,088
threads) on killeroo-gold; for mega-ser-flat Nsight lists the dispatch
as ONE block of 512 threads at 255 registers, 338 ms on ganesha and
68.8 ms on killeroo-gold -- that is how a pipeline with shader execution
reordering (SER, the sort of the paths by material at the call cursor)
appears to the profiler, not a grid of its own; the duration is the
frame's and the lanes, instruction counts and stalls are the launch's.

**The distortion, and the measurement that avoids it.** Under the full
section set the wavefront's trace launch on ganesha ran 20.17 ms, 47
times its 430 us, with 1,867 cycles of load latency and 1,263 of
traversal wait per issued instruction and an L2 hit rate of 47%; its
launch 2 ran 8.25 ms against 262 us. The same launch on killeroo-gold
ran 283 us under the full set, its listing's 285, and the megakernel's
frame on ganesha 384 ms both ways. What the distorted launches did
that the others did not: read system memory over PCIe --
`lts__t_sectors_aperture_sysmem_lookup_miss` 7.8 M sectors (250 MB)
for ganesha's launch 0 and 3.4 M for its launch 2, against 904 for
killeroo-gold's trace and 3,101 for the megakernel's frame. The cause
is on the profiler's side: Nsight's kernel replay runs the launch once
per pass (some forty for the full set) and saves and restores the
memory it may write between the passes; with the counter sections only
(a handful of passes) the launch ran 15.3 ms and with the full set and
the caches left warm 14.5 ms, so it is the multi-pass restore, not the
cache flush and not the source counters -- what of the renderer's
memory ends up on the host, and why on ganesha and not on killeroo-gold
or under the megakernel, I did not pin down (no managed memory in the
runtime; the card has 32 GB, the scene 196 MB). Application replay,
which re-runs the renderer for every pass and restores nothing, is
refused for our OptiX launches by this driver as it was for pbrt's
this morning: Nsight lists only the compute kernels and the
acceleration builds as profilable. What is true is a run of ONE pass,
which restores nothing: the one-pass listing's 430 us, and a metric
group small enough for one pass -- the duration, the cycles per issued
instruction, the warps active and the issue slots busy together (422
us), the lanes and the instruction counts together (430 us), but the
five stall ratios together needed more than one pass (16 ms), and one
of them, the load latency (`long_scoreboard`), needs two passes even
alone -- asked for by itself, with its raw counters, or through the
sampler (`smsp__pcsamp_aggregated_passes` = 2), its run took 15 ms
every time. So `--single-pass-timing`: after the full set, the timing
metrics are measured again in renderer runs of one pass each -- the
timing group, then each of the five drawn stall ratios on its own --
and merged into the .raw.csv over the full set's values (kept beside
it as .multipass.raw.csv); a run whose duration is off the timing
run's by more than a fifth took more than one pass and is not merged,
and if exactly one drawn ratio fails that way, every other stall
reason is measured in a one-pass run of its own (thirteen more, all
true at 430 us) and the failed one is the remainder: the cycles per
issued instruction less the sixteen measured reasons, 78.66 - 42.14 =
36.52 for the load latency here; the .raw.csv carries a
`bonsai__timing_provenance` column saying so, which the figure's .txt
prints. `--merge-only` redoes the merge from the single-pass files
beside the report, without the card -- the afternoon's measurements
were made by the check scripts under apps/pbrt/scratch/ and merged
that way; the tool's own run of the launch, one command, waits for
the two-minute slot bonsai-ac grants after their remeasure (~19:50).
The SASS and the per-instruction counts are counts, not cycles, and
stand from the full set. Only ganesha's wavefront trace needed this;
the other five launches of the figure are the full set's, and the
distorted kernel-replay files are kept under
apps/pbrt/scratch/profile-trace-check/. One slip to own: the last
90-second run was announced to bonsai-ac at 15:31 and did not start
until 16:16 -- the command sat queued in my session and I did not
watch for its start -- so their three-and-a-half-hour remeasure waited
45 minutes on my 'done'.

**What the figure shows.** On ganesha the wavefront's trace kernel (the
first band's closest-hit trace, 1,036,800 rays in 430 us) is a memory
machine at full lanes: 78.7 cycles per issued instruction at 31.2 lanes
of 32, 53% of them memory latency (the ray read from its queue, the
hit's gathers, the interaction written -- 36.5 cycles of load latency
by the remainder, 2.5 of load-queue and 2.3 of memory-unit throttling),
39% the wait on the traversal hardware (30.7 cycles), 1% the fetch
(1.1 cycles over 15k SASS instructions), the rest 7%; 15.9 warps per
SM of the 16 the 128 registers allow, issuing in 5% of the cycles. It
is pbrt's findClosest shape of this morning (85 cycles per instruction:
54% load latency, a third barrier, 31 lanes) with more of the wait at
the traversal and less at the loads. Against it the megakernel's frame
on ganesha: 30.8 cycles per issued instruction at 9.1 lanes, 46% the
fetch over 330k SASS instructions, 30% the traversal wait, 10% memory;
with SER 47.8 cycles at 15.0 lanes, 84% the fetch over 349k
instructions, the traversal wait gone from the stall counters.

On killeroo-gold the trace kernel is the same machine as on ganesha and
as pbrt's: 62 cycles per issued instruction at 31.3 lanes, 63% of them
memory latency, 23% the traversal wait, 3% the fetch, 15k SASS
instructions; it moves rays and hit records and waits, and its warps
are full. The megakernel's frame on killeroo-gold costs 19.8 cycles per
issued instruction at 14.5 lanes (the raygen's prologue up to the
camera ray's trace at 31.9 lanes, the continuations after a trace at
8.9 and 11.9), 18% of them the fetch, 29% the traversal wait, 27%
memory, over 341k SASS instructions; with SER 23.3 cycles at 23.2
lanes (the continuations at 14-23), half of them the fetch, the
traversal wait gone from the stall counters (a reordered trace does not
wait at a barrier; its cost is elsewhere), 360k instructions. On
ganesha the megakernel's frame costs 30.8 cycles per issued instruction
at 9.1 lanes (the continuations after the first trace at 6.0), 46% of
them the fetch and 30% the traversal wait, over 330k instructions; with
SER 47.8 cycles at 15.0 lanes (continuations at 9.4-11.4), 84% of them
the fetch, 349k instructions. Read across the two scenes: the
megakernel's lanes are what differ (14.5 and 23.2 of 32 on killeroo-
gold, 9.1 and 15.0 on ganesha) and with them the fetch's share (a fifth
to a half of the cycles without SER); the wavefront's trace pays
neither -- full lanes, 15k instructions -- and pays instead a launch
per queue per bounce and the queues' traffic, which this figure does
not show and the sweep figure prices. SER lifts the lanes on both
scenes (9.1 to 15.0, 14.5 to 23.2) and removes the barrier stall, and
triples the fetch cycles per instruction (14.0 to 40.4 on ganesha, 3.5
to 11.9 on killeroo-gold): the sorted warps run the arm their material
chose, so a warp's instruction stream is a different region of the
349k-instruction raygen from its neighbours', and the instruction cache
serves them worse -- the counters say the fetch grew; that explanation
of why is mine, not measured. The figure's lanes panel and the stall
panel are the morning's reading (a), (b), (c) of ba02adc6 and
0e41adf5 as a picture: the raygen's size is the fetch, the register
union holds the occupancy that would hide it, and the lanes after the
first bounce are the width every instruction is paid at.

**Registers: both nights at OptiX's choice.** The run was to settle
whether the SER megakernel's 255 registers and the raygens' 128 were a
cap's doing: bonsai-ac found on 10-28 that OptiX ignores the PTX's
`.maxnreg`, so --gpu-max-registers reaches OptiX only since 66b6590d.
This run passed no cap (BONSAI_GPU_MAX_REGISTERS=0, as pbrt builds its
own OptiX modules, OPTIX_COMPILE_DEFAULT_MAX_REGISTER_COUNT in

The profiles show the counts 10-28's showed: 128 for the wavefront's
trace and the flat megakernel, 255 for the SER pipeline, on both scenes.
So the night of 10-27's tables under 39c67ab9 were at OptiX's choice too
(the 128 the harness asked for never arrived), and what differs between
the two nights is the compiler alone, 39c67ab9's exit funnel against
7af5bd86's exit merge. gpu_compare.sh's default cap is now 0, its
comment saying why; BONSAI_GPU_MAX_REGISTERS=N is a real cap from now on,
and the log's compiler line and the table's footer say which.

## 10-29, midday: one colour scheme for the four figures, the sweeps' .txt files reading each scene, and the question of larger scenes

**The ask (the user, 10-29 noon).** (a) The colour schemes consistent
across the pbrt plots -- the GPU and CPU sweeps assigned colours
differently and it was confusing; (b) the .txt files explaining why
different schedules are best on different scenes; (c) is
sanmiguel-courtyard the most complex scene, the sweep does not go far
enough in complexity -- ten scenes with five larger ones, or eight, or six?
No card time: python and text only, bonsai-ac holding the lock for their
compiler work (matplotlib pinned to core 0 by agreement).

**(a) What was wrong, and the scheme.** Each sweep laid the one YlGnBu
ramp over its own bars in drawing order (the CPU figure classes 0..7 over
its eight Bonsai sides, the GPU figure 0..8 spread over its eight), so the
same colour named a different schedule on each figure -- the mid teal was
wf-t-s-ps on the CPU and mk-ser on the GPU -- and the two palest classes
were 4.7 apart under deutan simulation and 5.6 under normal vision (OKLab
x100, the dataviz validator): mk-b-s-ps against wf-b-s-sp on the CPU, mk
against mk-pass on the GPU, hard to tell apart. Now (figure_style.py,
SCHEDULE_COLOURS): two sequential ramps, one per family, each darker with
every scheduling step down the legend -- the megakernels on ColorBrewer
YlOrBr (six colours at equal OKLab spacing between its classes 2.5 and 8),
the wavefronts on YlGnBu (seven, between classes 3 and 8; the heatmap's
ramp, the heatmap being the wavefront's figure) -- so the family is read
from the hue and the variant from the lightness, and the same schedule has
the same colour everywhere: mk (gpu-optix-mega) and mk-b-s-ps (scalar)
the palest warm; wf (gpu-optix) and wf-b-s-sp (wavefront-frame) the palest
cool; wf-sort and wf-t-v-ps-sort the darkest cool; pbrt's bars black. The
profile figure's size and lanes bars take their launch's schedule colour
(wf trace teal, mk-flat and mk-ser-flat the two darkest warm) and its
stall shares are greys, so colour there names a schedule and nothing else.
The exploration sides borrow the CPU variants' shades (never on one
figure). Chosen by scratch/palette_pick.py over the validator's distances
(Oranges, YlOrBr, OrRd, YlOrRd and PuRd tried against three starts of the
cool ramp): bars side by side are at least 9.0 (GPU) and 8.0 (CPU) apart
under protan/deutan simulation and 11.2 / 9.4 under normal vision, every
warm colour at least 12.2 from every cool one; the validator's categorical
floor of 15 between neighbours is out of reach for six or seven ordered
shades (the bar order within every group, keyed by the legend, is the
second encoding), and its lightness-band and chroma checks fail a
sequential ramp by design. Redrawn 12:27, all four figures.

**(b) The .txt files.** Each sweep's .txt now carries, after the
statistics and the pairwise comparisons: "why: the mechanisms" (WHY in the
plotter -- what the megakernel pays and what the wavefront pays, the
megakernel's shapes, the sort, the spp trend; on the CPU the bands against
the per-thread queues, the drains' vectorization, the sort, the chunk's
queues), then "which schedule is best on each scene, and why": for every
scene the computed best side at each sample count with the runner-up, and
under it the scene's reading (READINGS, keyed by scene) from the measured
causes in this file -- the GPU: the killeroos' cheap trace and two
materials and the SER megakernel's full warps (14.7 -> 23.3 lanes on
killeroo-gold's profile), book's shading equal to its trace and the fused
raygen's 29-31% there, ganesha's 9.2 lanes and 44% fetch over a 330k
program against the trace kernel's 15k at 31 lanes, sanmiguel's two-level
latency-bound trace and four materials; the CPU: the killeroos' chunk
queues outgrowing the cache at 64/128 spp, book's and ganesha's heavier
shading paying for the vectorized drains, sanmiguel's incoherent rays and
heaviest shading paying for the sort. A scene without a reading prints

names the table each figure was drawn from. The heatmap's .txt gains its

## 10-29, afternoon: the sweeps go to eight scenes at 16 and 128 spp -- the choice, the scene statistics file, one-line scene names

**The word (the user, 10-29 afternoon).** "Let's do 8 x 2 spp. Choose
roughly evenly spaced scenes, ideally that have different shapes of their
performance eval across the different schedules. Start with GPU because I
think that's faster, and we'll just use the same 8 x 2spp for CPU for
consistency. Do 8 scenes at 16 and 128 spp. Definitely add kroken and
landscape, and make sure the script generates a scene_statistics.txt file
in the pbrt/plots directory that gives information on each scene, like
triangle count, material count, instance count, and any other useful
statistics." And: "to save whitespace, please don't have that weird scene
text rendering that splits the scene name in half (two lines) for no
reason."

**The eight, in the figures' order (pbrt --gpu's wall at 128 spp, the
heatmap of 10-29).** Of the five, four stay, each with a measured shape
of its own on the GPU figure: killeroo-gold (532k triangles, 1.22 s; the
SER flat megakernel wins every cell, 3.66x at 16 spp; the profile
figure's scene), book (21k, 1.33 s; the wavefront wins with the flat
megakernel within 7% and SER buying nothing -- the one such scene),
sanmiguel-courtyard (2.5M in 796 meshes, 69,040 instances; 1.34 s; the

trace latency-bound), ganesha (4.3M, 1.53 s; the wavefront by the most,
every megakernel below pbrt). killeroo-simple goes: its shape is
killeroo-gold's (the SER megakernel wins by the cheap trace) and it is the

triangles in 1,693 meshes, 133 materials, 20,638 area lights -- the light
sampling's scene; 2.79 s), landscape/view-0 (27.9M triangles, 30,034

(288M triangles, 248M of them from displacement, 2,175 area lights, depth

**The fit.** Eight scenes x two sample counts x nine sides: 177 bar

## 10-30, morning: the CPU sweep stopped at landscape; the packet schedules' crash and wrong images were one backend bug, a gang's gather reading its 32-bit lane offsets as signed; fixed, tested, dragon_10 in landscape's place

**Where the CPU sweep stood when it was stopped (08:36).** Started 16:37
the evening before into cpu-compare-out-eight: six scenes complete at
both sample counts, landscape at 128 spp on its ninth row of ten, kroken
and watercolor not begun, 108 rows. Landscape at 128 spp alone was a
ten-hour block -- a 3840x2160 frame at 128 spp is 1.06 billion camera
paths a render, pbrt's own render 1,463 s (24 min), ours 878-1,582 s,
each side rendered three times, ten sides a cell block (eight of ours,
pbrt's wavefront and pbrt's volpath): pbrt-wavefront + wavefront-frame
3 h 0 min, frame-packet 1 h 38, frame-packet-reorder 1 h 8, thread 49 min,
thread-packet 53, thread-packet-reorder 1 h 4, thread-packet-sort 46,
pbrt-volpath + scalar from 08:00. Nothing single-threaded: pbrt at 65
threads on 31 of 32 cores, the load 30-31 all night. The 13-16 h estimate
of the evening came from the five earlier scenes, 1080p-class frames at
15-220 s a render; kroken and watercolor would each have been a day or
more. The user (10-30, 08:3x): "Don't use landscape for the schedule
sweep, that's too big. Maybe replace it with dragon_10? Also, you need to
pause, find the simplest scenes the packet schedules segfault and/or fail
on, and cleanly debug them." Stopped; the lock to 'hold' for debugging;
bonsai-ac told (their 6 h rtq remeasure waits for 'done').

**What the CSV had.** Every packet schedule (frame-packet,
frame-packet-reorder, thread-packet, thread-packet-reorder,
thread-packet-sort) on bistro at 16 and at 128 spp: `compare.sh exit
139`, a segfault after "lights and film", before a pixel -- ten empty
cells. The same five on landscape at 16 spp: `FAILED: 8137227 pixels
received light here against pbrt's 8073772; a gap of 63455 where 8074
was allowed`, the count identical across the three that had run, so
deterministic; at 128 spp `the image is 1.36690x pbrt's on average`. The
non-packet schedules (scalar, wavefront-frame, wavefront-thread) matched
pbrt on both scenes. And scalar on sanmiguel at 16 spp `FAILED: 853108
pixels received light here against pbrt's 856648; a gap of 3540 where
1143 was allowed` -- the same numbers as the 10-28 run's, pre-existing,
passing at 128 spp, a scalar schedule with a texture pool under 1 GB:
not this bug, still open.

**The hunt (scratch/packet_hunt.sh, pfm_diff.py; 08:39-08:46).** The
simplest failing scene, found by running every heatmap scene at one
sample through wavefront-thread-packet and its twin wavefront-thread
(the same program, the same sampler; the twin's only difference is the
gangs), smallest geometry first, from the sweep's prebuilt renderers, and
diffing the two radiance images: twenty-seven scenes agree to the noise
two gangs' rounding orders make of a Monte Carlo estimate (mean ratio
within 0.3%, the lit-in-one-only counts symmetric), kroken among them
(1.00016); bistro_cafe and bistro_vespa both crash; landscape's packet
image is 1.42x the twin's (mean 0.702, 326,056 lit only in the twin
against 728,947 only in the packet's); watercolor's 1.4% brighter with
the lit-only counts asymmetric 17,634 against 35,057. The small
normal-map test scene (scenes/normalmap.pbrt, one of bistro's maps over a
quad) renders identically through both. So no small scene fails: the
failing set is exactly the three scenes whose converted texture bytes
pass 2 GB -- bistro 3,318,768,817, watercolor 3,064,429,339, landscape
3,049,000,501 -- where every other scene's pool is 920 MB or less
(sanmiguel), kroken's 298 MB.

**The crash (gdb on bistro).** SIGSEGV in `normal_map$gang16_v0_v1$masked`
at a `vgatherdps (%rcx,%zmm5,4),%zmm4{%k4}`, the mask register 0xffff
(every lane on), the fault address 0x7ffebbed57cb against a base of
0x555555867310 -- a lane's index far outside anything mapped. The
gather is `texture_bytes[byte]` of level_texel (textures.bonsai), `byte =
3u * texel`, a u32 past 2^31 for a pool over 2 GB.

**The bug: the addressing model read its 32-bit lane offsets as signed.**
A gang's gather or scatter is one base pointer and a 32-bit offset per
lane (CodeGen_LLVM::element_addresses' model, ISPC's default): the x86
gather instruction sign-extends its dword indices, and so does a GEP its
index. The comment on the model had recorded the consequence as a known
edge -- "a byte offset must fit in 31 bits: an array over 2 GB is
addressed wrongly past that, in a gather" -- and the three pools found
it. Before and after, per lane:

    before:  addr = base + sext64(offset) * scale
             offset >= 2^31  ->  addr below base by up to 2^31 * scale
    after:   addr = (base + 2^31 * scale) + sext64(offset xor 2^31) * scale
                  = base + offset * scale      for every offset < 2^32

The scalar path never had the limit (widen_index zero-extends a u32 to
the pointer's width), which is why scalar and the non-gang wavefronts
rendered bistro and landscape right, and the GPU paths form no such
addresses (CodeGen_PTX and CodeGen_OptiX do not call gather_indexed or
element_addresses; no GPU golden moved). So only the five vectorized CPU
schedules failed, and only on the three scenes: a crash where the wrapped
address was unmapped (bistro), wrong texels where it landed in other
mapped memory (landscape's leaves' alpha and colour, read from garbage,
let light through: 1.37x pbrt's image; watercolor 1.4%).

**The fix (CodeGen_LLVM::unsigned_lane_offsets; CodeGen_LLVM.cpp,
CodeGen_X86.cpp, CodeGen_LLVM.h).** The offsets stay 32 bits -- the
reason for the model, one register of indices against two of pointers --
and are read unsigned: the base is moved up by 2^31 units of the scale
(a scalar add, loop-invariant, which LLVM hoists; several goldens gained a
preheader for it) and the offset vector has its top bit flipped (one
`vpxord` per gather, shared by every gather over the same offsets: the
seventeen re-blessed goldens show 62 moved bases and 17 xors). The GEPs
formed from a moved base are no longer `inbounds` (the base lies past the
end of any array under 2 GB). Applied in the three places lane offsets
become addresses: the x86 gather intrinsic path, the generic masked-gather
path, and element_addresses, which the scatters and the per-lane byte
reads go through. The reach is now 4 GB of bytes, the reach of the u32
arithmetic that forms an offset; ISPC takes its 32-bit offsets signed and
leaves anything past 2 GB to `--addressing=64`, which would cost every
gather two registers of 64-bit indices for arrays that are almost never
that large.

**Tests.** `correctness/cpp/vectorize_gather_unsigned` maps 2 GB and a
megabyte (MAP_NORESERVE; only the pages written cost), writes known
values on both sides of the mark and reads them back through three
vectorized functions -- bytes at u32 indices (the pool's shape), a field
of an eight-byte element at indices whose byte offsets straddle 2^31, and
a scatter of words past the mark -- each lane checked against its own
index; `backends/llvm/vectorize_gather_unsigned` golden-diffs the IR's
`_up` and `_flip`. Seventeen LLVM goldens re-blessed after reading every
changed line (backends/llvm: defer-gang, defer-gang-bools, ptr-rows-packet,
sub-word-gather, vectorize_call_guard, vectorize_calls, vectorize_gather,
vectorize_loop, vectorize_packet_any, vectorize_packet_traversal,
vectorize_packet_wide, vectorize_pure_call, vectorize_soa,
vectorize_vector_index; correctness/llvm: x86-gather-avx2,
x86-gather-avx512, x86-gather-avx512-16): the moved base, the flipped
offsets (folded into the constants where the offsets were constant
ramps), `inbounds` gone from those GEPs, a preheader where the base was
hoisted, and nothing else. Suite 1944 of 1944 on the build of the last
edit.

**Verified on the scenes.** wavefront-thread-packet rebuilt under the fix
and run at one sample against the twin: bistro renders, mean 1.00066;
landscape 1.00002 (from 0.702); watercolor 0.99990 (from 0.986), the

**After the sweep: killeroo-coated-gold, clouds and frame542 on the GPU
(10-30, 17:16-17:45; scratch/post_sweep_gpu.sh; gpu-compare-out-coated,
gpu-compare-out-two, scratch/post-sweep).** Three short runs for the
user's two questions of the afternoon, the eight GPU schedules of the
figure at 16 and 128 spp, three repeats, the renderers reused from
gpu-compare-out-six, no profiler. (1) *Why killeroo-gold alone favours
the megakernel:* killeroo-coated-gold is killeroo-gold's geometry (532k
triangles, 4 meshes, 2 disks), lights (one area light and one other)
and camera with CoatedConductor in place of the Conductor (3.63 rays a
camera ray against 3.75). pbrt --gpu pays 8% at 128 spp for it (1.32 s
to 1.42; kernel 1197 ms to 1327); our wavefront 21% (0.581 s to 0.706;
0.078 to 0.094 at 16), the sort 12%; and every megakernel 2.0-2.7x --
the SER flat one 0.474 s to 1.269 (0.060 to 0.158 at 16), the flat 0.696
to 1.516, the pass 0.722 to 1.566, the blocked 0.907 to 1.825, the SER
1.066 to 2.255, the per-sample 1.479 to 3.895. On the coated scene the
wavefront is best (2.34x and 2.01x), the SER flat megakernel 1.39x and
1.12x, the flat 1.16x and 0.94x, the per-sample 0.46x and 0.36x -- so
the Conductor's closed-form BSDF is what let the megakernel win
killeroo-gold, and pbrt's layered BSDF, a stochastic random walk through
the coat (CoatedConductor here, CoatedDiffuse on ganesha and book),
costs a megakernel two to three times what it costs a wavefront, whose
material kernel runs the walk with every lane on the same material
(ganesha's profile, 9 lanes active and 44% no-instruction stalls in the
megakernel, is consistent with this; not a proof). SER buys less once
the walk diverges after the regrouping: the SER flat over the flat
1.20x here against 1.44-1.47x on gold. (2) *"What if you added clouds
and frame542":* **clouds** (a volume: one sphere, one Diffuse material,
one light, depth 50, 7.29 rays a camera ray, 1920x1080; pbrt --gpu
1.03 s and 7.54 s) -- the wavefront 1.57x and 1.44x (the heatmap's
1.58x and 1.45x), the sort 1.20x and 1.10x, every megakernel 0.37-0.58x
with the plain per-sample one the least bad (0.58x and 0.56x) and the
SER ones 0.39-0.44x: the medium's delta-tracking walk diverges inside a
megakernel's bounce loop and SER has no surface hit to regroup by (a
reading; not profiled). **frame542** (transparent-machines: 1.3M
triangles in 229 meshes, 5 instances, Dielectric and Diffuse, one

## 10-31, the night: the CPU sweep of plume and frame542, pbrt disagreeing with itself on the plume, two compiler fixes for the wavefront variants

**The CPU sweep of plume and frame542** (23:34-02:12, cpu-compare-out-two,

everything a CPU schedule uses). Both scenes read as the six did. plume
(a participating medium under an interface, 1.44M pixels): pbrt's CPU
wavefront 39.5 s / 314.6 s; the frame wavefronts 1.75-2.18x (the packet
frame wavefront best of them at 2.18x/2.16x); the per-thread wavefronts
5.6-7.8x, the packet per-thread one best at 7.83x/7.26x, the reorder a
wash (7.81x/7.27x), the sort behind (7.61x/6.78x); the scalar, pbrt's own

reads the same way: every megakernel loses on plume). frame542 (the

frame wavefronts 1.75-2.25x; per-thread 6.4-8.3x, the plain per-thread
wavefront best (8.26x/7.94x) with the packet one a hair behind at 16 spp
and ahead at 128 (8.07x/7.25x), the reorder last (7.20x/6.41x); the
