VolPath (3.32 s / 26.72 s) -- the CPU's version of the GPU reading, a
deep scene paying the wavefront's rounds. Thirty-eight of the forty
rows' images match pbrt's. The two that did not are the plume's scalar
cells, and they are not ours.

**pbrt disagrees with itself on the plume.** The scalar schedule's
image check compares against pbrt's CPU VolPath integrator, the renderer
it is timed against, and read 0.93345x / 0.93350x of it. Measured from
the cached renders with compare_gbuffer.py, pbrt's own wavefront is
0.93383x / 0.93354x of pbrt's own VolPath on plume (agreeing to 1e-3 on
1% of pixels), where on frame542 the two agree to 0.99996x (86.6% of
pixels to 1e-3). Our scalar image is 0.9999x of pbrt's wavefront, as our
wavefront schedules' are (all eight matched). The program follows the
wavefront where pbrt's two integrators differ (the ruling of 09-25, the
catalogue above: an interface crossing costs the wavefront a bounce, the
wavefront rolls Russian roulette after a medium scatter and adds no
emission at the last bounce; a medium scene is where all three bite), so
on a medium scene the scalar schedule renders the wavefront's image and
the VolPath reference is the wrong one to fail it against. Two things
were tried. First the rule the GPU table has had since 10-18 (the
spread: a failing check is held against pbrt's other integrator's render
of the same cell, and passes when pbrt's two disagree by more than ours
does with the timed one), which compare.sh and cpu_compare.sh never
applied: compare.sh gained `--pbrt-spread`, and the plume's scalar cells
measured again under it (02:29-02:33) still failed -- by noise: ours
0.93345x / 0.93350x of VolPath against pbrt's own 0.93383x / 0.93354x,
two independent estimates of the same image a few ten-thousandths apart,
ours the further by a coin's toss. The rule is strict by design and
stays as the user set it. The right reference for the scalar's image is
simply the wavefront's, by the ruling of 09-25 that the program's images
are compared against `pbrt --wavefront`: compare.sh now also takes
`--check-against-wavefront` -- the time is the timed CPU integrator's,
the image check's reference pbrt's wavefront render (from the
--pbrt-cache by the timed run's key with `--wavefront` toggled, which a
cell has by the time the scalar runs, that being why the scalar runs
last in a cell; else rendered once untimed), and compare_gbuffer.py
names the reference in its verdict (`--reference-name`), so the row
reads "ok: the image matches pbrt's wavefront" and no reader takes it
for a check against the CPU integrator. cpu_compare.sh passes it for the
scalar cell and `--pbrt-spread` for every cell (a failing wavefront cell
is held against the CPU integrator's render, as the GPU table's are),
and reads the last verdict line. plume's two scalar rows are measured a
third time under it after the night's GPU run; their times stand within
the sweep's protocol either way (6.50 s / 53.06 s at 02:30, against
6.61 s / 56.02 s at 00:17, a quieter machine).

**Two compiler fixes, for the three wavefront variants the user asked
for (b72c215b).** The variants: `gpu-optix-fused` (the material stage
fused into the trace program: compiled and ran at 1 spp, 2.41x on
killeroo-simple), `gpu-optix-fused-ser` (that, with shader execution
reordering by material before the shading: OptiX refused the module,
"Illegal call to optixReorder in function __closesthit__trace", as on
10-24) and `gpu-optix-pass` (a band of pixels times four samples per
round of launches, a quarter of pbrt's rounds: the compiler refused it,
"the caller's storage, of which there is one per call, is made once per
iteration of a loop").

The first fix, in the pass that moves allocations out of loops. The
pass-of-four schedule's queue is sized by the product of the two split
counts, a multiply the deferral puts at the head of the band loop, and
the pass hoisted only an allocation whose size was already known before
the loop, so the queue stayed inside it and the GPU storage rule refused
it. Before:

    func render(...) {
      parfor band in bands {
        n = pixels_in_band * 4      // the queue's size, computed in the loop
        rays = alloc n              // so the queue's storage was made once per band
        ...
      }
    }

After:

    func render(...) {
      n = pixels_in_band * 4        // moved to the entry with the allocation it sizes
      rays = alloc n                // once per call
      parfor band in bands { ... }
      free rays
    }

The pass now moves the pure arithmetic a size depends on along with the
allocation -- loop-invariant code motion (Allen and Cocke 1971; Muchnick
ch. 13): an operand may move when it is a constant, a definition from
before the loop, or a pure instruction (add, multiply, shift, select,
cast and the like; never a load) over operands that may move. Each
moved instruction is moved once however many sizes share it. The golden
of tests/bonsai/ssa/defer-nest-guard changed the same way, as it should:
a chunk's twelve-slot record is now one allocation per call rather than
one per chunk (at the LLVM level, four mallocs at the entry where the
constant-size record had folded to stack arrays).

The second fix, in the pass that turns a trace's continuation into the
closest-hit program (the shape pbrt's trace kernel has). The fused SER
wavefront's continuation begins with the reordering hint, and OptiX
allows that hint in a raygen program alone. Before:

    raygen:      trace(ray); on a miss, push the escaped ray
    closest-hit: reorder by material key   // illegal here: the module fails to build
                 shade(...)

After, the pass refuses a continuation that reaches a reordering hint
(BONSAI_EXPLAIN_HIT_CONTINUATIONS=1 says so), and the loop keeps the
raygen shape, as the SER megakernels have it:

    raygen:      hit = trace(ray)
                 if hit { reorder by material key; shade(...) } else { push the escaped ray }
    closest-hit: record the hit alone

Tests: tests/bonsai/ssa/hoist-size-arithmetic (the product at the entry,
the allocations after it, the round loop after them) and
tests/bonsai/ssa/hit-continuation-reorder (the generic closest-hit
program alone, no hit copy of the shading function, the hint in the
raygen before the call). The suite's 1950 tests pass. The variants' run
under the fixed compiler follows (post_fix_gpu.sh: a 1 spp check of each,
then the ones that run on the eight scenes at 16 and 128 spp); its
reading is the next paragraph.

**The three variants measured (02:33-02:59 and 09:00-09:20).** All three
compile under b72c215b (the pass variant's compiler error is gone: 434 s
to compile, as the others), and two run. The fused wavefront
(gpu-compare-out-wf3, 02:48-02:59, the eight scenes at 16 and 128 spp,
three repeats, every image matching pbrt's): 2.63, 2.17, 2.19, 2.01,
1.87, 2.02, 2.42, 1.76x at 16 spp and 2.01, 1.60, 1.54, 1.69, 1.50,
1.67, 1.92, 1.68x at 128 spp over pbrt --gpu, in the figure's scene
order -- against the matched wavefront's bars of 10-30, 0.85-0.97x on
killeroo-gold, book, ganesha, dragon_10 and plume (a cheap trace: the
material stage inside the trace program lengthens the raygen's
continuation, which runs once the warp's traversals are back, and pays
for the hit queue it removes), 1.04-1.13x on sanmiguel, bistro and
frame542 (a heavy or deep trace, where the hit queue's round trip was the
larger cost). That is the 10-24 reading of the fused wavefront, now with
the gain side measured. The fused wavefront with reordering by material
(gpu-compare-out-wf3b, 09:06-09:20, every image matching): 1.99, 2.33,
2.15, 1.89, 1.92, 2.00, 2.06, 1.42x at 16 spp and 1.98, 1.75, 1.53,
1.61, 1.54, 1.64, 1.64, 1.36x at 128 spp -- against the fused wavefront
without it 1.03-1.09x on book and dragon_10, a wash on sanmiguel and
plume (0.98-0.99x), a loss on ganesha (0.94-0.95x), bistro (0.85x),
frame542 (0.81x) and killeroo-gold at 16 spp (0.76x; 0.99x at 128).
Where the SER megakernel buys 1.14-1.46x over its flat sibling by
refilling warps whose lanes have diverged over whole paths, the fused
wavefront's raygen holds one bounce: a trace, one material's evaluation,
a push -- too little work after the reorder to repay a sort of the
launch's rays every bounce (a reading from the walls; not profiled). The
two sides go into the GPU sweep figure as `wf-fused` and `wf-fused-ser`
in the user's order. **The pass-of-four wavefront** matched pbrt at 1 spp
on killeroo-simple (0.59x -- one sample, a quarter-filled band) and died
on every sweep cell at 16 and 128 spp at the first copy back,
`cuMemcpyDtoH failed: CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`. At 1 spp the sample
loop's split (groups of four with a tail guard) has one group of one
sample; at 16 spp four full groups, so a band's queues -- owned by the
band loop and sized pass_pixels x 4 since the hoist -- hold four rays a
pixel. The probe (scratch/pass_spp_probe.sh, 09:21: killeroo-simple at 4,
8 and 16 spp with the sweep's renderer) fails at 4 spp already, the first
full group, so it is not the reuse of the storage across groups but its
size. And the size is the driver's: an extern queue's capacity is only
known at run time, so the header says each array's element bytes and the
driver multiplies by "the capacity it computes as the program does"
(SSA/QueueStorage.cpp) -- and the driver computes the pass of pixels,
pbrt's maxQueueSize (render_hook.cpp, the queue_capacity lambda), which
was the program's capacity in every schedule until this one. The pass
schedule's program fills pass_pixels x 4 entries into storage of
pass_pixels: four rays a pixel into room for one, hence the illegal
address at the first full group and a clean run at 1 spp (one ray a
pixel). The header shows the shape, too: the pass renderer's entries
carry three slot indices (`_slot`, `_slot1`, `_slot2`) where the matched
wavefront's carry one. The root fix is the interface, not the schedule:
the compiler knows the capacity as an expression over the exported
function's parameters (the hoisted product is one), so the header should
print it -- `BONSAI_render_<queue>_CAPACITY(params)`, say -- and the
driver multiply by that rather than by a rule of its own; a driver that
guesses the program's capacity is the kind of hidden coupling the
storage argument was meant to remove. That is a compiler (CodeGen/CPP)
and driver change for the user's eyes; until it lands the pass side stays
out of the figure with a note (plots.sh, plot_gpu_wavefront.py).

## 11-01, the capacity in the header: the pass-of-four wavefront rendered, and what it costs

The user, 10-31 late: "Please make that fix you suggested with the driver
and the C++ codegen, it should be clean and minimal." Committed e08e0195.
The change is to the interface between a program whose queues live in the
driver's memory and the driver that allocates them. Before, the generated
header gave each queue array's element size and the driver chose the count
by a rule of its own:

    // the header, per queue array
    #define BONSAI_render_rays_ray_o_ELEMENT_BYTES sizeof(std::array<float, 3>)
    // render_hook.cpp
    capacity = width * scanlines_per_pass    // pbrt's maxQueueSize, computed again here
    bytes    = capacity * ELEMENT_BYTES

After, the header states the count too, as the program computes it from
the function's own parameters, and the driver multiplies:

    // the header, per queue array
    #define BONSAI_render_rays_ray_o_ELEMENT_BYTES sizeof(std::array<float, 3>)
    #define BONSAI_render_rays_ray_o_CAPACITY ((width * (((height + (((height
        + max(1u, 1048576u / width)) - 1u) / max(1u, 1048576u / width))) - 1u)
        / (((height + max(1u, 1048576u / width)) - 1u) / max(1u, 1048576u / width)))) * 4u)
    // render_hook.cpp
    bytes = CAPACITY * ELEMENT_BYTES

(the pass renderer's: pbrt's pass of pixels, times the four samples a
group holds; the matched renderer's is the same without the `* 4u`; a
schedule that states a constant capacity prints that constant). Where the
count comes from. The storage pass turns an Extern queue's array into a
parameter of the exported function; the value that sized the array is
arithmetic computed at the function's entry (the hoist of 10-31 put it
there when it was not). The resolver that gives a kernel launch its block
size -- a value of the body computed again on the host from the captures,
Briggs, Cooper and Torczon's rematerialization (PLDI 1992) -- is run on
the entry block with every parameter a capture and no loop index, and
yields an expression over the parameters and constants, or the reason it
cannot (a value read from memory, a call, something merged inside a loop).
The parameter carries the expression as its `capacity`, the IR argument
carries it on to the C++ backend, which prints the macro, and the SSA and
IR printers show it after the parameter's type (`sums_k_0 : mut i32[]
capacity (n << 1)`). A capacity that cannot be so expressed is refused
where the parameter is made, with the reason: the caller has to be told how
much to allocate, and only arithmetic over what it passes can be printed
for it. Three tests: the SSA golden ssa/queue-storage-capacity (the
capacity on the parameters of a function whose loop runs `n * 2` times),
the refusal error/queue-storage-extern-capacity (a loop bounded by
`out[0]`), and the execution test correctness/gpu/queue-extern-capacity-cpp,
whose C++ driver allocates by the header's capacity over `n` and prints
it (8 entries of 4 bytes, the sums of queue-extern-cpp). The driver's
lambda that recomputed pbrt's pass of pixels is gone; its queue_buffer
takes the header's capacity. Suite 1956.

**The pass-of-four wavefront under it** (scratch/check_pass_capacity.sh,
23:59-00:22). killeroo-simple at 1, 4 and 16 spp matches pbrt (0.38x,
0.36x, 0.58x of pbrt --gpu; the crash at 4 spp is gone), and the
eight-scene sweep at 16 and 128 spp, three repeats, matches on all sixteen
cells (gpu-compare-out-wf3c). It is slow: 0.17, 0.10, 0.28, 0.09, 0.25,
0.28, 0.16, 0.79x at 16 spp and 0.75, 0.45, 0.99, 0.50, 0.94, 1.01, 0.72,
2.62x at 128 (figure order), below every other wavefront on every scene but
frame542 at 128 spp, where it is the best wavefront. The cause is in the
header the fix prints. Every queue array is allocated at the band's
capacity -- 1,950 arrays, 15,650 bytes an entry summed across them (the
material queues are one per material under each texture evaluator, each
at the full capacity, as pbrt's are) -- and four samples a pixel makes
4,147,200 entries on book (1920x1080, pass_pixels 1,036,800): 60.4 GB of
managed memory, against the matched renderer's 1,644 arrays, 14,394 bytes
an entry, 13.9 GB, on a card of 32.6 GB. The pages migrate as the kernels
touch them: the wall time exceeds the renderers' own kernel statistics by
0.6-2.4 s a render (killeroo-gold 0.87 s, book 2.03 s, bistro 2.35 s,
frame542 1.29 s at 16 spp), the same at 16 and 128 spp -- a cost paid once
a render, not per sample -- where the matched renderer's wall is within
0.02 s of its kernels on book; and a single trace launch takes 57-126 ms
(the raygen's maximum in the statistics) where the matched renderer's
longest is 0.42 ms. The schedule's comment said the card has the memory
pbrt's cap guards against; it does not, and the comment now says what was
measured. A quarter of the rounds is bought with four times the queue
memory, so the only scene the pass wins is the one whose cost is all
rounds: frame542 at 128 spp, 256 bounces, 2.62x against the matched
wavefront's 1.62x and the fused wavefront's 1.68x (the megakernel with
reordering is still 20.4x there). No profiler was run; this is the
renderers' own statistics and the header's arithmetic.

**The figure.** wf-pass joins the GPU sweep (plots.sh, GPU_TABLES gains
gpu-compare-out-wf3c/table.tsv; the notes that left it out are gone),

## 11-01 afternoon, the schedule exploration: which compositions of the directives are sometimes best

The user's ask (11-01, after the capacity fix): "do a little bit better
schedule (NOT LAYOUT) exploration. Using the existing scheduling commands
that we have, and compositions of them, with no changes to the tree, what
sometimes-optimal schedules can you find across these sweep scenes?
Ideally each sweep has a few mk and wf variants each." Then the rule for
the GPU figure: "Obviously any schedule that is the winner on at least one
configuration ... If there are less than 8, we should select the others to
approximately balance out the number of wf versus mk schedules. And of
course, the sweep needs to include the matching schedule to PBRT"; seven
rather than eight once wf-sort, which never wins, went ("it makes the
legend look weird"); and for the CPU, "we NEED an exactly matching
schedule to the megakernel approach ... the first Bonsai bar of the
chart", with pbrt's doubling waves left out ("don't worry about the
doubling-waves part. Just match the schedule otherwise with the tiling").

Every schedule below is a file under schedules/ made of directives the
language already had -- `defer` removed to fuse a stage, `reorder` and
`collapse` for a launch's order, `sort` for a reordering hint, `split` and
`bind` for tiles -- with nothing added to the language and the trees
untouched. Each file's header says what it changes and why.

**The GPU variants, and what each one is.** The matched wavefront
(gpu-optix.bonsai) gives every stage pbrt's queue and kernel. Fusing a
stage is removing the `defer` that put it on a queue, so that the call
runs where the program wrote it:

    before (gpu-optix):            after (gpu-optix-fused-route):
      trace program: route hit ->    trace program: route hit ->
        push onto hits / escaped /     material, light sample, shadow push,
        emissive queue                  next ray push; a miss or an emissive
      hits kernel per material:        hit handled right there
        material, light sample,
        shadow push, next ray push
      escaped kernel, emissive kernel

- gpu-optix-fused-route: the material stage in the trace program (10-24's
  gpu-optix-fused) and the two one-line routings beside it, a miss's
  infinite-light contribution and an emissive hit's. Drawn as wf-fuse-mat.
- gpu-optix-fused-shadow: gpu-optix-fused with the shadow ray traced in
  the trace program too, a second optixTrace in the same raygen.
- gpu-optix-bounce: the ray queue alone, every other stage fused -- the
  samples, the media, the routing, the material, the shadow ray, the
  subsurface chain -- one launch per bounce, specialized by the scene's
  media and subsurface flags as the megakernels are. Laine, Karras and
  Aila's one-logic-kernel wavefront (HPG 2013) without their path
  regeneration. Drawn as wf-bounce.
- gpu-optix-mega-flat-samples: the flat megakernel (one launch over every
  (pixel, sample) pair of the frame) with a pixel's samples adjacent in
  the launch instead of a row's pixels -- the "samples order", a warp of
  32 being one pixel's samples at 128 spp. Drawn as mk-flat (the pixel
  order of 10-27, gpu-optix-mega-flat, is mk-flat-px from now on).
- gpu-optix-mega-ser-ray-flat: the SER flat megakernel (reordering by
  material before the material switch) with a second reordering before
  every trace, by where the next ray starts and heads (the top sixteen
  bits of the coarse two-point Morton key), on every call that continues
  the path -- 10-24's mega-ser-ray idea on the flat launch. Drawn as
  mk-flat-ser-ray-px.
- gpu-optix-mega-ser-flat-samples and gpu-optix-mega-ser-ray-flat-samples:
  the two SER shapes in the samples order. Drawn as mk-flat-ser and
  mk-flat-ser-ray.

The samples order is `collapse(p, s, ps)` with the pixel loop outside, and
the collapse is refused on the loops as written: the pixel loop zeroes the
pixel's film slots before its sample loop, and a collapsed loop would zero
them once per sample (SSA/CollapseLoops.cpp, correctly). `reorder(p, s)`
moves the sample loop outside and leaves that prologue in a pixel loop of
its own -- gpu-optix-mega-flat's shape -- and `reorder(s, p)` puts the
pixel loop outside again, now a perfect nest, so `collapse(p, s, ps)` is
allowed: two interchanges for a fission the language has no directive
for. The generated code confirms the order (the collapsed index splits as
pixel = index / spp, sample = index % spp; scratch/explore-1101/compile/
ssa/).

**The two GPU runs** (scratch/explore-1101/gpu_explore.sh: each schedule
compiled, checked on killeroo-simple at 1, 4 and 16 spp against pbrt,
then the eight scenes at 16 and 128 spp, the least of three, every image
checked): gpu-compare-out-explore3 (10:54-12:07) the first five above,
gpu-compare-out-explore4 (12:13-13:04) the two samples-order SER shapes
beside gpu-optix, gpu-optix-mega-flat and gpu-optix-mega-ser-flat
measured again in the same run. 160 cells, 158 matching pbrt's image; the
two that do not are gpu-optix-fused-shadow on plume, where the first
kernel fails with `CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_FAILED (unspecified launch failure)`
at both counts -- the media path with the shadow trace inside the raygen;
open, below. The three re-measured incumbents reproduced their 10-30
cells within 2% by wall and 1% by kernel time (scratch/explore-1101/
compare_tables.py prints the two side by side), so the tables of 10-30
and 10-31 stand and the plotter takes the later rows for those three.

**What was found**, by kernel time where the wall's spread would hide it:

- The samples order is ahead of the pixel order on every megakernel at
  every cell but one: by 4-80% on the flat launch (book the 4%, frame542
  at 16 spp the 80%), 2-37% on the SER one, 2-26% on the ray-reordered
  one; the exception is frame542 at 128 spp, where the pixel order is
  ahead by 4-8% (not measured why). A pixel's samples leave the camera
  through one footprint and hit one surface, so the warp's first trace
  and first material are as coherent as camera rays get; the reading from
  the kernel times, not a profile.
- The reordering by ray before every trace, on top of the one by
  material, is worth 1.2-1.4x on book, sanmiguel and bistro, 1.4x on
  ganesha, 1.6x on dragon_10 and 1.9x on plume -- the heavier the trace,
  the more a warp of rays walking one part of the tree is worth -- and
  costs 7-8% on killeroo-gold, where the conductor's closed-form BSDF
  leaves the warps little divergence for a second sort to regroup (a
  reading). It is the best megakernel on seven of eight scenes, and the
  schedule with the highest geomean of any in the sweep (mk-flat-ser-ray
  2.28x against the matched wavefront's 1.94x), with its losses on
  ganesha, dragon_10, plume and bistro intact.
- wf-fuse-mat is 1.00-1.04x of wf-fused by kernel time on every scene
  (1.14x on frame542): the two routing stages cost a launch and a queue
  each and did nothing a fused program minds. It takes bistro at both
  counts (2.44x, 1.94x) and draws in wf-fused's place.
- wf-bounce is the best wavefront on frame542 (2.65x, 2.57x against the
  matched 1.66x, 1.59x: a fifth of the launches a round) and level with
  the matched one on killeroo-gold at 16 spp; elsewhere below wf-fuse-mat,
  worst on ganesha and dragon_10 (0.69x, 0.67x of wf at 128 spp), where
  the fused program's size cost most on 10-31 too. It matches wf-pass on
  frame542 at 128 spp without the paging and beats it everywhere else, so
  wf-pass is out of the figure.
- wf-fused-shadow is 0.64-0.88x of wf-fused everywhere but frame542
  (1.27x): the trace program's lanes wait on a second traversal before
  they push the next ray. Not drawn.

**The figure** (plots/pbrt-gpu-sweep.pdf, redrawn 14:25, 112 drawn bars
all matching): the per-cell winners are the matched wavefront (ganesha,
dragon_10, plume), wf-fuse-mat (bistro), mk-flat-ser (killeroo-gold,
4.06x and 3.13x), mk-flat-ser-ray (book 3.28x and 2.59x, sanmiguel 2.62x
and 1.97x, frame542 at 16 spp 20.1x) and mk-flat-ser-ray-px (frame542 at
128 spp, 21.2x); wf-bounce and mk-flat fill to three wavefronts and four
megakernels. plots.sh names the seven (GPU_SIDES) and the two new tables
(GPU_TABLES); figure_style.SCHEDULE_COLOURS lays the ramp over them, the
wavefronts the three greens and the megakernels the four blues, skipping
one shade between the families. The labels are the user's short ones: a
flat megakernel is in the samples order unless it says -px, and
wf-fuse-mat is the material stage fused (with the routing). The axis is
cut at 5x (GPU_YMAX; the user: "remove that pesky 4.1x speedup label"),
so only frame542's megakernel bars are cut. The .txt's WHY and READINGS
carry the above per scene.

**The CPU: the match that was missing.** Reading pbrt's source for the
tiling (cpu/integrators.cpp, ImageTileIntegrator::Render; util/
parallel.cpp, ParallelFor2D) showed that the schedule the CPU figure had
called the megakernel match, scalar.bonsai, is not pbrt's shape: pbrt
hands its threads square tiles of `clamp(sqrt(pixels / (8 * threads)), 1,
32)` pixels a side -- 32 on this machine for every sweep scene -- walks a
tile's pixels row by row, and renders in waves of samples over the whole
frame (1, 1, 2, 4, ... 64 a wave; pbr-book 4ed, 1.3.4: previews during
rendering, and "a cost for threads to acquire work for a new image tile"
that the growing waves amortize), while scalar.bonsai takes a pixel's
samples in turn in the runtime's chunks of about 8,100 pixels. The match
is scalar-tiled.bonsai: `split(p, p_ty, p_in_band, tile_band_pixels)`
(bands of 32 rows; `tile_band_pixels = width * 32u` is a program value
beside `pass_pixels`, computed as pbrt computes its tile), `split(p_in_
band, p_iy, p_x, width)`, `split(p_x, p_tx, p_ix, 32)`, `reorder(p_iy,
p_tx)`, `collapse(p_ty, p_tx, p_tile)`, `bind(p_tile, CPUThread)` -- the
rows had to come from a band of rows rather than the frame, since a split
needs a constant stride and a row loop's stride is the frame's width.
The waves are not expressible (a split whose pieces grow) and the user
set them aside; the one residue is the runtime's chunk of the tile loop
where pbrt's threads claim one tile at a time. It goes first in the CPU
legend as the megakernel match, scalar.bonsai staying as the variant it
is (a pixel's samples in one visit, best on three scenes on 10-30).

**The CPU variants** (the sweep running at the time of writing,
scratch/explore-1101/cpu_explore.sh, 13:52-, resumed into
cpu-compare-out-six and -two so that every new cell is timed against the
pbrt wavefront time cached in its cell): scalar-sample-outer (the sample
loop outside, every pixel once per sample), scalar-waves16 (waves of
sixteen samples, pbrt's wave count at 128 spp), scalar-chunk1024 (1,024
pixels a task, pbrt's grain in one dimension), scalar-collapsed (the
pixel and sample loops collapsed, the CPU's flat launch, by the same two
interchanges), and the per-thread vectorized wavefront with 256 and 4,096
pixels a thread instead of 1,024 (wavefront-thread-packet-chunk256,
-chunk4096) and with the material stage in the trace drain's gang
(wavefront-thread-packet-fused). Their numbers and the CPU figure's new
selection follow in the next entry.

**Two compiler findings on the way, and the fixes.** The vectorized
megakernels -- packet.bonsai, perlane.bonsai and a gang of sixteen pixels
(perlane-pixels.bonsai) -- were refused on volpath: the gang reaches
`nanovdb_grid`, a foreign function (docs/foreign-functions.md), which the
vectorizer could not give a lane's arguments. Specializing the integrator
copy by `have_media` (packet-media-scalar.bonsai) did not help, and the
reason is worth writing down:

    func render(..., have_media):                 // the schedule's specialize(have_media)
        parfor p: parfor s: path_step(ray, have_media, ...)   // copies this loop per value
    func path_step(ray, have_media, ...):          // but the flag is a PARAMETER here
        if have_media and ray.medium >= 0: medium_sample(...)   // reaches nanovdb_grid

The copy for `have_media = false` passes a constant, but the vectorizer
built one sixteen-lane `path_step` for both copies, keyed only by which
arguments vary, so the branch and the foreign call were still in it. The
user: "Specialization should constant-propagate the value through";
"shouldn't vectorization of an extern function just scalarize that
chunk?" Both are in SSA/Vectorize.cpp now (built and tested after the
sweep; this entry is extended with the suite's count): (a) a constant a
call hands a parameter that the callee's control depends on is part of
the gang variant's key (VariantKey::constants, parameter_steers_control),
and the clone substitutes the constant for every use of the parameter and
simplifies before it is vectorized, so the arm no caller of the clone can
reach is gone -- LLVM's function specialization, weighed the same way by
the branches a constant decides; the GPU already had this through its
always-inline device functions, the CPU gang path did not; (b) a callee
with no body -- a foreign function -- gets a wrapper variant that makes
the scalar call once per lane that is on, in lane order, each lane's
arguments extracted, each result shuffled into its lane, the lanes the
mask has off skipped (specialize_foreign): ispc's `foreach_active`,
written by the compiler. Tests: ssa/vectorize-constant-argument (the two
clones of a flag-branching callee, no select left), ssa/vectorize-
foreign-call (the per-lane wrapper under a mask, four lanes; the former
error test foreign-vectorized retired), correctness/cpp/
vectorize_constant_argument and foreign_gang (run against drivers that
count the foreign calls: eight when the flag is on and none when off; the
four even lanes in order and no other).

**gpu-optix-fused-shadow's launch failure on plume: found by reading, fix
built, verification pending (11-01 evening).** The user: "afterwards, it
would be good to debug why". The bare error (`cuMemcpyDtoH failed:
CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_FAILED`, the first kernel) says nothing; the cause is in
runtime/bonsai_optix.h's pipeline creation: `link.maxTraceDepth = 1` for
every module -- "a raygen program traces; the hit programs it runs do not"
-- and the continuation stack sized by optix_stack_size.h's formula for
depth one. That was true of every schedule until the fused ones: in
gpu-optix-fused the material stage runs inside the closest-hit program
(the launched body's own continuation, SSA/HitContinuations.h; 10-24
found the same when the reordering hint landed in `__closesthit__trace`),
and gpu-optix-fused-shadow casts the shadow ray from there -- a trace
nested in the raygen's, depth two, which the pipeline was never linked
for. Undefined behaviour that ran on the stack's slack on the seven
surface scenes and overflowed on the plume, whose shadow walk through the
medium (vol_shadow_track: the ratio-tracking steps and a trace_any past
each interface) is the heaviest hit continuation of the eight. The fix at
the root: the compiler states the depth. CodeGen_OptiX counts it -- two
when any hit or miss program it adds to a module traces, itself or through
what it calls (`traces`, the walk `queries_traced` makes), one otherwise
-- and the generated prologue passes it to `bonsai_optix_load(ptx,
payload_values, trace_depth)`, where the runtime links the pipeline with
it and sizes the stack for it (the formula with the depth: the raygen's
continuation plus the hit/miss programs' once per level past the first,
plus the larger of theirs and the intersection plus any-hit programs').
Every schedule that traces from the raygen alone keeps depth one and the
stack it had. **Verified in part (21:00).** Under the fix the trace
raygen's pipeline links at depth two with a 2,176-byte continuation stack
(BONSAI_OPTIX_STATS: cssRG 192 + CH 992 + 992; every other pipeline of the
renderer at depth one as before), the build and the suite pass (1962),
and the plume render still fails: at 1 spp, with the renderer rebuilt,
the first round's trace raygen (`__raygen__rays$False`, 720k threads) is
launched twice and the next device-to-host copy reports an unspecified
launch failure, under OptiX's validation mode (BONSAI_OPTIX_VALIDATION,
every exception on) without a word from OptiX -- so a device fault in the
hit program's continuation rather than a stack or depth exception. What
that continuation does on this scene and no other is walk the medium for
the shadow ray (shadow_radiance under have_media: vol_shadow_track's
ratio-tracking steps over the uniform grid and a trace_any past each
interface) inside the closest-hit program. The depth fix stands on its
own -- a pipeline has to be linked for the traces it makes -- and the
plume failure is open; the next step is the fault's address, which wants
compute-sanitizer or cuda-gdb on the renderer, neither run without the
user's say-so (10-20). The schedule is not in the figure (a loss on every
scene but frame542 where it runs).

## 11-01 evening, the CPU exploration measured: smaller per-thread queues, the fused material stage, and pbrt's tiles

The sweep (scratch/explore-1101/cpu_explore.sh, 13:52-17:47; eight new
schedules on the eight scenes at 16 and 128 spp, the least of three,
resumed into cpu-compare-out-six and -two against the pbrt times cached
in each cell on 10-30 and 10-31): 128 cells, all matching pbrt's image.
The user followed it scene by scene; the readings below are the
figure's .txt's (plot_cpu_wavefront.py, READINGS), and
scratch/explore-1101/scene_report.sh prints any scene's cells against
both of pbrt's integrators.

**What won.** Two of the per-thread wavefront's variants take cells from
the schedules the figure had, and the megakernels keep theirs:

- 256 pixels a thread (wavefront-thread-packet-chunk256, wf-t256-v-ps):
  the best side at 16 spp on killeroo-gold (10.09x over pbrt's wavefront
  against wf-t-v-ps's 7.05x; 1.56x pbrt's megakernel), book (8.11x against
  6.91x), ganesha (6.54x against 5.51x) and plume (8.20x against 7.83x),
  and at both counts on dragon_10 (3.38x, 3.34x) and plume (7.33x at 128).
  A thread's queues hold chunk x spp entries; at 16 spp 256 pixels make 4k
  entries where 1,024 make 16k, and a round's working set -- the records
  written by one drain and read by the next -- fits the core's own L2 at
  the smaller size and not at the larger (a reading from the gains; not
  profiled). At 128 spp both sizes overflow and the chunk is worth 1-4%
  (killeroo-gold, book, ganesha, plume) or nothing (bistro, frame542);
  4,096 pixels a thread (-chunk4096) loses at every cell, 0.80-0.97x of
  the 1,024-pixel chunk.
- the material stage in the trace drain's gang (wavefront-thread-packet-
  fused, wf-t-v-ps-fuse: the hit queue gone, the CPU's gpu-optix-fused):
  the best side at 128 spp on killeroo-gold (9.12x against 6.67x; 1.36x
  pbrt's megakernel), book (6.74x against 6.47x) and ganesha (6.34x against
  5.72x), and level with the chunk at 16 spp on killeroo-gold (9.63x) and
  ganesha (6.22x). It saves the hit record's write and reload where the
  trace is cheap and the materials few; on sanmiguel (four material kinds)
  and bistro (133 materials) it is within 2% of the unfused wavefront, the
  gang's material switch divergent with or without the queue.
- the sorted per-thread wavefront (wf-t-v-ps-sort) keeps sanmiguel (3.81x,
  3.94x) and bistro (3.53x, 3.72x) at both counts, 1-18% over every other
  wavefront: the two scenes where the sort's coherence for the packet
  traversal is worth more than a smaller footprint or a saved queue.
- the megakernels keep frame542 (9.21x and 8.94x, the collapsed loop
  scalar-collapsed by 0.1-0.6% over the untiled scalar -- noise) and tie
  dragon_10 (a pack of five within 1%), where the dielectric paths split
  the gangs and the subsurface bounce costs every schedule the same.

**pbrt's megakernel, matched** (scalar-tiled, mk-b-s-ps-tiled; the
section above says how it is written): 1.03-1.40x pbrt's own megakernel on
seven scenes (killeroo-gold 1.19x/1.16x, book 1.38x/1.40x, sanmiguel
1.03x/1.07x, ganesha 1.13x/1.17x, dragon_10 1.21x/1.24x, bistro 1.06x/
1.13x, frame542 0.97x/0.98x) and 0.87x/0.90x on plume, the medium march
the untiled scalar lost on too (0.92x/0.95x). Against the untiled scalar
(mk-b-s-ps) the tiles are a wash on six scenes (within 4%, ahead at 128
spp on ganesha and bistro) and a loss on plume (0.95x) and frame542 (0.86x
at 16 spp, 0.88x at 128): with depth 256 and short dielectric paths, a
thread's run of 8,100 consecutive pixels keeps more of the machines in
cache than a 32x32 tile does (a reading). The megakernel's other shapes:
waves of sixteen samples (scalar-waves16) and the collapsed loop
(scalar-collapsed) are 1-5% ahead of the untiled scalar on the cheap
scenes and level elsewhere; 1,024 pixels a task (scalar-chunk1024) is
level; the sample loop outside (scalar-sample-outer, every pixel once per
sample) is 4-8% behind everywhere, the frame streamed once per sample,
and the one megakernel at parity with or below pbrt's on ganesha,
sanmiguel and bistro.

**The CPU figure** (plots.sh CPU_SIDES, in legend order; the user, 11-01:
every schedule best on at least one cell, both of pbrt's integrators

## 11-02, the vectorized CPU megakernels debugged: ten compiler faults, eight fixed, two open

The user, 11-01 22:40: "first debug the vectorized CPU megakernels, then
investigate wf-fused-shadow as you need to." The three schedules --
packet-media-scalar, perlane-media-scalar, perlane-pixels (schedules/) --
had stopped on two faults of the gang's short-vector handling. Each fix
uncovered the next; the chain so far, each fault stated as the program
shape that trips it, with what the compiler did before and does now.
Three compiler commits: 1ab9281e (faults 1-4), 1f5c68b1 (5-6), and the
third of this morning (7-8); faults 9 and 10 are open at the time of
writing. Every fix has a test at the IR level and, where it runs, at the
LLVM and execution levels, the execution tests checking the gang against
the same program one lane at a time.

**1. A gang's lane adding a short vector into its own slot.** The path's
radiance is a `vec4f` reduced into a per-sample slot through a `reduce(+)`
parameter; in the gang the slot is per-lane memory behind one pointer,
and the value a struct of four gang vectors (one per component). Before:
widening kept the accumulate whole, `acc.add slot value$v16`, and no
backend can add a struct to a struct. After: one masked accumulate per
component, `acc.add slot.k value.k mask` for k in 0..3. The same for a
scalar accumulated into a vector slot (`tMax *= 1 + 2 gamma(3)` in the
box test): the scalar's one gang vector is what every component takes.

**2. A gang storing a lane's short vector into an array of vectors.** Found
by the new test, not by pbrt: `out[i] = v` with `v` a per-lane `vec3f`
stored the struct of planes whole -- every lane's x over the first
elements of the array, the last elements untouched. After: the mirror of
the strided read the splitter already had, one store per component into
the array viewed as floats, the element's width asked of the backend
(twelve bytes of data in sixteen of storage). Fault 5 is the same for an
accumulate (`normal_out[p] += w * n`, the film's normal buffer at each
lane's pixel).

**3. Not a vectorizer fault: a vector scaled by a scalar through an
accumulate.** `tMax *= 1 + 2 * gamma(3)` (stdlib/intersects.bonsai) is a
`vec3f` place accumulated with an `f32` value. Every backend loaded and
stored the place in the value's shape, one float: every scalar and GPU
traversal compiled until 11-02 applied pbrt's robust slab factor to
`tMax.x` alone. The factor is 1 + 3.6e-7, a few ulps on `y` and `z`; every
image check passed before and after, and no timing moves. The SSA builder
now broadcasts the scalar over the place's components, as `tMax * s`
always was. The user decides whether anything is remeasured for this;
rtq's and wosx's traversals are their own transcriptions of Embree's and
FCPW's box tests, not stdlib's, and both peers confirmed their LLVM
unchanged.

**4. A constant lost at a callee that only passes it on.**
`render[VolPath][False]` calls `li_vol_path` with `have_media = false`;
`li_vol_path` hands it to `vol_path_step`, which branches on it. Before: a
callee was cloned for a constant argument only when its own control
depended on it, so `li_vol_path` got no clone, `vol_path_step` received a
parameter, and the gang kept the whole media walk -- down to the NanoVDB
grid handle, a foreign value no gang can hold one of per lane. After: an
argument handed on as it is to a callee whose control depends on it
counts as steering control; the clone chain folds the media arms away,
and a foreign-typed result per lane is a clear error.

**6. A bypass landing on a join that keeps its arguments.** The lens walk
(`trace_lenses_from_film`, camera.bonsai) has a uniform `if is_stop` whose
join merges the hit point from both arms, so the fold keeps the join and
its arguments; the else arm holds the quadratic's divergent early return
and work worth skipping, so the rest of the arm gets a BOSCC gadget (a
test of the arm's mask, skipping the arm when no lane is on) whose one
exit is that join. Before: the guard's bypass jump into the join carried
nothing of the join's own, and the next pass met a jump of 14 values into
a block of 31. After: the bypass hands the join, per argument, the one
definition every edge threads under the argument's name where there is
one (the counter, the live mask, the exit flags) and an undefined value
where the arms merge different values -- no lane is active on a bypass,
so no lane reads what the skipped arm would have merged.

**7. What the code after a divergent loop reads of the loop.** Uniformizing
a loop the lanes leave at different iterations moves every exit to the
header's test and carries each value read after the loop out through a
tracker, one per argument of the exit edge. Three reads were not
arguments and were missed, each a stale resolution from the time the
body dominated the code after it: a read pointing at the loop's
instruction itself (the alpha test's ray, `q.ray`, computed in the body of
the per-lane traversal's node loop and read in the leaf loop after it,
where the body is out of scope), a block's name table saying the name
meant that instruction (which the threading took at its word), and a
cloned instruction whose owner block was another function's, which the
invariance test took for a value from outside the loop (the lens walk's
constant normal). The threaded copy also has a name of its own now,
`x!out`: under the loop's own name the per-lane tracked copy of a uniform
value -- gamma(3), computed from eps inside the body -- and the scalar
itself became one variable of the backend's, of one type, and a
broadcast met a vector.

**8. A join every edge threads the same name through.** Such a join loses
its argument and the blocks below keep naming the value, on the promise
that a dominator declares the name. When that dominator's argument had
already been blended (a select over the lanes' sources), its rewrite had
skipped this join's subtree because the join still declared the name;
once the join dropped it, nothing reached the subtree. The join now
applies the name's current meaning, found up the dominator chain, as it
drops the argument.

**9. Open: a guard's bypass handing a landing a scalar for a per-lane
argument.** In `render`'s gang body, the guard of the arm that makes the
path's call (`!then_28!any`) bypasses to `!merge_29(have_media!False!skip
: boolx16)` with `(bool)0`. Widening's last pass broadcasts a uniform value
handed to a per-lane block argument and did not here; why is not yet
found (the jump is a dispatch target, which that pass walks).

**10. Open: a landing argument passed by a block that does not have it.**
In the path step's `have_media = false` clone, `!merge_171!inl2` hands
`!merge_173!inl2` the landing argument `!live.upd!skip1`, which no block
on the way declares; the LLVM lowering finds it unbound. The linearizer's
threading of a value through nested landings is where to look.

**Found and left for the user:** the promotion pass (SSA/PromoteAllocas)
leaves a `mut` local declared in a loop header block in memory -- the
header is in its own dominance frontier and the entry edge "never
assigned" it -- so the loopified traversal's `tMax`, `tMin`, `gamma` and
`aabb_span` slots are memory in every scalar traversal; LLVM's own
promotion cleans it up in the backend, and no measurement should move,
but the SSA shows accumulates into memory where values would do. A wide
change (every traversal's code) and the tables' provenance, so not made.
apps/benchmarks.txt (the schedule index the user asked for, 11-01) is
written but `*.txt` is ignored by .gitignore; not force-added.

**The user's asks of 11-02 afternoon, done the same evening.** "How did
the `*=` not apply to the whole vector; is it totally fixed?" The whole
chain: the frontend builds `t *= s` as an accumulate statement of the
place `t` by the value `s`; `t * s` goes through the binary operation's
constructor, which broadcasts a scalar against a vector, but the
accumulate's constructor did not, and the SSA builder passed the scalar
on; every backend then read and wrote the place in the value's shape --
one float, the first component. Now closed at every road (014d544c): the
SSA builder broadcasts (1ab9281e), the statement constructor broadcasts
wherever an accumulate is built, and the LLVM backend refuses a scalar
value for a vector place rather than truncating in silence. Tests at the
IR, LLVM and execution levels (accumulate-vector-scalar). "A variable is
within a scope; a local declared in a loop body must not carry across
iterations": the promotion pass now skips the declaring block as a join
(a local is born at its declaration), so every loopified traversal's

and execution levels; fourteen goldens re-blessed, reviewed. "PBRT must

apps/benchmark.sh (57d9c42a) with apps/pbrt/figures.sh holding what the
